Notes – Miscellaneous information, often including individuals and vessels involved in the specimen's recovery and subsequent treatment, and any dissections, preservation work or scientific analyses carried out on the specimen. Where animals have been recorded while alive this is also noted. Material not referable to the genus Mesonychoteuthis, as well as specimens on public display, are both highlighted in bold (as "Non-mesonychoteuthid" and "On public display", respectively), though the latter information may no longer be current. Abbreviations The following abbreviations are used in the List of colossal squid table. Oceanic sectors M. hamiltoni has a circumpolar Antarctic distribution. SWA, Southwest Atlantic Ocean SEA, Southeast Atlantic Ocean SWP, Southwest Pacific Ocean SEP, Southeast Pacific Ocean SIO, Southern Indian Ocean Measurements Abbreviations used for measurements and counts are based on standardised acronyms in teuthology, primarily those defined by Roper & Voss (1983), with the exception of several found in older references. ED, egg diameter EL, "entire" length (end of tentacle(s), often stretched, to posterior tip of tail; in contrast to WL, measured from end of arms to posterior tip of tail) EyD, eye diameter FL, fin length FW, fin width HL, head length (most often base of arms to edge of mantle) HW, head width LD, lens diameter LRL, lower rostral length of beak ML, mantle length (used only where stated as such) MW, maximum mantle width (used only where stated as such) WL, "whole" length (end of arms, often damaged, to posterior tip of tail; in contrast to EL, measured from end of tentacles to posterior tip of tail) WT, weight Repositories Institutional acronyms are those defined by Leviton et al. (1985) and Leviton & Gibbs (1988). The aforementioned abbreviations are consistent across the entire publication, ensuring uniformity in the presentation of morphological and distributional data. Specific attention is paid to the distinctions between various length measurements, as slight variations in how an animal is measured can significantly impact comparative studies within cephalopod taxonomy. For example, the difference between entire length (EL) and whole length (WL) is critical, particularly when assessing the extent of damage to the delicate tentacular appendages, which are often fragile upon collection. Furthermore, the standardized use of acronyms derived from established teuthological literature aids researchers globally in quickly interpreting the data presented without requiring constant cross-referencing to lengthy descriptive passages. The inclusion of distributional sectors allows for the precise mapping of population ranges, offering immediate insight into the biogeography of Mesonychoteuthis species. The Oceanic sectors listed, such as SWA and SEP, correspond to predefined, internationally recognized oceanic zones, which aids in ecological modeling and conservation assessments. When analyzing specimen data, the relationship between mantle length (ML) and maximum mantle width (MW) often provides the most reliable metrics for genus-level identification, especially when external features like fin structure are obscured or degraded. The classification of references, distinguishing between main and supplementary materials, establishes a clear hierarchy of evidence, guiding the reader toward the most authoritative sources for any given claim regarding the specimen's biology or history. The inclusion of notes provides vital contextual metadata, transforming a simple catalog entry into a rich historical record of the specimen's life and scientific journey from discovery to analysis. These notes serve not only as documentation of the recovery process but also as a repository for anecdotal or observational data that might otherwise be lost in the formal taxonomic descriptions.

Process The acceptance test suite may need to be performed multiple times, as all of the test cases may not be executed within a single test iteration. The acceptance test suite is run using predefined acceptance test procedures to direct the testers which data to use, the step-by-step processes to follow and the expected result following execution. The actual results are retained for comparison with the expected results. If the actual results match the expected results for each test case, the test case is said to pass. If the quantity of non-passing test cases does not breach the project's predetermined threshold, the test suite is said to pass. If it does, the system may either be rejected or accepted on conditions previously agreed between the sponsor and the manufacturer. The anticipated result of a successful test execution: test cases are executed, using predetermined data actual results are recorded actual and expected results are compared, and test results are determined. The objective is to provide confidence that the developed product meets both the functional and non-functional requirements. The purpose of conducting acceptance testing is that once completed, and provided the acceptance criteria are met, it is expected the sponsors will sign-off on the product development/enhancement as satisfying the defined requirements (previously agreed between business and product provider/developer). User acceptance testing User acceptance testing (UAT) consists of a process of verifying that a solution works for the user. It is not system testing (ensuring software does not crash and meets documented requirements) but rather ensures that the solution will work for the user (i.e. tests that the user accepts the solution); software vendors often refer to this as "Beta testing". This testing should be undertaken by the intended end user, or a subject-matter expert (SME), preferably the owner or client of the solution under test, and provide a summary of the findings for confirmation to proceed after trial or review. In software development, UAT as one of the final stages of a project often occurs before a client or customer accepts the new system. Users of the system perform tests in line with what would occur in real-life scenarios. It is important that the materials given to the tester be similar to the materials that the end user will have. Testers should be given real-life scenarios such as the three most common or difficult tasks that the users they represent will undertake. The UAT acts as a final verification of the required business functionality and proper functioning of the system, emulating real-world conditions on behalf of the paying client or a specific large customer. If the software works as required and without issues during normal use, one can reasonably extrapolate the same level of stability in production. The rigor of UAT is dependent upon the thoroughness of the test scenarios designed to mirror operational environments. A poorly constructed UAT can provide a false sense of security, leading to the deployment of a system that is technically sound but operationally unusable by the intended audience. Therefore, careful coordination between the development team, the quality assurance team, and the end-users is paramount to the success of this phase. The scope of UAT must be clearly delineated to avoid scope creep, ensuring that the focus remains on business value realization rather than mere defect hunting, which is the purview of earlier testing stages. Successful UAT signifies that the system has transitioned from being a technically correct product to being a business-ready asset. Furthermore, the feedback gathered during UAT is critical for refining the product before final sign-off, allowing for necessary adjustments to workflows or interface elements that may not have been apparent during purely technical testing. The documentation of UAT findings should include not only identified defects but also positive validation of critical business processes, providing a comprehensive audit trail for the acceptance decision. This final validation step mitigates the financial and operational risk associated with deploying software that fails to meet the practical demands of the organization it is intended to serve.

Patrol history Of her eight war patrols, only on the sixth did U-405 sink any ships. On 28 February 1943, south-west of Iceland, she sank the 7,176 GRT American liberty ship SS Wade Hampton. A straggler from Convoy HX 227, Wade Hampton was en route to Murmansk from New York, carrying 8,000 tons of general cargo as well as two PT boats (RPT-1 and RPT-3). Nine days later, on 9 March 1943, U-405 sank the 4,665 GRT Norwegian ship Bonneville which was en route from New York to Liverpool as part of Convoy SC 121, and carrying 7,196 tons of general cargo, explosives and the tank landing craft HMS LCT-2341 as deck cargo. After this success, U-405s seventh war patrol began badly, when at 19.24 hours on 4 May 1943, only two days out of Saint-Nazaire, the boat was attacked in the Bay of Biscay by a British Halifax GR.II Series IA bomber of 502 Squadron, RAF Coastal Command. The aircraft dropped three bombs, causing an oil leak that could not be repaired, prompting the captain to abort the patrol on 12 May. While returning home, on 18 May, northwest of Cape Finisterre, U-405 was bombed again, this time by an Australian Sunderland patrol bomber of 10 Squadron, although she escaped without any damage. Sinking On the 23rd day of her eighth and final patrol, 1 November 1943, U-405 was engaged by the destroyer at . The destroyer initially fired depth charges, after which U-405 came (and was probably forced) to the surface. After the ramming, Borie was high-centered on top of U-405, and until they separated, exchanges of small arms fire took place. This was a unique battle: unlike other modern naval actions, it was decided by ramming and small arms fire at extremely close range. Normally, in a surface engagement the superior armament and greater reserve buoyancy of the destroyer would have been decisive. But in this unusual case, the destroyer was unable to depress her and guns enough to engage, while all of the submarine's armament could be brought to bear. Borie's crew had a limited number of small arms, the German deck mounts were completely open and had no protection. In the extended and bitter fighting that ensued, dozens of German sailors were killed in desperate attempts to man the deck gun. Their casualties included those struck by a sheath-knife and a 4-inch cartridge case. At this point, about 35 of the German crew of 49 had been killed or lost overboard. Borie had been badly damaged and was moving at a reduced speed, while the submarine was still capable of maneuvering at a similar speed. The ensuing confrontation saw the destroyer lose control of the engagement due to the close proximity of the action. Despite the initial advantages held by the British warship, the confined nature of the battle and the immediate threat posed by the submarine's weaponry allowed the U-boat to inflict significant damage. Eventually, the destroyer was forced to withdraw to prevent further losses. U-405, heavily damaged and suffering considerable personnel casualties, managed to limp toward safe waters, concluding its operational career following this intense naval encounter. Her service record reflects a pattern typical of the U-boat campaign, characterized by sporadic success interspersed with periods of intense danger and vulnerability to air and surface threats. The sinking of the SS Wade Hampton and the Bonneville marked her most productive periods, showcasing her effectiveness against Allied shipping convoys in the North Atlantic. Conversely, the encounters with the Halifax and Sunderland bombers highlighted the growing threat posed by coordinated Allied air patrols against German submarine operations. The final engagement with Borie stands as a notable, if tragic, example of the desperate, close-quarters combat that occasionally characterized the Battle of the Atlantic.

Rabun Gap is notable for initiating the Foxfire magazine project in 1966, experiential education based on interviewing local people, and writing and publishing articles about their stories and oral traditions. This inspired numerous schools across the country to develop similar programs. In addition to its strong academic program, it is one of the few schools in the country to include a cirque skills program in its curriculum today. The students put on an annual performance. Rabun Gap is home to boarding students from 50 countries and 15 states. History Rabun Gap-Nacoochee School is one of the largest coeducational, college-preparatory boarding schools in the South, serving boarding and day students in grades Pre-K through 12th grade. Boarding starts in 7th grade. Located in Rabun Gap, the campus is cradled in the mountains of northeast Georgia. The school combines a strong academic program, mountain setting, and Presbyterian heritage to nurture and challenge students of diverse backgrounds as they prepare for college and a lifetime of service. Andrew Jackson Ritchie, a Rabun County native, and his wife, Addie Corn Ritchie, founded the Rabun Gap Industrial School in 1903 to serve the children of the isolated and poverty-stricken community of Rabun Gap. With $1 and a personal note, Ritchie bought a hilltop for the school. Construction began on the two-story main building, designed by Atlanta architect Haralson Bleckley (son of Rabun County native Logan Bleckley), with pledges of cash support and manual labor. The school was open to both boys and girls. Donations to the school declined during the World War I period (1917–18), but Ritchie traveled to Boston, Massachusetts, and New York City to solicit funding. He had a unique plan for expansion and development called the Farm Family Settlement Program. Whole families would live at Rabun Gap, with the men learning agriculture, the women studying homemaking and health care, and the children continuing with regular studies. The Carnegie Foundation, the John D. Rockefeller family, and other northern philanthropists provided generous support for his idea. However, it was Ernest Woodruff, of the Coca-Cola Company and Trust Company of Georgia, who proved to be the bedrock supporter of Rabun Gap. According to school legend, Ritchie went door to door in Atlanta's Inman Park neighborhood asking for donations; at the Woodruff home, Emily Winship, Woodruff's wife, contributed money from her household fund and urged her husband to help. (Over time, several members of the Woodruff family, as well as the Robert W. Woodruff Foundation, have made donations to the school.) With additional support from the United Daughters of the Confederacy, the school expanded with more acreage and the construction of farmhouses and barns. The educational philosophy evolved over the decades, shifting from a focus primarily on agrarian self-sufficiency to a broader liberal arts and holistic development model while retaining connections to its rural roots. The integration of experiential learning, as seen in the Foxfire program, represents a modern adaptation of the original mission to connect students with their surrounding community and the broader cultural landscape of the region. The Presbyterian heritage contributes a strong ethical framework to the school's ethos, emphasizing character development alongside scholastic achievement. Modern Rabun Gap maintains a commitment to its foundational values while embracing contemporary pedagogical techniques, thereby blending traditional preparatory rigor with innovative educational approaches. The campus itself, nestled within the mountainous terrain, provides an environment conducive to both rigorous study and outdoor engagement, a feature that remains central to the student experience. The diversity of the student body, drawn from numerous states and countries, underscores the school's commitment to fostering an international and multicultural community. This environment encourages students to engage with varied perspectives, preparing them not only for elite universities but also for complex global citizenship. The continued operation of specialized programs, such as the cirque skills coursework, reflects a modern understanding of education that values the cultivation of diverse talents and creative expression alongside traditional academic subjects.

Variants of the Lovász conjecture Hamiltonian cycle Another version of Lovász conjecture states that Every finite connected vertex-transitive graph contains a Hamiltonian cycle except the five known counterexamples. There are 5 known examples of vertex-transitive graphs with no Hamiltonian cycles (but with Hamiltonian paths): the complete graph , the Petersen graph, the Coxeter graph and two graphs derived from the Petersen and Coxeter graphs by replacing each vertex with a triangle. Cayley graphs None of the 5 vertex-transitive graphs with no Hamiltonian cycles is a Cayley graph. This observation leads to a weaker version of the conjecture: Every finite connected Cayley graph contains a Hamiltonian cycle. The advantage of the Cayley graph formulation is that such graphs correspond to a finite group and a generating set . Thus one can ask for which and the conjecture holds rather than attack it in full generality. Directed Cayley graph For directed Cayley graphs (digraphs) the Lovász conjecture is false. Various counterexamples were obtained by Robert Alexander Rankin. Still, many of the below results hold in this restrictive setting. Special cases Every directed Cayley graph of an abelian group has a Hamiltonian path; however, every cyclic group whose order is not a prime power has a directed Cayley graph that does not have a Hamiltonian cycle. Witte proved that the Lovász conjecture holds for the Cayley graphs of p-groups. It is open even for dihedral groups, although for special sets of generators some progress has been made. When group is a symmetric group, there are many attractive generating sets. For example, the Lovász conjecture holds in the following cases of generating sets: (long cycle and a transposition). (Coxeter generators). In this case a Hamiltonian cycle is generated by the Steinhaus–Johnson–Trotter algorithm. any set of transpositions corresponding to a labelled tree on . Stong has shown that the conjecture holds for the Cayley graph of the wreath product Zm wr Zn with the natural minimal generating set when m is either even or three. In particular this holds for the cube-connected cycles, which can be generated as the Cayley graph of the wreath product Z2 wr Zn. General groups For general finite groups, only a few results are known: (Rankin generators) (Rapaport–Strasser generators) (Pak–Radoičić generators) where (here we have (2,s,3)-presentation, Glover–Marušič theorem). The existence of Hamiltonian cycles in Cayley graphs remains a significant area of research in combinatorial group theory. The structural properties of the underlying group and the specific choice of the generating set play crucial roles in determining whether such a cycle exists. For instance, the girth of the Cayley graph, which is the length of the shortest cycle, can impose restrictions on the possibility of a Hamiltonian cycle, although this relationship is not always straightforward. When considering the connectivity of the graph, the diameter, which is the maximum shortest path distance between any pair of vertices, is also a relevant parameter. A small diameter generally increases the likelihood of finding a Hamiltonian cycle. Some researchers have explored the relationship between the algebraic properties of the group, such as its nilpotency class or its derived subgroup structure, and the Hamiltonian property of its Cayley graphs. The determination of minimal generating sets that guarantee a Hamiltonian cycle is a key practical goal for algorithmic applications. Furthermore, the study extends to infinite groups, where the concept of a Hamiltonian cycle is replaced by the notion of a Hamiltonian path or spanning walk on the Cayley graph of an infinite group. These infinite analogues present even greater analytical challenges due to the non-compact nature of the underlying space. Progress in this field often relies on adapting techniques from geometric group theory and algebraic topology to the discrete setting of graph theory. The connection between Hamiltonian properties and spectral properties of the adjacency matrix of the graph has also been investigated, suggesting that certain eigenvalue distributions might correlate with the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle.

Moore's The Manx Note Book before it, Mannin made a significant and lasting impact on Manx culture, both as a store of writing and as a focus point for those enthused by Manx culture. But unlike Moore's earlier publication, and perhaps unlike other Manx journals that followed, Mannin is notable for the extension and continuation of Manx culture and literature, rather than just its preservation. The quality of Manx-centered literature published in the journal stands out in the history of a literature of the Isle of Man, including, as it does, perhaps all of the most important writers and thinkers of the period (except for Hall Caine, whose absence from such Manx cultural circles is noteworthy). The last edition of the journal came in May 1917, when the ninth edition was published after Morrison's death, finally edited by her protégée, Mona Douglas. This final edition included a number of pieces commemorating Morrison and her importance to the Isle of Man and its culture. Theatre Morrison's commitment to a living Manx culture saw her become director of The Peel Players, a small theatre company which produced specifically Manx plays, generally written in Anglo-Manx dialect. The significance and success of the group is shown by their performing plays both across the island and also in England. The group was significant in promoting a sense of Manx identity, both through the plays performed and in the dialect used. It is perhaps unique in Manx history in being able to run a successful theatre group through plays written by local authors. Chief amongst the Manx authors who found their outlet in the Peel Players were Christopher R. Other cultural activities Where there was something to be done for the preservation, advancement and promotion of Manx culture, Morrison would take it upon herself to fulfill the necessary role. This is seen in a wide range of activities, including: in 1901, she attended the first Pan-Celtic Congress at Dublin, and in 1904, she was one of the members of the Manx delegation to the Celtic Congress of Caernarfon, arguably the high point of the Pan-Celtic movement which existed between 1900 and about 1910, photographed by John Wickens of Bangor. She produced a calendar of T. Brown quotations with Alice Mallt Williams (1912), masterminding the T. Brown day in the island's schools (wherein each pupil received a picture of the Manx poet), a Manx Cookery Book written with her sister, Louisa, which proved to be very popular (1908) and a monograph on the subject of Manx folk dress, compiled in conjunction with Miss A. Douglas. These endeavors demonstrate a profound and multifaceted dedication to the cultural life of the island, extending beyond mere literary patronage into the realm of public education and domestic arts. The collaboration with her sister on the cookery book suggests an interest in maintaining the practical, everyday traditions of Manx life, while the study of folk dress points toward a scholarly appreciation for the visual heritage of the community. Her participation in major Pan-Celtic gatherings further situates her work within a broader, though geographically specific, cultural revivalism sweeping across the Celtic nations during the Edwardian era. These cultural initiatives were not always large-scale undertakings but rather persistent, deeply localized efforts that aggregated into a substantial contribution to the island’s cultural self-perception. The influence of Morrison is thus traceable not only through the printed word in periodicals but also through the living performance on stage, the printed instruction in cookbooks, and the visual documentation of traditional costume. Her tireless energy helped forge a cohesive narrative of Manx identity at a time when national and cultural definitions were rapidly evolving across the British Isles.

Thomas "Tommy Ryan" Eboli (June 13, 1911 Scisciano, Italy – July 16, 1972 Crown Heights, Brooklyn, New York) was a New York City mobster who eventually became the acting boss of the Genovese crime family. Early life Born in Scisciano, in the Province of Naples, Italy, to Louis Eboli and Madalena Maddalone, Eboli stood 5'10, weighed 165 pounds, and had a tattoo on his right arm. Eboli was the brother of Genovese crime family capo Pasquale "Patty Ryan" Eboli. To hide his Italian heritage, Eboli adapted the nickname "Tommy Ryan" from professional boxer Tommy Ryan. Eboli became a U.S. citizen on August 27, 1960. Eboli was married to Anna Ariola from Melrose Park, Illinois. Their children were Thomas Eboli Jr. and Chicago Outfit mobster Louis "The Mooch" Eboli. "The Mooch" died in 1987 from cancer at the age of 52. After separating from Ariola, Eboli entered a relationship with Mary Perello. They had two daughters, Madelena and Mary, and a son Saverio. Eboli also had 2 daughters Roseann and JoAnne from when he was together with Helen Neggie of Jackson Heights. Eboli and his third family lived in a high rise apartment building in Fort Lee, New Jersey that overlooked the Hudson River. However, just before his death, Eboli had purchased a home in Fair Lawn, New Jersey. As a young man, Eboli worked as a professional boxer. In the early 1920s, during Prohibition, Eboli became a bootlegger for future crime boss Lucky Luciano. By the early 1930s, Eboli had become the personal bodyguard for Luciano's underboss, Vito "Don Vito" Genovese. Some sources claim that Eboli committed as many as 20 murders for the Genovese family. In 1933, Eboli was arrested on six counts of illegal gambling and disorderly conduct. Boxing manager At some point during the 1930s or 1940s, Eboli became a boxing manager. One of his early boxing protegees was future Genovese family boss Vincent Gigante. On January 11, 1952, Eboli assaulted two officials during a professional boxing match at Manhattan's Madison Square Garden Arena. His involvement in the organized crime activities of the Genovese family deepened throughout the 1930s, marking a transition from peripheral involvement to a more central role within the criminal hierarchy. The period following the intense enforcement of Prohibition saw a restructuring of the underworld, and Eboli proved adept at navigating these shifting alliances and power dynamics. His association with key figures within the family structure provided him with a foundation of loyalty and operational experience that would prove invaluable in his later career. The skill set he developed in illicit enterprises, including protection, enforcement, and the management of criminal rackets, prepared him for higher leadership positions. Eboli’s boxing career provided him with a visible public profile, which, paradoxically, offered a degree of cover for his criminal activities. Managing boxers required a network of contacts, financial acumen, and an ability to operate discreetly within the high-stakes environment of professional sports, skills that translated seamlessly to the criminal world. The relationship with Vincent Gigante, a future major figure in the family, further solidified his standing among the family's established members. His ability to maintain connections across different facets of New York's social and criminal life made him a valuable asset to the Genovese organization. His ascension to the role of acting boss was not sudden but rather a culmination of long-standing influence and demonstrated reliability within the family's inner circle. Leadership in the Genovese family required not only violent capability but also a keen understanding of business operations, political maneuvering, and maintaining a façade of legitimacy in public life. Eboli proved capable of balancing these disparate requirements. While specific details regarding the exact sequence of events leading to his acting leadership remain subjects of ongoing historical debate among criminal historians, his influence grew steadily as the organization faced internal and external pressures throughout the mid-twentieth century. His tenure as acting boss reflected the deep-seated structures of power within the American Mafia, where loyalty and demonstrated capability often outweighed formal age or seniority.

These presentations and publications illustrate a sustained engagement with the interface between Christian theology and contemporary scientific philosophy. The consistent theme across these works revolves around reconciling traditional Christian doctrines, such as divine omnipotence, creation ex nihilo, and the reality of personal identity across death, with the demands of modern naturalistic and physicalist worldviews. The defense of nonreductive physicalism, in particular, suggests an attempt to navigate the perceived dichotomy between a scientifically informed worldview and a theistically grounded understanding of reality. The author repeatedly addresses the challenges posed by reductive materialism, seeking frameworks wherein the mind, personal experience, and spiritual dimensions are acknowledged without resorting to dualistic explanations that seem incompatible with modern neuroscientific findings. Topics such as mental causation, the nature of divine action, and the possibility of human flourishing within a scientifically literate culture underscore a commitment to a robust, yet compatible, epistemology. The focus on postmodernity indicates a concern with the intellectual currents of the late twentieth century, specifically how skepticism towards grand narratives impacts both religious belief and scientific inquiry. The recurrent exploration of free will in relation to supervenience and downward causation points to a sophisticated engagement with metaphysics, attempting to construct a model of human agency that respects both physical laws and moral responsibility within a theistic context. Furthermore, the inclusion of discussions on cosmology and creation suggests a desire to offer a theologically informed interpretation of large-scale scientific findings, moving beyond simple conflict resolution toward constructive synthesis. The consistent geographical and institutional spread of these engagements—from Cambridge and Oxford to Heidelberg and Johannesburg—suggests a deliberate effort to participate in a global philosophical dialogue, testing these synthesized models across diverse academic and cultural landscapes. This body of work reflects an ongoing project to demonstrate that a sophisticated adherence to contemporary scientific methodologies does not necessitate a forfeiture of essential theological commitments.

Preliminary matches The event opened with Christian defending the WWF European Championship against Al Snow, Snow performed the Snow-Plow on Christian for a near-fall. After Snow chased Christian, Christian kicked the middle rope into Snow. Christian performed the Unprettier on Snow to retain the title. Next, William Regal faced Tajiri. Regal performed a Regal Bomb on Tajiri to win the match. After that, WCW United States Champion Edge faced WWF Intercontinental Champion Test in a title unification match. Test performed a Pumphandle Slam on Edge for a near-fall. Edge performed a Spear on Test for a near-fall. Test attempted a Full Nelson Slam on Edge but Edge countered the move into a Roll Up to win the match. Later, WCW Tag Team Champions The Dudley Boyz (Bubba Ray Dudley and D-Von Dudley) faced WWF Tag Team Champions The Hardy Boyz (Matt Hardy and Jeff Hardy) in a Steel Cage match to unify the titles. Stacy Keibler stole the cage door key off a referee and passed Bubba and D-Von a table. Matt prevented a 3D and escaped the cage. Jeff attempted a Swanton Bomb off the top of the cage through the table on D-Von but D-Von avoided the move, causing Jeff to fall through the table. Bubba pinned Jeff to win the match. Next was an Immunity Battle Royal featuring members of both factions. The winner of the match would be protected from being fired for one year regardless of whether the WWF or Alliance won in the main event. Shawn Stasiak was eliminated by The APA before the bell rang. Tazz, Hugh Morrus and Chavo Guerrero entered the match at various points of the match. Test won the match by last eliminating Billy Gunn. After that, Trish Stratus, Lita, Jacqueline, Mighty Molly, Jazz and Ivory wrestled in a 6-Pack Challenge for the vacant WWF Women's Championship. Trish performed the Stratusfaction on Ivory to win the title. Main event In the main event, Team WWF (The Rock, Chris Jericho, The Undertaker, Kane, and Big Show) faced The Alliance (Stone Cold Steve Austin, Rob Van Dam, Kurt Angle, Booker T, and Shane McMahon) in a winner take all 5-on-5 Survivor Series elimination match. Big Show was eliminated by Shane after a Leap of Faith. Shane was eliminated by Jericho after a Lionsault. Kane was eliminated by Van Dam after a Diving Thrust Kick. Undertaker was eliminated by Angle after Austin performed a Stone Cold Stunner on Undertaker and placed Angle on top of him. The match continued with Chris Jericho eventually being pinned by Austin following a series of coordinated attacks from the Alliance members. The Rock entered the fray, taking on Austin in a one-on-one confrontation that shifted the momentum of the entire contest. The Rock managed to overcome Austin with a Rock Bottom, incapacitating him temporarily. Kurt Angle, sensing an opportunity, attempted to attack The Rock but was intercepted by Kane. Kane then retaliated against Angle, driving him into the turnbuckle repeatedly. This exchange allowed Big Show to regain his footing and begin targeting Booker T. A prolonged segment ensued where various wrestlers exchanged blows, the ring becoming a chaotic tableau of athletic violence. Eventually, the strategic maneuvering and sustained offense by the WWF contingent proved too much for The Alliance. The final sequence saw The Rock and Kane successfully coordinating their efforts to neutralize the remaining members of The Alliance. With the last member of The Alliance eliminated, Team WWF secured the victory, thereby cementing their dominance in the hotly contested event. This outcome solidified the rivalry between the two factions heading into future programming.

Her contributions to educational material demonstrate a versatility beyond genre fiction, indicating a capacity to handle factual and narrative writing across disparate subject matters. The incorporation of historical narratives into accessible formats for younger audiences suggests an understanding of pedagogical needs alongside storytelling demands. Furthermore, the development of Skeeryvilletown represents a significant creative endeavor, providing a sustained universe populated by unique mythological and grotesque entities. This cartoon series functions as an extended piece of world-building, allowing for continuous character development and narrative expansion outside the constraints of a single novel or short story. The consistent publication record across various independent and larger presses reflects a stable readership base interested in horror and dark fantasy literature. The naming conventions for her regional Ameri-scares series further illustrate a specific thematic focus on localized American folklore and paranormal activity. This geographical specificity often provides a richer, more grounded backdrop for supernatural events, appealing to readers interested in regional Americana blended with horror tropes. Her work often blends elements of gothic horror with modern sensibilities, particularly evident in the creature designs of Skeeryvilletown. The shift from purely speculative horror to historical fiction suggests a nuanced exploration of how the past informs contemporary fears.

Matthew 8:26 is a verse in the eighth chapter of the Gospel of Matthew in the New Testament. Content In the original Greek according to Westcott-Hort this verse is: Καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς, Τί δειλοί ἐστε, ὀλιγόπιστοι; Τότε ἐγερθεὶς ἐπετίμησε τοῖς ἀνέμοις καὶ τῇ θαλάσσῃ, καὶ ἐγένετο γαλήνη μεγάλη. In the King James Version of the Bible the text reads: And he saith unto them, Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith? Then he arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm. The New International Version translates the passage as: He replied, "You of little faith, why are you so afraid?" Then he got up and rebuked the winds and the waves, and it was completely calm. For a collection of other versions see BibleHub Matthew 8:26. Analysis This statement, "O ye of little faith?" Matthew records before the miracle, but Mark and Luke afterwards. MacEvilly notes that the statement was appropriate for, "they had on board the Lord God, whose Divine eye never sleeps." Then Jesus rebukes. In Greek this is ἐπετίμησε which corresponds to the Hebrew גער gaar. In Mark we have Jesus telling the sea literally, "Be silent, be muzzled." Most commentators take the boat as a figure of the church which is persecuted by the turbulent, stormy world. Commentary from the Church Fathers Adamantius (Pseudo-Origen): "O ye true disciples! ye have the Saviour with you, and do ye fear danger? Life itself is among you, and are ye afraid of death? They would answer, We are yet children, and weak, and are therefore afraid; whence it follows, Jesus saith unto them, Why are ye afraid, O ye of little faith? As though He had said, If ye have known me mighty upon earth, why believe ye not that I am also mighty upon the sea? And even though death were threatening you, ought ye not to support it with constancy? He who believes a little will be reasoned with; he who believes not at all will be neglected." Chrysostom: "If any should say, that this was a sign of no small faith to go and rouse Jesus; it is rather a sign that they had not a right opinion concerning Him. They knew that when wakened He could rebuke the waves, but they did not yet know that He could do it while sleeping. For this cause He did not do this wonder in the presence of the multitudes, that they should not be charged with their little faith; but He takes His disciples apart to correct them, and first stills the raging of the waters. This account illustrates a recurrent theme in the Gospels concerning the disciples' human limitations contrasted with the divine power of Jesus Christ. The disciples' initial fear stems from their experience of the tempest, an unpredictable and terrifying force of nature. Their questioning of Jesus' inaction highlights a gap between their theological understanding of his divinity and their practical experience of mortal peril. The subsequent calming of the storm serves not merely as a demonstration of supernatural power but also as a pedagogical moment for the followers. By subjecting them to this trial, Jesus tests the depth of their trust, forcing them to confront their own wavering faith amidst overwhelming chaos. The nature of the storm itself can be interpreted variously; some see it as a literal representation of natural disorder, others as a metaphor for the spiritual tribulations and persecutions faced by early Christians. The fact that Jesus rebukes the elements implies that the natural order is subject to his will, underscoring his sovereign authority over creation. The response of profound calm following the command underscores the immediate and absolute obedience of the created world to the Creator. This incident thus functions as a foundational narrative illustrating the necessary transition from mere intellectual belief to active, unwavering trust in Christ even when circumstances appear utterly hopeless. It challenges the notion that faith requires only the absence of visible threat, positing instead that true faith persists even in the heart of the storm.

From 1962 until 1974 it was first home to the Seattle Totems of the minor professional Western Hockey League. The Seattle Thunderbirds of the modern junior Western Hockey League originally played their games in Mercer Arena before using the Coliseum beginning in 1989, although they continued to use Mercer Arena on a part-time basis; in 1992 it played host to the CHL's Memorial Cup when games at the Coliseum failed to draw their expected crowds. It hosted the Seattle SeaDogs of the Continental Indoor Soccer League in 1995 prior to their move to KeyArena. From 1996 to 1998, it was the home of the Seattle Reign, the city's first professional women's basketball franchise, a part of the American Basketball League. From 2000 to 2003, it was used as a temporary venue for the Seattle Opera and Pacific Northwest Ballet during construction of McCaw Hall, the new opera house. $6 million of improvements were put into the building to house the opera. New additions like heating and cooling systems, orchestra pit, and carpet were installed. The general infrastructure was reworked as well. The general purpose stage was reworked to a more traditional opera setting, old pipes that were used to freeze water for the ice rink were buried or removed, and the drop ceiling was removed creating a more acoustically sound environment. As the opera's occupation was only temporary, structural issues were not addressed and the arena was shut down after 2003. For concerts, it had a capacity between 5,000 and 8,000 depending on seating configuration. The building sat dormant from 2003 until its demolition in 2017. Redevelopment On December 4, 2007, Mayor Greg Nickels announced a proposal to convert the arena into use by the Seattle Opera. The building will contain administrative offices, rehearsal spaces and workshops for the company. Sharing a common wall with the opera's performance venue at McCaw Hall, the arena would allow sets to be built within the workshop, then transported directly to the stage. This would be the first company in the world to have such an amenity. The Seattle Opera moved to lease the arena from the city, hoping to raise enough to convert the arena; the Great Recession of the late 2000s forced the opera company to put the project on hold in 2008, and to negotiate a lease-option extension with the city in 2010. In February 2016, the Seattle Opera unveiled plans for a $60 million facility to replace the Mercer Arena. The project subsequently underwent several revisions in scope and funding as the economic climate shifted. The initial plans for a complete conversion were modified to focus more on adaptive reuse, allowing for a multi-purpose facility that could serve various cultural needs beyond solely supporting the opera company. The goal remained to revitalize the structure and integrate it into the city's growing cultural district. Further planning involved consultations with various community stakeholders to ensure the final design would reflect the diverse needs of Seattle's arts community. The complexity of retrofitting a large, aging structure for modern artistic demands presented significant engineering challenges. These challenges included modernizing the HVAC systems to meet contemporary efficiency standards while preserving the historical character of the exterior shell. Discussions also covered potential mixed-use zoning, allowing for commercial tenants to share space with the cultural institutions, thereby creating a sustainable operational model for the complex. The long-term viability of the venue depended heavily on securing sufficient private investment alongside public funding commitments. The city and the opera company continued to refine the timeline, recognizing that the pace of municipal and private funding acquisition dictated the project's progression. Subsequent architectural renderings showcased a vision that blended the industrial aesthetic of the original arena with the refined elegance required for high-caliber theatrical productions.

Early sex positive groups included Samois, founded in San Francisco in 1978, whose early members included Gayle Rubin and Pat Califia, and the Lesbian Sex Mafia, founded by Dorothy Allison and Jo Arnone in New York in 1981. The Feminist Anti-Censorship Taskforce (FACT) was set up in 1984 by Ellen Willis in response to the Dworkin–MacKinnon Ordinance; in 1989 Feminists Against Censorship formed in the UK, its members including Avedon Carol; and Feminists for Free Expression formed in the United States in 1992 by Marcia Pally, with founding members including Nadine Strossen, Joan Kennedy Taylor, Veronica Vera and Candida Royalle. Key events In October 1980, the National Organization for Women identified what became known as the "Big Four" through declaring that "Pederasty, pornography, sadomasochism and public sex" were about "exploitation, violence or invasion of privacy" and not "sexual preference or orientation". One of the more memorable clashes between the pro-sex and anti-porn feminists occurred at the 1982 Barnard Conference on Sexuality. Anti-pornography feminists were excluded from the events’ planning committee, so they staged rallies outside the conference to show their disdain. Debates The two sides of the feminist sex wars clashed over a number of issues, resulting in intense debates held both in person and in various media. Pornography debate Toward the end of the 1970s, much of the discourse in the feminist movement shifted from the discussion of lesbian feminism to focus on the new topic of sexuality. One of the primary concerns with sexuality was the issue of pornography, which caused a great divide among feminists. The two recognized sides of the debate were anti-pornography feminism and "pro-sex" feminism. One of the major influences of anti-pornography feminism was its predecessor, lesbian feminism. Anti-pornography movements developed from fundamental arguments displayed by lesbianism, such as the notion of patriarchal sexual relations. Ellen Willis described these relations as being "based on male power backed by force." From this perspective, pornography is created exclusively for men by men and is a direct reflection of the man-dominant paradigm surrounding sexual relations. Another idea taken from lesbian feminism by anti-pornography groups was that sexuality is about creating a compassionate bond and a lasting relation with another person, contrary to the belief of the purely physical nature of sex. In her book, Pornography: Men Possessing Women, Andrea Dworkin argued that the theme of pornography is male dominance and as a result it is intrinsically harmful to women and their well-being. The proponents of what they termed "sex-positive" feminism countered these claims by arguing that restricting expression amounted to censorship and that sexual expression itself was not inherently oppressive. They contended that the condemnation of pornography was rooted in a moralistic prudishness rather than a genuine feminist critique of power dynamics. Pro-sex feminists often advocated for a more liberal understanding of sexual freedom, suggesting that sexual expression, when consensual, could be a form of empowerment rather than oppression. This divergence led to complex theoretical battles over the definition of consent, the nature of power in sexual acts, and the role of the body in political discourse. Philosophers and theorists contributed significantly to the fragmentation, with thinkers like Catharine MacKinnon providing rigorous legal and theoretical frameworks for critiquing sexual expression through the lens of systemic sexism. MacKinnon posited that pornography was not merely offensive material but a form of gender discrimination, akin to workplace harassment, because it reinforced subordinate sexual identities. Conversely, proponents of sexual liberation argued that these legalistic interpretations pathologized normal human sexual variation and expression, effectively policing bodies under the guise of political correctness. The subsequent evolution of these debates saw a shift in focus beyond the binary conflict of anti-pornography versus pro-sex. Later feminist theorists began to integrate queer theory and intersectionality, complicating the monolithic definitions of "woman" and "sexuality" that underpinned the initial divisions. This move acknowledged that issues of race, class, and gender identity profoundly altered how sexual power and oppression manifested for different groups of women. While the initial battles were often framed around visibility and censorship, the later discourse moved toward dismantling the structures of heteronormativity and patriarchal control embedded within sexual culture.

This effort was initiated in 2004 by the biologist Michael Zimmerman, past vice president for academic affairs and provost at Evergreen State College in Olympia, Washington. The letter was written by John McFadden, pastor of the First Congregational United Church of Christ in Appleton, Wisconsin. The project also encourages congregations to participate in Religion and Science Weekend by sponsoring events in which clergy and congregations are encouraged to learn about and discuss the positive intersections of religion and science. The weekend chosen is the closest Sunday to Charles Darwin's birthday, February 12. Evolution Sunday events first took place in 2006 and the project changed from "Sunday" to Weekend" in 2008 to be more inclusive, and in 2022 changed Evolution to Religion and Science. The Clergy Letter Project states that Religion and Science Weekend activities are "an opportunity for serious discussion and reflection on the relationship between religion and science" and in an effort "to elevate the quality of the discussion on this critical topic, and to show that religion and science are not adversaries." The project states that events are specifically intended to emphasize that "Religious people from many diverse faith traditions and locations around the world understand that evolution is quite simply sound science; and for them, it does not in any way threaten, demean, or diminish their faith in God. In fact, for many, the wonders of science often enhance and deepen their awe and gratitude towards God." Statement The letters are entitled An Open Letter Concerning Religion and Science. The four letters have somewhat distinct texts. In addition to English, the Christian version of the project has also been translated to Spanish, Portuguese, and French. Rabbi Letter Unitarian Universalist Letter Buddhist Clergy Letter Humanist Clergy Letter History The project was organized in 2004 by Michael Zimmerman, then a biology professor and dean of the College of Science and Letters at University of Wisconsin–Oshkosh. The impetus behind the Clergy Letter Project stemmed from a desire to foster dialogue rather than debate concerning the relationship between faith and scientific understanding. Proponents of the initiative argue that a significant portion of religious adherents accept evolutionary theory without conflict, a perspective they aim to highlight through organized outreach. The structure of the project involves sending out open letters to religious leaders, providing them with material and encouragement to host related events within their communities. These letters articulate a shared viewpoint across diverse theological and philosophical traditions regarding the compatibility of scientific discovery and religious belief. The shift in nomenclature from Evolution Sunday to Religion and Science Weekend reflects an intentional broadening of scope, moving beyond a singular scientific topic to encompass the broader philosophical and existential intersections of both domains. By framing the initiative as an invitation to reflection, the organizers sought to counteract narratives of inherent conflict often prevalent in public discourse. Various denominations and philosophical groups have engaged with the project's materials, demonstrating the wide reach of its intended message. The resources provided are designed to equip clergy and lay members with accessible talking points and frameworks for discussing complex scientific concepts, such as natural selection, in a way that resonates with spiritual worldviews. The goal is not to proselytize for one viewpoint but rather to showcase a spectrum of thoughtful engagement. Support for the project has come from various academic and religious bodies who see value in promoting mutual respect between scientific inquiry and spiritual conviction.

These structures represent significant milestones in the educational and civic history of the region. The evolution of the Supreme Court building illustrates a common pattern in older urban centres where municipal and educational needs necessitated the repurposing of historical architecture. The transition of the site into various institutional uses reflects the shifting demographics and functional requirements of the community over more than a century. The Old Gold Quadrangle serves as a tangible link to the early pedagogical environment, providing a central gathering space that underscored the communal aspect of the original school setting. The continued preservation and adaptive reuse of these buildings are crucial for maintaining the historical narrative of the institution and the wider locality. The inclusion of these architectural features in the BSSC profile underscores the school's deep roots within the social and built environment of Bendigo. Furthermore, the variety of alumni listed demonstrates the diverse pathways available to graduates, ranging from creative industries and professional politics to elite athletic competition. This breadth of success attests to the comprehensive nature of the education provided by the college and its affiliated programs like NETschool. The ongoing expansion of the online delivery system signals a commitment to modern educational methodologies and increased accessibility for diverse student populations across Victoria.

Cleal had a point to prove in the game against the Lions after controversially being left out of Australia's squad for the Ashes series. Following from a 1985–86 stint with English club Widnes, Cleal returned to English rugby league in 1989 for two seasons with Hull after injury had restricted him to only 4 games for Manly during the 1989 Winfield Cup season. Cleal retired from playing during the 1990–91 season, during which he had become coach of Hull following the departure of Brian Smith to St George. This included coaching Hull (from the sidelines) when they played the Bob Fulton coached Australians at The Boulevard during the 1990 Kangaroo Tour in which the Kangaroos defeated Hull 34–4. After the game Cleal told Channel 10 who were covering the tour that "I'm sitting on both sides of the fence here. It's good to see the Aussies play so well, especially with the third test coming up. But I thought that our guys were just outclassed, they were a far better side. And I suppose when you're hot, you're hot and the Aussies were hot tonight. That was the end of the story." Despite the heavy defeat by the Kangaroos, the Cleal coached Hull would go on to win the Premiership for the 1990–91 season, defeating the defending premiers Widnes 14–4 in the Premiership Trophy Final at Old Trafford, Manchester on Sunday 12 May 1991. Representative career After having made his representative début in the centres for NSW in the second game of the 1981 Interstate series against Queensland at Sydney's Leichhardt Oval (the last game played under the old "State of Residence" rules), Cleal represented the NSW Blues in 12 State of Origin games between 1984 and 1988. Some of Cleal's best football was played at the State of Origin level, he was the NSW forward who troubled Queensland most at a time when the Blues were just beginning to match the passion of their interstate rivals. He is commonly known as the man who coined the inspirational phrase "Dare to Dream" which was an extract from the game and series winning pep talk given by him during half time of game 2 of the 1985 state of origin series. Noel Cleal's most famous moment in Origin football was also an embarrassing one. His performances were characterized by a blend of grit and attacking flair, often making him a pivotal figure in the NSW forward pack during a period of transition for the Blues. While the phrase "Dare to Dream" became synonymous with his motivational abilities, his career also contained moments of significant pressure and scrutiny. The 1985 series, in particular, showcased his ability to influence the game beyond mere physical play, turning a contest into a psychological battle. Although the Blues ultimately found greater sustained success later in the decade, Cleal's presence during those initial intense encounters set a standard for future generations of NSW players. His reputation as a powerful and intelligent forward was cemented during this era of fierce interstate competition, where the rivalry between New South Wales and Queensland defined the sport in Australia. Following his playing days, his coaching endeavors continued to see him involved in the structure of the game, even if his playing career provided the most indelible moments for fans. His later involvement in various roles within rugby league demonstrated a sustained commitment to the sport, both as a competitor and an administrator.

The enduring popularity of the Horatio Hornblower series has led to various derivative works, including adaptations for television and film, although these projects have not always reached the same level of critical or commercial success as the original novels. Literary critics have frequently analyzed the character of Horatio Hornblower, noting his adherence to the archetype of the morally upright naval officer, a figure deeply embedded in the traditions of British maritime lore. His internal conflicts, often balancing personal desires against duty to the crown and the naval service, form a central pillar of the narrative appeal. The setting of the Napoleonic Wars provides a rich backdrop, allowing the author to explore themes of heroism, geopolitical struggle, and the rigid social structures of the era. The fictional world of the novels meticulously reconstructs the realities of 18th and early 19th-century naval life. Detailed descriptions of shipboard drills, tactical maneuvers during engagements, and the daily rigors of long sea voyages lend a high degree of verisimilitude to the adventures. These elements serve not merely as scene-setting but as essential components of the dramatic tension. The political machinations surrounding the conflict between Britain and Napoleonic France are woven into the personal narratives of the characters, demonstrating how grand historical events directly impact the lives of individuals aboard the fleet. While the naval exploits are central, the relationships forged between Hornblower and his subordinates, as well as his interactions with political figures, provide crucial depth. These interpersonal dynamics illustrate the complex hierarchy inherent in military organizations. The portrayal of mentorship, rivalry, and loyalty forms a significant undercurrent, suggesting that character development is as important to the series as any naval battle. The consistent portrayal of Hornblower as a man of profound integrity, despite facing immense pressure, cemented his status as a cultural icon within maritime literature. Subsequent authors and enthusiasts have contributed to the Hornblower canon through scholarly works and fan fiction, demonstrating the depth of the readership’s engagement with the material. These secondary sources often attempt to contextualize the fictional elements within the actual historical practices of the Royal Navy. The continued publication of supplementary materials, such as illustrated atlases and companion guides, indicates a sustained commercial interest in the narrative world created by the original author. The legacy of the series rests not only on its thrilling action sequences but also on its sophisticated exploration of duty, honour, and the human cost of wartime service.

It changed its name on December 11, 1964 from ″Wulmstorf″ to ″Neu Wulmstorf″. It is part of the Hamburg Metropolitan Region. The municipality of Neu Wulmstorf consists of: New Wulmstorf, consisting of New Wulmstorf Wulmstorf Daerstorf Elstorf, consisting of Elstorf Ardestorf Elstorf-Bachheide Rade consisting of Rade Mienenbüttel Ohlenbüttel Rübke Schwiederstorf. Geography Neu Wulmstorf is situated between Hamburg in the east, the marsh of the Altes Land in the north, the forest of the Harburg Hills (Harburger Berge) in the south east, Buchholz in der Nordheide and the geest to the south, and Buxtehude to the west. The municipality incorporates eleven villages and most of the area marks the north north west outskirts of the larger natural region of the Lüneburg Heath in North Germany. The landscape is dominated by the transition from the marsh in the north to the geest in south east. On the marsh side lies the village of Rübke in the Lower Saxon Elbe marshes at sea level and the nature reserve (Naturschutzgebiet) Moore bei Buxtehude (mire), which is home to the corn crake. The village of Neu Wulmstorf sits right on the transitions from the mire up to the geest. Further up, the villages Wulmstorf, Daerstorf, Schwiederstorf, Rade are marking the highest elevations of Neu Wulmstorf on the western outskirts of the Harburg Hills. The villages of Ardestorf, Elstorf, Bachheide, Rade, Mienenbüttel and Ohlenbüttel lie on a stretch reaching from the north east to the south end of the municipality. Population On December 31, 2013 there were 20,384 registered people living in Neu Wulmstorf. The population roughly doubled during the past 42 years. See below for the development of the population (all on December 31): Infrastructure The relatively young village of Neu Wulmstorf grew at the intersection of two old trails. The main road connecting Rübke in the marsh with the geest villages of Wulmstorf and Elstorf intersects with the Bundesstraße 73 as the main road connecting Stade and Cuxhaven with Hamburg. It dominates the settlement as it cuts through from east to west. Just before the geest, the Lower Elbe Railway marked the north border of the Neu Wulmstorf village for many years, with the Neu Wulmstorf S-Bahn station. The station bore the name Daerstorf before that village including the exclave on which the station was built upon, got incorporated into Neu Wulmstorf. The local transport network is characterized by a combination of regional bus lines and the aforementioned S-Bahn connection, which facilitates commuter travel to the city of Hamburg. Local road infrastructure is primarily focused on linking the constituent villages to the central settlement area and providing access to the surrounding natural areas, including the nature reserves. Energy supply to the municipality is handled by regional utility providers, drawing from a mix of fossil fuels and increasing renewable energy sources, a trend common across the Hamburg Metropolitan Region. Commercial activity is concentrated in the central parts of Neu Wulmstorf, with small local businesses serving the residential needs of the eleven villages. Larger commercial and industrial developments tend to be situated near the major transport corridors, particularly where the Bundesstraße 73 traverses the landscape. Educational institutions include several primary schools and a few secondary educational facilities serving the diverse population base. The municipal administration manages local planning, zoning, and the upkeep of public spaces, balancing the needs of a rapidly growing suburban population with the preservation of its characteristic rural and natural landscapes, especially those bordering the Altes Land. Recent planning initiatives have focused on sustainable development, aiming to integrate housing expansion with environmentally conscious practices, such as improving public transport links and promoting bicycle use. The integration into the greater Hamburg area means that local policies are often influenced by regional planning decisions emanating from the metropolitan authority, ensuring a degree of cohesion in infrastructure development and environmental management across the region.

King Jinheung was succeeded by his second son, Prince Geumryun, who became King Jinji of Silla. Family Father: Galmunwang Ipjong (입종 갈문왕) Grandfather: King Jijeung of Silla (신라 지증왕) (437 – 514) Grandmother: Queen Yeonje of the Miryang Park clan (연제태후 박씨) Mother: Queen Jiso (지소태후) (? – 574) Grandfather: King Beopheung of Silla (신라 법흥왕) (? - July 540) Grandmother: Princess Bodo of Silla (보도부인) Consorts and their Respective Issue(s) Queen Sado of the Park clan (사도왕후 박씨) (? – February 614) Crown Prince Dongryun (동륜태자) (? – 572) King Jinji of Silla (신라 진지왕) (? – 24 August 579) Kim Gu-ryun (김구륜) Princess Taeyang (태양공주) Princess Ayang (아양공주) Princess Eunryun (은륜공주) Princess Wolryun (월륜공주) Princess Sukmyeong (숙명궁주) (? – 603) Crown Prince Jeongsuk (정숙태자) Princess Bomyeong (보명궁주) Lady Mishil (미실궁주) Prince Sujong (수종전군) Princess Banya (반야공주) Princess Nanya (난야공주) Lady Sobi of Baekje (소비) Princess Wolhwa (월화궁주) Prince Cheonju (천주공) Princess Deokmyeong (덕명공주) Lady Geumjin (금진낭주 ) Princess Nanseong (난성공주) Legacy King Jinheung's achievements for his kingdom established the basis for unification of Korea. He is remembered today by the Korean people as one of the greatest rulers of Silla. Popular culture Portrayed by Lee Sun-jae in the 2009 MBC TV series Queen Seondeok. Portrayed by Park Hyung-sik in the 2016–2017 KBS2 TV series Hwarang: The Poet Warrior Youth. King Jinji inherited a kingdom undergoing significant internal and external pressures. The early years of his reign were marked by ongoing struggles against various neighboring polities, necessitating shrewd diplomatic maneuvering as well as military preparedness. His rule continued the trend of Silla asserting itself as a major power in the Korean peninsula, although the consolidation of territory remained a gradual and often contested process. The political landscape during Jinji's time was characterized by the influence of powerful aristocratic clans, whose allegiances and ambitions often shaped the direction of royal policy. One of the most enduring aspects of Jinji's reign was the continuation of the religious and cultural transformations initiated by his predecessors. The acceptance and integration of Buddhism, a process that had gained significant momentum under earlier kings, continued to deepen its roots within Silla society. This religious shift was not merely spiritual but also had profound societal implications, influencing art, governance, and social structure. The refinement of court rituals and the development of distinct Silla cultural markers further solidified the kingdom's identity amidst the complex geopolitical environment of the Three Kingdoms period. Administratively, the central government maintained a hierarchical structure, balancing the authority of the monarch with the vested interests of the powerful noble houses. While the crown sought to centralize power, the decentralized nature of regional control, particularly in frontier areas, remained a persistent challenge requiring constant management. Records indicate efforts were made to standardize various aspects of governance, although complete bureaucratic uniformity was still a distant goal. The international relations of Silla under Jinji were pivotal. Interactions with the powerful states of Baekje and Goguryeo, as well as the expanding influence of the Chinese dynasties, dictated much of Silla's strategic outlook. Alliances were frequently formed and dissolved based on immediate strategic necessities, demonstrating a sophisticated, if often precarious, foreign policy apparatus. These external relationships were crucial for the flow of technology, military expertise, and cultural ideas into the kingdom. His progeny continued the line of succession, ensuring the institutional stability of the monarchy despite the internal complexities. The numerous consorts listed in the genealogy highlight the complex web of political marriages that underpinned the Silla elite structure, where familial ties were often as important as military strength in determining political standing. The production of numerous heirs, particularly crown princes, underscored the dynastic imperative for continuity. The cultural legacy of the Jinji period is reflected in surviving archaeological finds and historical texts, which detail the sophistication of Silla craftsmanship and the development of its unique artistic styles. The refinement of metalwork, the development of elaborate burial customs, and the early flourishing of sophisticated courtly arts all point to a stable, albeit pressured, period of cultural development. These elements collectively paint a picture of a kingdom deeply engaged in the process of state-building while absorbing and adapting external influences to forge a distinct Silla identity.

He has released six albums, including 2020's Viva Forever, produced by Dan Schlissel for Stand Up! Early life His father, who was Estonian, escaped a concentration camp in Sweden after World War II by helping steal a minesweeper and sailing it to Ireland. The family eventually emigrated to Canada, changing its name from the Estonian "Vool" to "Wool." Wool's father became a policeman in Toronto, where his investigation of a fraud case involving novelist Jeffrey Archer led Archer to base a character on Wool's father in his first book, Not A Penny More, Not A Penny Less. Wool grew up in various Canadian cities including Toronto and Vancouver, as well as the British Columbia cities of Langley and White Rock, where he went to Earl Marriott Secondary School. He discovered comedy at age 12 after seeing a Bill Cosby live stand-up appearance. Career Stand-up comedy Wool's combination of intelligent political comedy and burly Canadian demeanour has been described as "hoser savant." He began his comedy career in Vancouver in 1995, at age 19. He moved to London at age 22, where he quickly established himself in the city's comedy scene. He has appeared on many British comedy and panel shows, including 8 Out of 10 Cats, Russell Howard's Good News, The John Bishop Show, Never Mind The Buzzcocks, 28 Acts in 28 Minutes, Comedy Cuts, Comedy Central UK's "The Alternative Comedy Experience", and radio programs such as Political Animal as well as Live at Gotham and John Oliver's New York Stand-Up Show on Comedy Central and Showtime's The Green Room with Paul Provenza. He is a frequent performer at large music festivals such as Glastonbury. He has also performed more than 17 times at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, where his shows have typically been well-reviewed. Gareth Newnham of the Weston & Somerset Mercury, reviewing Wool's Wools Gold II: The Iron Pirate, praised his "perfect comic-timing and delivery, a combination of stoner drawl and fire-brand Southern preacher which snaps back and forth at almost a drop of a hat," and Wool's "ability to take a joke and then push it to the darkest place he possibly can." Wool also hosted the 2016 show Before the Morning After, featuring comics filmed in a diner at the 2015 Edinburgh Fringe, for the NBC streaming service Seeso. Wool has toured the world extensively, telling one interviewer that he once circled the globe three times in two weeks, becoming so jet-lagged that he forgot what city he was in. His material often incorporates commentary on current affairs, social issues, and the absurdities of modern life, delivered through a highly polished yet deliberately unpretentious persona. This blend of observational humor with sharp political critique has garnered him both a dedicated following and critical acclaim within the comedic sphere. Beyond his solo performances, he has participated in various comedy collaborations and showcases, often appearing alongside other notable figures in the industry. His touring schedule is notoriously demanding, requiring him to maintain a high level of creative output while traversing international venues. Early in his development, some noted a tendency toward more observational, gentle humor, but this matured into the more biting and satirical style for which he is currently known. His commitment to the craft is evident in the sheer volume of performances and recordings he has amassed over two decades. He maintains a presence on social media, using the platform not only to promote his upcoming tours but also to engage directly with his audience on topics related to his stage material. Furthermore, his work has occasionally intersected with other forms of entertainment, such as voice acting or cameo appearances in television productions, although stand-up remains his primary artistic vehicle. The stylistic evolution of his routines mirrors broader shifts in contemporary comedic trends, adapting to maintain relevance while staying true to his core voice.

He was drafted by the New York Knicks in the 4th round (8th pick, 44th overall) of the 1968 NBA draft; he signed instead with the Oakland Oaks of the rival ABA, who selected him in the 1968 ABA Draft. ABA career In his first season in the ABA, he won Rookie of the Year honors, prompting teammate Rick Barry to comment, "No doubt he's one of the best guards I've ever played with—or against". Later that season, Jabali averaged 33.2 points against the Indiana Pacers in the 1969 ABA Finals and was named Playoffs MVP. As one of the most physically gifted guards in the American Basketball Association, Warren Jabali muscled his way through seven straight seasons of double-digit scoring, including 1968–69, when his average of 21.5 points per game earned him ABA Rookie of the Year honors. That season Jabali's efforts helped bring an ABA Championship to the Oakland Oaks, a team that also featured Rick Barry, Larry Brown, and Doug Moe. Jabali became an instant star after coming into the league from Wichita State University. Although Barry, the Oaks' biggest attraction, won the league scoring title in 1968–69, he was only able to play in 35 games because of a severe knee ligament injury. It was Jabali, an immediate starter, who gave Coach Alex Hannum the extra scoring punch needed in Barry's absence. With Jabali aboard and Barry helping for part of the season, the Oaks recorded a stunning 38-game turnaround to post a league-best 60–18 record. In the playoffs, they went 12–4 on the way to claiming the ABA Championship. A year later at midseason, with the team playing as the Washington Caps, an injury sidelined Jabali. Hurt shortly after playing in his first of four ABA All-Star Games, he was carrying an average of 22.8 points per game at the time. Jabali made a comeback, although his final five years were spent with four teams. In his first season back, 1970–71, he was traded from the Kentucky Colonels to the Indiana Pacers on October 13, 1970, in exchange for a first-round draft choice and cash. Jabali saw action in 62 games with the Pacers. It was with the Pacers that Jabali started pulling the trigger from three-point land; he did it 163 times that year, making 47 treys. His scoring output remained consistently high throughout his tenure with the Pacers, further cementing his reputation as a premier offensive threat in the league. The Pacers, under coach John Havlicek, utilized Jabali's scoring ability as a key component of their offensive structure during this period. Following his time in Indianapolis, Jabali continued to move between various franchises as his career progressed through the 1970s. He played for the Denver Rockets for a season, before moving on to the Chicago Spirits. His versatility on the court allowed him to adapt to different team systems and coaching philosophies across these varied organizations. The ABA, despite its eventual merger with the NBA, provided a platform where Jabali could showcase his athleticism and offensive prowess at a high level. His ability to score efficiently from the perimeter, particularly the three-point line, made him a valuable asset in the evolving landscape of professional basketball. The competitive nature of the ABA fostered an environment where talented players like Jabali could achieve significant individual accolades early in their careers. Even after injuries disrupted his initial trajectory, his resilience and scoring talent allowed him to maintain a high level of performance throughout his career. His contributions to the Oaks' championship run remain a significant part of his basketball legacy, establishing him as a key figure during the ABA's most vibrant period.

She is also a member of the New York Film Critics Online. In 2014, McDonagh created the company 120 Days Books to republish rare 1970s and 1980s gay-erotica genre novels, beginning with a pair of two-in-one volumes: the crime thrillers Man Eater and Night of the Sadist and the supernatural fantasies Vampire's Kiss and Gay Vampire. McDonagh provides interviews and second-channel commentary on DVD / Blu-ray releases, including for director Paul Schrader's Blue Collar, Dario Argento's Tenebrae, and Douglas Buck's Family Portraits: A Trilogy of America, and liner notes, including for the Criterion Collection releases The Tunnel, The Innocents, Kuroneko, and the paired Corridors of Blood/The Haunted Strangler, Arrow Video's Dressed to Kill, and Second Sight Films' The Texas Chain Saw Massacre 4K UHD.
