This versatility has allowed him to collaborate with artists across diverse genres, demonstrating an adaptability that remains a hallmark of his career. His involvement in archival restoration underscores a deep respect for musical history, positioning him not merely as a modern producer but as a guardian of sonic heritage. The process of handling such fragile, aged media demands a rare combination of technical knowledge and meticulous patience, qualities which critics have repeatedly highlighted. His contribution to the Basement Tapes project is often cited as a benchmark for historical audio recovery in the music industry. Beyond commercial successes, his dedication to preserving the integrity of original recordings provides a vital service to musicologists and devoted fans alike. His sustained output demonstrates a commitment to craft over fleeting trends, a principle that resonates throughout his extensive discography. In 1925, Dean married Lady Mercy Greville (3 April 1904 - 21 November 1968; known by her acting name, Nancie Parsons), daughter of Francis Richard Charles Guy Greville, 5th Earl of Warwick and his wife, the former Frances Evelyn Maynard. Dean and Parsons had one daughter, Frances Elizabeth Tessa, before their marriage was dissolved in 1933. In 1929, after he had directed Coward's The Vortex on Broadway, introducing Coward as an actor to American audiences, and three Coward plays in London – Easy Virtue, The Queen Was in the Parlour and Sirocco, the last of which was a conspicuous failure – Dean and Rea dissolved their partnership. Dean became chairman and joint managing director of Associated Talking Pictures (later Ealing Studios) in 1929. During the 1930s, his career alternated between cinema and theatre. For a while his films did well, particularly those starring Gracie Fields, but his flair for theatrical staging did not extend to the cinema, where his work as director was uninspired: the biographer Alan Strachan writes, "most of his films are inert with next to no rhythm or comedic flair", and Fields's biographer David Bret writes that Dean was "positively renowned for his complete lack of sense of humour". In the late 1930s, Dean fell out with Ealing Studios, where his colleagues felt that he was neglecting films in favour of his theatrical work; he was obliged to resign. In 1934 Dean married the Canadian-born Victoria Hopper (1909–2007). This, his third and final marriage, was dissolved in 1948. Second World War and ENSA As the Second World War loomed, Dean published his suggestions on how the entertainments industry could help to sustain the morale of the civilian public and members of the armed forces when war came. For this he was derided by some colleagues, such as George Black of the London Palladium, who were convinced there would be no war. Dean ignored his critics and formed an alliance with the comedian and theatre owner Leslie Henson, who had been a leading figure in entertainments for the troops in the First World War. When the war started, Dean, after lobbying the government, was appointed director of the entertainment branch of the Navy, Army and Air Force Institutes, which was named ENSA (Entertainments National Service Association). Drury Lane was requisitioned as the organisation's headquarters. Dean worked with Henson and other experts in their theatrical or musical spheres, including Black (now firmly behind Dean's ideas), Lena Ashwell, Harold Holt, Jack Hylton, Sir Harry Lauder and Dame Sybil Thorndike, organising entertainment in Britain and overseas for the troops and civilians throughout the war. His contributions to ENSA were significant, encompassing the organization of countless performances ranging from large-scale musical productions to intimate dramatic readings designed to provide escapism and emotional support to service members in various theaters of operation. The scale of the undertaking was immense, requiring logistical planning on a global level, coordinating artists and venues across occupied and Allied territories. Dean's administrative acumen proved invaluable in navigating the complex political and military structures inherent in wartime entertainment provision. The work provided a vital connection to home and normalcy for personnel facing the rigors of military life. Following the cessation of hostilities, the management and structure of ENSA underwent significant transformation, adapting to the post-war cultural landscape. While the immediate wartime imperative subsided, the infrastructure and expertise developed during the conflict laid groundwork for future state-sponsored cultural initiatives. His involvement underscored the growing recognition by authorities that the arts held a critical function beyond mere diversion during periods of national crisis. After the war, Dean returned more fully to theatrical pursuits, though his association with major studio power structures had been permanently altered by his wartime service. His subsequent directorial efforts reflected a mixture of his earlier dramatic inclinations and the large-scale organizational experience gleaned from the ENSA endeavor. He remained an influential, albeit sometimes controversial, figure within British cultural circles for the remainder of his life.

His eight shutouts in 1905 was tops in the American League. Suspension in 1906 Killian started only 16 games in 1906 and finished 10–6 with a 3.43 ERA. He missed several weeks of the season in August and September. He was suspended after a series of incidents in which he destroyed a telephone and various articles of furniture in the clubhouse in a rage, showed up on multiple occasions not "in condition to play ball", and trouble under the grandstand in which officers had to be called to prevent Killian from going on the field. During the suspension, Killian left Detroit and pitched semipro ball in Chicago (for $100 per game) and did not pitch in a game for the Tigers until September 19. 1,001 innings without a home run Between September 19, 1903, and August 7, 1907, a span of nearly four years and 1,001 innings, he did not allow an opposing batter to hit a home run. In his entire career, he allowed only nine home runs – an average of one home run every 178 innings. According to BaseballLibrary.com, he was "the hardest pitcher to homer against in ML history." He reportedly used a "sinkerball" to induce batters to hit groundballs. Three consecutive American League pennants In 1907, Killian had the best season of his career. He started 41 games and compiled a 25–13 record with a 1.78 ERA. His ERA was 81 points lower than the league average of 2.59. He ranked among the American League's leaders with his 1.78 ERA (second), 25 wins (third), 29 complete games (sixth), and 1,270 batters faced (sixth). Killian also excelled as a batter in 1907, compiling a .320 batting average and .410 slugging percentage. His batting average was 73 points higher than the league average of .247. Killian's 8.0 wins above replacement (WAR) in 1907 was the highest of any player in the American League at any position, higher even than teammate Ty Cobb. Only Honus Wagner in the National League had a higher WAR rating at 9.0. Killian's performance helped lead the 1907 Tigers to their first American League pennant and was one of the best pitching performances in the club's history. His continued excellence contributed to the team's dominance in the late 1900s. The Detroit Tigers secured another American League pennant in 1908, with Killian maintaining a high level of performance, though his statistics did not reach the heights of his 1907 campaign. In 1908, he pitched in 38 games, recording a 21–11 record and posting a respectable 2.51 ERA. While his ERA rose slightly from the previous season, his contributions remained vital to the team's competitive standing. He continued to demonstrate proficiency at the plate, though his offensive numbers were less spectacular than in 1907. The 1908 season saw the Tigers remain a formidable presence in the league, a testament to the consistent high caliber of play provided by Killian and his teammates. The 1909 season brought another pennant for the club, and Killian was again a central figure in the rotation. He pitched in 33 games, finishing with a 20–12 record and an ERA of 2.18. This performance underscored his enduring effectiveness as a frontline pitcher. His ability to maintain elite performance levels across multiple seasons, despite the personal distractions and suspensions, solidified his place as a premier hurler of his era. These consistent contributions were instrumental in establishing the Tigers as a perennial powerhouse during this period of baseball history.

Use in early Europe A French book named La catoptromancie grecque et ses dérivés (which translates in English to "Greek catoptromancy and its derivatives") by Armand Delatte from 1932 details the history of catoptromancy in the context of early European history. Dellate wrote that, in the Middle Ages, mentions of the divinatory mirror appear, "obscure and also uncertain", in the canon of an Irish council "whose convocation is reported by tradition". Historical criticism shows that the collection of these texts cannot go back further than the beginning of the 6th11th century, although certain canons can claim to a more remote antiquity. Here is an example: I translate literally: 'the Christian, it is said, who believes that there is a witch (lamia or striga) in a mirror, will be anathema, anyone who launches this insult against a person; and he cannot be received into the church before having personally retracted the accusation he has made and thus having done penance with all desirable zeal'. The absence of connection, in the first sentence, between the two relative clauses, as well as the mention of a single measure of reparation and penance, which consists of the retraction of an insult, clearly shows, despite the clumsiness of the editorial, that we cannot dissociate the two faults referred to in this canon: it is the same person who claims to see a witch in a mirror and who, in relation to this first error (as shown by the words this insult), launches against others an accusation of witchcraft. To express our thoughts clearly, sin consists, according to us, of trying to recognize a witch with the help of a magic mirror. Certain modern superstitions and customs can be cited in support of this interpretation. In Thuringia, in Scotland and in the country of Cornwall, we encountered, not long ago, diviners who had the power to make witches and evil people appear, either in an ordinary mirror or in a mirror specially consecrated by magical rites, as well as the author of a theft or any other secret thing. Frazer reports, according to Miss Gordon Cumming, that a family of Nairn in Scotland possessed in the last century 'a crystal ball which, immersed in a bucket of water, becomes a magic mirror reflecting the face of the evil neighbor who bewitched the cattle'. Here we encounter for the first time an example of those combinations of lecanomancy with crystallomancy or catoptromancy to which I alluded previously. The text of the Irish canon therefore seems to me to target a particular use of divination by the mirror, one of those which was considered more dangerous by the Church of the first centuries, because it favored belief in magic. These practices, which involve using reflective surfaces for scrying or divination, present a complex intersection of pre-Christian magical beliefs and subsequent Christian theological prohibitions. The ecclesiastical condemnation detailed in the Irish canon directly addresses the perception of mirrors not merely as reflective objects but as conduits to supernatural or malign forces, thereby facilitating accusations of witchcraft. Such condemnations were not isolated incidents but reflected a broader cultural tension regarding the boundaries between natural perception and occult foresight. The historical trajectory of catoptromancy reveals a continuous negotiation between indigenous belief systems, which often incorporated the power of reflective surfaces for prognostication, and the dominant religious doctrines that sought to marginalize or eradicate such practices as heretical or demonic. Beyond the documented medieval instances, the concept of the divinatory mirror surfaces in various folk traditions across Europe, often evolving alongside other forms of divination like scrying in water or bone. These variations demonstrate a pragmatic adoption of a powerful, yet inherently ambiguous, tool. The specific focus on identifying malefactors, such as witches or thieves, points toward the deeply ingrained social anxieties of agrarian societies, where the threat of unseen harm—from blight to magical assault—was a constant existential pressure. The convergence of lecanomancy, crystallomancy, and catoptromancy, as noted by Dellatte, suggests a dynamic syncretism in magical practice, where different modes of divination were combined to achieve a more potent or specific result. This combination was particularly fraught with danger in the eyes of the institutional Church, which viewed any attempt to bypass divinely ordained channels of knowledge as an act of profound transgression against the established cosmic order.

Nas began to make appearances on other artists' work, including "Fast Life" on Kool G Rap's "4,5,6" and "Verbal Intercourse" on Raekwon's Only Built 4 Cuban Linx... (1995). Nas began to dub himself as Nas Escobar on these guest appearances. Meanwhile, his excessive spending habits had left him with little money, as Nas had to ask for a loan to purchase clothes to wear to the 1995 Source Awards. The success of fellow East Coast act The Notorious B.I.G. at the awards show sent a message to Nas to change his commercial approach, resulting in his hiring of Steve "The Commissioner" Stoute as manager. While Illmatic attained gold status, Stoute convinced Nas to aim his efforts in a more commercial direction for his second album, after which Nas enlisted production team the Trackmasters, who were known for their mainstream success at the time. Meanwhile, Brooklyn-based female rapper Foxy Brown was brought to the attention of the Trackmasters, who were working on LL Cool J's Mr. After impressing the production team with an on-stage freestyle rap, she earned a guest appearance on Mr. Smith, contributing a verse to the remix of "I Shot Ya". Throughout 1995 and 1996, Brown appeared on several platinum and gold singles, including Jay-Z's "Ain't No Nigga" and the remix of Toni Braxton's "You're Makin' Me High". Her appearances sparked a recording company bidding war in early 1996, leading to her signing to Def Jam Recordings. The success of "I Shot Ya" prompted her inclusion, along with rappers AZ and Cormega, in collaborating with Nas on the song "Affirmative Action" for his second studio album, It Was Written (1996). The collaboration came in the wake of the critical success of AZ's debut album Doe or Die (1995). He initially garnered attention with his appearance on Nas' "Life's a Bitch" (1993). Cormega, whose rapping career had been put on hold due to his incarceration during the early 1990s, was referenced by Nas on "One Love" (1994), and was released from jail in 1995. Dre gave a reason why the album was a failure. "When we were doing that record, it was a lot of problems in the studio. I only spent maybe four days in the studio with the artists and we're supposed to do a record with them for days. He came in and did his thing. Foxy missed like 5 airplanes to getting to the studio. She's in here like 1 hour so we got to work with her 1 hour. The noted production issues and scheduling difficulties contributed to the album's underwhelming reception despite the individual talents of its featured artists. This period marked a significant transition point for both Nas and his contemporaries, as the East Coast hip hop landscape began to evolve in response to changing commercial demands and industry pressures. While Nas's artistic trajectory continued to diverge from purely underground aesthetics, he maintained a level of lyrical complexity that distinguished him within the increasingly polished soundscapes of the mid-1990s. Foxy Brown, meanwhile, capitalized on her momentum, becoming a prominent figure in mainstream hip hop through her association with established acts and her own burgeoning singles. Her success demonstrated a growing appetite for female voices within the genre, a trend that would become more pronounced in the subsequent years. The incorporation of artists like AZ and Cormega on It Was Written served to broaden the sonic palette of the album, bringing in different regional flavors and stylistic approaches to complement Nas's established lyrical prowess. This convergence of established veterans and rising stars defined the commercial peak of many East Coast acts during this transitional era. The business aspects of the music industry, as evidenced by the recording company bidding wars, reflected the heightened market value of successful rappers who could cross over from critical darlings to mass-market attractions.

In recent decades, topics regarding class, capitalism, and social structure gave way to studies of the cultural history of urban life, as well as the study of groups such as women, prostitutes, migrants from rural areas, and immigrants from the Continent and from the British Empire. The urban environment itself became a major topic, as studies of the material fabric of the city, and the structure of urban space, became more prominent. Historians have almost always focused on London, but they have also studied small towns and cities from the medieval period, as well as the urbanization that attended the industrial revolution. In the second half of the 19th century, provincial centres such as Birmingham, Glasgow, Leeds, Liverpool, and Manchester doubled in size and became regional capitals. They were all conurbations that included smaller cities and suburbs in their catchment area. Available scholarly materials have become quite comprehensive today. United States Urban biography Urban biography is the narrative history of a city and often reaches a general audience. Urban biographies cover the interrelationships among various dimensions, such as politics, demography, business, high culture, popular culture, housing, neighbourhoods, and ethnic groups. It covers municipal government as well as physical expansion, growth and decline. Historians often focus on the largest and most dominant city—usually the national capital—which geographers call a "primate city." Some representative urban biographies are: Edwin G. Gotham: a history of New York City to 1898 (2000) S. Checkland, The Upas Tree: Glasgow, 1875-1975 (1981) Geoffrey Cotterell, Amsterdam, The Life of a City (1972) Janet Abu-Lughod, Cairo; 1001 Years of City Victorious (1971) Diane E. Davis, Urban Leviathan: Mexico City in the Twentieth Century (1994) Constance McLaughlin Green, Washington, Village and Capital, 1800-1878 (1962) Christopher Hibbert, London, the Biography of a City (1969) Robert Hughes, Barcelona (1992) Colin Jones. Paris: Biography of a City (2004) Blake McKelvey. Rochester (4 vol, 1961), Rochester NY Simon Sebag Montefiore, Jerusalem: The Biography (2012) Bessie Louise Pierce, A History of Chicago (3 vol 1957), to 1893. Roy Porter, London: A Social History (1998) Alexandra Ritchie, Faust's Metropolis: A History of Berlin (1998) James Scobie, Buenos Aires: Plaza to Suburb (1974) Ronald Taylor, Berlin and its Culture: A Historical Portrait (1997), considers literature, music, theater, painting, and decorative arts. Historians have developed typologies of cities, emphasizing their geographic location and economic specialization. In the United States Carl Bridenbaugh was a pioneer in historiography. He emphasized the major port cities on the East Coast, the largest of which were Boston and Philadelphia, each with fewer than 40,000 people at the time of the American Revolution. These early metropolitan centers exhibited distinct characteristics rooted in their mercantile functions and burgeoning colonial connections. The examination of urban forms in the United States has often centered on the interplay between mercantile capitalism and evolving social hierarchies within these coastal hubs. Subsequent scholarly endeavors have broadened this focus to include the interior cities and the dynamics of westward expansion, linking urban development to broader patterns of American settlement and economic diversification. The study of urban infrastructure, such as transportation networks, sanitation systems, and communication channels, has also become a critical component of modern urban history. These material aspects reveal much about the administrative capabilities of nascent municipal governments and the lived experiences of diverse populations navigating rapidly changing physical landscapes. The concept of the metropolis itself has been theorized through various lenses, ranging from functionalist models emphasizing economic specialization to more critical perspectives focusing on power dynamics and social reproduction within the urban fabric. Furthermore, the influence of global trade routes on the morphology and social character of cities cannot be overstated, as port cities served as crucial nodes connecting regional economies to international markets. These interactions brought with them not only goods but also new social groups, cultural practices, and ideologies that transformed the urban milieu. The diversity fostered by immigration and internal migration has consistently been a central theme, highlighting the continuous process of social negotiation within the expanding city limits.

It is also one of the medications that can cause toxic epidermal necrolysis or Stevens–Johnson syndrome. The pediatric version of cefdinir can bind to iron in the digestive tract; in rare cases, this causes a rust or red discoloration of the stool. Blood typically appears dark brown or black in stool, and testing may confirm which is present. If the reddish stool is accompanied by abdominal pain, weight loss, diarrhea, etc., a Clostridioides difficile infection caused by the antibiotic could be signified. Mechanism of action Society and culture Economics As of 2008, cefdinir was the highest-selling cephalosporin antibiotic in the United States, with more than $585 million in retail sales of its generic versions. Available forms Cefdinir is administered orally. It is available as capsules and a suspension. Dosage, schedule, and duration of therapy varies according to the type of infection. Warner-Lambert licensed the drug for marketing in US from Fujisawa. Abbott obtained U.S. marketing rights to cefdinir in December 1998 through an agreement with Warner-Lambert Company. It was approved by the FDA on December 4, 1997. It is available in US as Omnicef by Abbott Laboratories and in India as Cednir by Abbott, Kefnir by Glenmark, Cefdair by Xalra Pharma and Cefdiel by Ranbaxy. Synthesis Acylation of the primary amine 1 with 4-bromo-3-oxobutanoyl bromide (2) leads to the amide (3). The active methylene group in that product is then nitrosated with sodium nitrite; the initial product spontaneously tautomerizes to afford the oxime (4). The structure of cefdinir belongs to the aminopenicillins, a class of antibiotics characterized by a modified beta-lactam ring. Its efficacy stems from its ability to inhibit the synthesis of bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan. This inhibition occurs through the binding of the drug to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) located within the bacterial cell membrane. By interfering with transpeptidases, cefdinir prevents the cross-linking of glycan strands, leading to a compromised cell wall structure and subsequent bacterial lysis. The drug exhibits enhanced stability against beta-lactamase enzymes compared to earlier cephalosporins, which contributes to its broader spectrum of activity against resistant strains. Resistance mechanisms in bacteria can include the production of beta-lactamase enzymes that hydrolyze the antibiotic or alterations in the PBPs themselves that reduce the drug's binding affinity. The specific chemical synthesis pathway detailed involves several key reactions, starting with the acylation of a primary amine to form an amide intermediate. This intermediate then undergoes nitrosation, a process involving the introduction of a nitroso group, which facilitates the formation of the final oxime structure. The industrial production of cephalosporins often requires stringent quality control measures to ensure purity and consistent pharmacological activity across batches. Clinical guidelines recommend appropriate dosing regimens based on the severity of the infection, patient age, renal function, and susceptibility testing results obtained for the causative pathogen.

Foner's comprehensive work offers an extensive examination of the evolving role of the Republican Party within the broader context of American political development. The party's ideological shifts, particularly concerning sectionalism, industrialization, and the expansion of federal authority, are meticulously traced through various historical periods. Early on, the party coalesced around anti-slavery sentiments, a core tenet that defined its initial rise and subsequent national prominence. This foundational commitment to preventing the expansion of slavery into new territories served as a powerful unifying force during the tumultuous decades preceding the Civil War. The ensuing conflict irrevocably altered the party's character, forcing a national reckoning regarding the nature of American citizenship and federal supremacy. Following Reconstruction, the Republican Party navigated a complex landscape marked by industrial expansion, urbanization, and the growing influence of economic interests. This era witnessed significant debates over protective tariffs, internal improvements, and the regulation of burgeoning corporate power. The Progressive Era presented another major crucible for the Republican Party, challenging its established doctrines with calls for governmental reform and greater social regulation. Figures within the party advocated for measures designed to curb the excesses of industrial capitalism and address social inequities that were becoming increasingly apparent in the rapidly modernizing nation. This period saw a gradual diversification of the party's platforms, moving beyond purely economic concerns to encompass issues of public health, labor rights, and democratic accountability. Subsequent decades saw the party engage in intense ideological contests, balancing the imperatives of business interests with the growing demands of organized labor and a more socially conscious electorate. The trajectory of the Republican Party through the twentieth century demonstrates a pattern of both steadfast adherence to certain core principles, such as fiscal conservatism and a belief in limited government intervention in the economy, and significant adaptation to prevailing national concerns. The New Deal era, though often characterized by Republican opposition, forced a reevaluation of the role of the federal government in economic stabilization and social welfare. The party's response to these challenges contributed to periods of significant realignment in American political alignments. Modern analysis of the party highlights the constant tension between its traditional roots as a party of free labor and its evolving relationship with corporate power and national security concerns. The ability of the Republican Party to maintain relevance across such profound societal transformations underscores its resilience within the American political system.

The album is often cited by scholars of American alternative rock as a transitional work, bridging the gap between the more straightforward, melodic rock of the late 1970s and the increasingly electronic textures that would define the 1980s alternative scene. Its willingness to incorporate synthesized sounds, while simultaneously retaining strong song structures and accessible melodies, placed it at a fascinating intersection of musical trends. Some listeners appreciated the dynamic range, moving from intimate, subdued moments to bursts of energetic, keyboard-laden chorus work. Conversely, others found the density of the instrumentation and the pervasive nature of the electronic elements to be overproduction, detracting from what they perceived as the core songwriting strengths. The collaboration with numerous session musicians and programmers suggests an ambition to create a highly polished, contemporary soundscape, albeit one that proved divisive among reviewers. Despite the mixed critical response, the album maintained a cult following among dedicated fans of 1980s New Wave and power-pop, establishing a recognizable sonic palette for Matthew Sweet's subsequent musical endeavors. This period of prolific, though commercially challenging, output informed the stylistic shifts that would characterize his later work.

Bishop Patrick Hepburn (1538–73), the last Roman Catholic bishop at Spynie, installed wide-mouth gun loops to boost the castle defences and enlarges some windows. He continued to live at Spynie for a period after the Reformation. English prisoners were held at Spynie during the war known as the Rough Wooing, including Edward Sutton, 4th Baron Dudley who was taken at Hume Castle in December 1548. Christopher Rokeby, an agent provocateur of Elizabeth I of England, who had tried to lead Mary, Queen of Scots, into a plot with English Roman Catholics, was imprisoned in Spynie Castle in 1566 for eighteen months during Bishop Patrick Hepburn's tenure. Hepburn fell foul of the Privy Council for sheltering his relative Bothwell at Spynie in 1567 who had fled from the battle of Carberry Hill first to Huntly Castle. Bothwell sailed to Orkney and Shetland, and finally to Denmark. As part of the pacification following the abdication of Queen Mary, Regent Morton, in a meeting of the Privy Council at Perth on 23 February 1573, ordered that the castle be made available to the Crown, if needed:the hous of Spyne salbe randerit and deliverit to oure Soverane Lord and his Regent foirsaid quhen it salbe requirite on XV dayis warning, without prejudice of ony partiis rycht. On 29 July 1587, King James VI gave the castle and estate to Alexander Lindsay, 1st Lord Spynie; and they remained in his hands until he surrendered them back to the Crown in December 1605. During this period in 1595, Spynie was one of the castles that had additional fortification installed as protection against a perceived threat from the Spaniards. 17th century In 1606, King James restored to the bishopric of Moray the endowments that remained. Bishop John Guthrie, who was a well-known royalist, ceased to be the bishop in 1638 when all bishops were deposed by the general assembly – he and his family continued to live at Spynie however. Guthrie refused to subscribe to the Covenant and prepared the castle for a siege which duly arrived in 1640 in the form of Covenanter Col. The period of the Scottish Wars of Religion witnessed numerous conflicts involving Spynie, reflecting its strategic location in the northeast of Scotland. The castle's architecture adapted over the centuries, transitioning from a medieval stronghold to a more fortified residence capable of resisting prolonged military action. Following the upheaval of the Civil Wars, the ownership and religious use of Spynie fluctuated according to the prevailing political climate and the decrees issued by the reigning monarch and the Scottish Parliament. The rebuilding and modification of the structure continued sporadically throughout the 17th century, often influenced by the fortunes of the families who held it, such as the Lindsays. These alterations reveal a history of strategic necessity mingled with residential comfort, as the structure served multiple functions throughout its long history. The Reformation fundamentally altered the institutional role of the castle, transforming it from a center of Catholic ecclesiastical power to a property managed under different legal and religious frameworks. The maintenance of the castle, even when under lay ownership, required considerable resources, often supplemented by grants or leases from the Crown. These changes underscore Spynie's enduring significance not merely as a defensive structure but as a persistent fixture within the sociopolitical landscape of Moray.

In the last 35+ years, GPC has continued to grow through the acquisition of other companies in the automotive industry, as well as in the industrial, office and electrical industries. Today GPC is a parts distributor with over 3,100 operations and approximately 48,000 employees. Subsidiaries The Automotive Parts Group distributes automotive replacement parts, accessory items and service items throughout North America, Australia and New Zealand. In North America, parts are sold primarily under the NAPA (National Automotive Parts Association) brand name. The company's GPC Asia Pacific business serves the Australasian markets primarily under the brand name Repco. The Automotive Parts Group supports over 6,000 NAPA AUTO PARTS stores throughout the United States, 700 wholesalers in Canada and 481 automotive locations in Australia and New Zealand. These stores sell to both the Retail (DIY) and Commercial (DIFM) automotive aftermarket customer and cover the majority of all domestic and foreign motor vehicle models. The Industrial Parts Group, operating under the name Motion Industries, offers more than 5.9 million industrial replacement parts and related supplies. The logistical network supporting this division is substantial, ensuring that complex and specialized parts can reach industrial clients efficiently across the continent. Further diversification has been evident in the company’s expansion into electrical and electronic materials, which complements the needs of both the automotive and industrial segments. This expansion allows the consolidated entity to offer a more comprehensive suite of supplies to its varied clientele. The continuous integration of these disparate yet synergistic businesses has allowed the corporation to maintain a diverse revenue stream insulated from fluctuations in any single market sector. Strategic acquisitions have been pivotal in this evolution, providing access to established market share, proprietary technology, and regional distribution hubs. The transition from a localized automotive parts depot to a multinational industrial and retail conglomerate reflects a profound organizational transformation over nearly a century. Ongoing efforts focus on enhancing supply chain resilience and integrating digital technologies into customer-facing operations to meet modern commercial expectations. The global reach, particularly through the Australasian operations, demonstrates a commitment to serving international markets beyond the core North American base.

In 1127, he reconquered Longares, but simultaneously lost all his Castilian possessions to Alfonso VII. He confirmed a treaty with Castile the next year (1128) with the Peace of Támara, which fixed the boundaries of the two realms. He conquered Molina de Aragón and populated Monzón in 1129, before besieging Valencia, which had fallen again upon the Cid's death. He went north of the Pyrenées in October 1130 to protect the Val d'Aran. Early in 1131, he besieged Bayonne. It is said he ruled "from Belorado to Pallars and from Bayonne to Monreal." At the siege of Bayonne in October 1131, three years before his death, he published a will leaving his kingdom to three autonomous religious orders based in Palestine and politically largely independent – the Knights Templars, the Hospitallers, and the Knights of the Holy Sepulchre, whose influences might have been expected to cancel one another out. The will has greatly puzzled historians, who have read it as a bizarre gesture of extreme piety uncharacteristic of Alfonso's character, one that effectively undid his life's work. Elena Lourie (1975) suggested instead that it was Alfonso's attempt to neutralize the papacy's interest in a disputed succession – Aragon had been a fief of the papacy since 1068 – and to fend off Urraca's son from her first marriage, Alfonso VII of Castile, for the papacy would be bound to press the terms of such a pious testament. Generous bequests to important churches and abbeys in Castile had the effect of making the noble churchmen there beneficiaries who would be encouraged by the will to act as a brake on Alfonso VII's ambitions to break it – and yet among the magnates witnessing the will in 1131 there was not a single cleric. In the event it was a will that his nobles refused to carry out – instead bringing his brother Ramiro from the monastery to assume royal powers – an eventuality that Lourie suggests was Alfonso's hidden intent. His final campaigns were against Mequinenza (1133) and Fraga (1134), where García Ramírez, the future king of Navarre, and a mere 500 other knights fought with him. The death of Alfonso in 1137 marked the culmination of a turbulent political and military career characterized by shifting allegiances and contested territories. His legacy remains a complex subject for medieval Iberian historiography, oscillating between that of a successful regional warlord and a highly pious, albeit controversial, sovereign. Contemporary chronicles offer differing accounts of his final years, with some emphasizing his piety and others highlighting his relentless military expansionism, particularly in the Pyrenean foothills. The strategic importance of the Val d'Aran, a region with strong connections to the French sphere of influence, played a critical role in his northern campaigns, suggesting a sophisticated understanding of trans-Pyrenean power dynamics. The delegation of his domains to religious orders, while appearing counterintuitive to the established feudal customs of the era, could be interpreted as a sophisticated political maneuver designed to create a decentralized buffer zone against encroachment from larger Christian kingdoms or the Papacy itself. This act of testamentary disposition effectively transformed his military conquests into ecclesiastical holdings, a unique fusion of temporal and spiritual authority. The internal resistance to the will, evidenced by the elevation of his brother Ramiro, suggests that while Alfonso possessed considerable regional power, he did not command absolute allegiance from the highest echelons of his aristocracy. The continuing struggle between the nascent Aragonese entity and the established Castilian power structure defined much of the geopolitical landscape of the early thirteenth century, a conflict in which Alfonso served as a powerful, volatile nexus. His patronage of local churches and monasteries provided him with a vital network of support, extending his influence beyond purely military might into the socio-religious fabric of his domain.

According to Alexis Petridis of The Guardian, "FutureSex/LoveSound" and the other opening songs of the album are heavily influenced by David Bowie's Diamond Dogs (1974). The song sounds "horny" which can be seen through the lines "Slide a little bit closer to me, little girl / Daddy’s on a mission to please." The chorus of the song reminded 411mania's Mikey MiGo of Prince's "New Power Generation". Critical response Mikey MiGo of 411mania wrote that the song is a "welcomed change" from Timberlake's past work. She stated that the song "has qualities of Prince that I've never seen anyone muster up before". Amanda Murray of Sputnikmusic called the song "musically and melodically great", but criticized its lyrics. She wrote that the lyrics sound like the dialogue of a "low-rent porn film", highlighting the lines: "She's pressed up on me; I think she's ready to blow?" and "All I need is a moment alone, to give you my tongue and get you out of control". According to Murray, "It makes one question exactly what films Timberlake was starring in during his sabbatical." She concluded that "FutureSex/LoveSound" establishes a pattern for the rest of FutureSex/LoveSounds: "infectiously catchy and in many cases accomplished pop music, marred by retardedly retarded lyrics". In a review of FutureSex/LoveSounds, Ben Williams of New York cited the album's first five tracks, including "FutureSex/LoveSound", as updating the early 1980s Minneapolis sound: "tense drum machines, high-pitched synth squiggles and staccato funk bass lines". While reviewing the album, Stephen Thomas Erlewine of Allmusic noted that the first three songs of the album include the word "sex" in their titles, "as if mere repetition of the word will magically conjure a sex vibe, when in truth it has the opposite effect: it makes it seem that Justin is singing about it because he's not getting it." Lucy Davies of BBC Music stated that it is initially "difficult to listen to the lyrics of the opening tracks and give an objective opinion". She wrote that it is like Timberlake is "trying to find redeemable qualities about some guy who has zero social skills and stares at women on his own from the corner of a bar. Only he seems to have found some similarly unreconstructed creepy friends shouting words of encouragement to his clunky chat-up lines, like Timbaland". Live performances "FutureSex/LoveSound" was used as the opening song on Timberlake's FutureSex/LoveShow in 2007. The visual presentation accompanying the album further contributed to its controversial reception. The music videos for several tracks utilized stylized, often sexually suggestive imagery, aligning with the perceived thematic content of the music. This aesthetic choice drew both praise for its boldness and criticism for its perceived vulgarity, mirroring the lyrical concerns raised by critics such as Amanda Murray. Timbaland's production style, a key component of the album's sound, was frequently cited as a defining element. His innovative use of programmed percussion and intricate sonic textures provided a modern, angular counterpoint to Timberlake's more conventional vocal delivery. This juxtaposition of avant-garde production with pop sensibility became a hallmark of the album's overall sonic identity. Furthermore, the album marked a significant stylistic departure for Timberlake following his earlier work with Justified, which had emphasized a more youthful, R&B-inflected sound. FutureSex/LoveSound introduced a greater degree of electronic complexity and a darker, more adult tone to his musical output. The album's commercial success, despite the polarized critical reaction, demonstrated its broad appeal to a mainstream audience eager for contemporary pop music infused with innovative production. Its sound was seen by many as a successful marriage between classic funk and cutting-edge digital music manipulation, even if the narrative elements proved divisive among reviewers. The thematic preoccupation with desire and seduction, whether celebrated as raw energy or dismissed as superficiality, formed the core tension surrounding the release.

In his memoirs, former U.S. Treasury Secretary Donald Regan recalls referencing a finding made in one of CTJ's reports when he explained to President Reagan that "your secretary paid more in federal taxes last year than ... Boeing, General Dynamics, and 57 other big corporations." After admitting that "I didn’t realize things had gotten that far out of line", Reagan threw his support behind the push to close corporate loopholes. McClatchy Newspapers has said that CTJ's work "sparked national outrage that helped pave the way for The Tax Reform Act of 1986." The Washington Post described the release of these reports as a "key turning point" in the process of enacting the Act. University of Connecticut law professor Richard Pomp described the CTJ studies as having had "a profound effect on educating the public and on shaping public opinion, unlike previous studies relying on only statistical aggregates", and declared that "one of the major catalysts for the corporate reforms made by the Tax Reform Act of 1986 was the disclosure by Citizens for Tax Justice (CTJ) of the nominal amount of income tax paid by some of the largest corporations in the country." A 1988 article in The Washington Monthly proclaimed CTJ was one of the "best public interest groups" in the nation. The magazine described CTJ's work as having "helped set the stage for one of the most dramatic defeats that special interest groups have ever suffered: the 1986 overhaul of the federal tax code." 2001 Bush tax cut debate In 2001, with Republicans in control of the White House and both houses of Congress, both the Treasury Department and the Joint Committee on Taxation were encouraged not to produce distributional tables explaining the impact of President Bush's proposed tax cuts. Republicans were reported to have "never liked that kind of measurement, saying it contributed to class warfare." As a result, data released by CTJ, produced using the ITEP Microsimulation Tax Model, was the primary source of information on which opponents of the tax cuts had to rely. The New York Times described CTJ's Director, Bob McIntyre, as having "no doubt ... exerted more influence on the tax debate this year than any lobbyist in town." In a similar vein, Senator Kent Conrad of North Dakota said "I don’t know what we’d do without Bob McIntyre. This level of influence extended beyond mere data provision; McIntyre and CTJ actively engaged in public discourse to interpret the complex economic modeling. Their reports often framed tax policy not merely as an economic adjustment but as a fundamental issue of social equity and fairness within the American system. Opponents of the tax cuts frequently cited CTJ findings to argue that the benefits of the proposed legislation would disproportionately accrue to the wealthiest segments of the population, while the burdens would fall upon middle and lower-income families. The reliance on non-partisan, academically rigorous analysis provided by CTJ gave critics a powerful, seemingly objective platform from which to launch their arguments against the Republican agenda. This dynamic illustrated a recurring pattern in American fiscal policy debates, where specialized, data-driven advocacy groups become essential counterweights to the legislative priorities of the ruling party. The use of microsimulation models, as employed by CTJ, allowed for a detailed, individual-level assessment of tax changes, offering a granularity of analysis that traditional aggregate statistics could not provide. This methodological approach was itself a significant contribution to the field of progressive tax research, moving the conversation beyond broad economic theory into the practical, lived experience of tax code alterations. The impact of this informational leverage suggests that the battle over tax policy is often won or lost not solely in the halls of Congress, but in the arena of public perception, shaped by accessible, compelling data.

Some of the 1980 constitution's original provisions, such as the presidential power of dissolving the Chamber of Deputies (the lower house of Congress) and serving eight-year terms with possibility of re-election, were modified or eliminated after 1990, when the country regained its democracy and the Congress was re-established. Results The results supplied by the Colegio Escrutador Nacional (National Election Observer Association) were as follows. Aftermath The new constitution took effect on 11 March 1981. On this date a transition period of eight years began, during which General Pinochet, acting as President of the Republic and the Military Regime (Junta), exercised constituent and legislative power. Accusations of fraud The results of the referendum were disputed by the political opposition, headed by former senator Patricio Aylwin, and 46 other representatives, who argued that there had not been any electoral records and that the only anti-fraud measure was an ink mark on the thumb, which was easily removed. These criticisms were rejected by the National Scrutinizing College, made up of the Comptroller General of the Republic, Osvaldo Iturriaga; the minister of the Court of Appeals of Santiago, Arnoldo Dreyse; and the secretary of the Supreme Court, René Pica. In Antofagasta, former deputy and former mayor Juan Floreal Recabarren denounced the possibility of voting numerous times by removing the adhesive seal from his identity card (delivered when he voted for the first time that day) and cleaning his thumb of the ink. He was later detained by the authorities. Other accusations of fraud are related to the fact that the mayors of the time (appointed by the dictatorship) held a lottery to define the members of each polling station, which were made up exclusively of supporters of the regime and collaborators belonging to large companies such as Soprole, Mingo, Neut Latour Forestal, Banco de Chile, BHC, Lan Chile, Banco Sud Americano and Embotelladora Andina, among others. The figure of the polling station representatives did not exist either, so the opposition did not have access to supervise the electoral process. In December 1987, Cauce magazine published a report prepared by Eduardo Hamuy in conjunction with the Academy of Christian Humanism in which observations made at 981 polling stations in Greater Santiago on the day of the 1980 plebiscite were compiled, and numerous cases of fraud were found. These allegations of systemic irregularities raised serious questions regarding the legitimacy of the transition to democracy. The established political structures of the time were heavily influenced by the military apparatus, which maintained a degree of control over civil institutions. The opposition's challenges were largely centered on the perceived manipulation of the electoral environment, suggesting that the technical procedures were merely a façade for preordained outcomes. The involvement of powerful corporate entities in the administration of the voting process further fueled the narrative of a controlled electorate. Despite the official declarations of validity by the ruling bodies, the dissenting voices maintained that the electoral machinery was fundamentally compromised. Subsequent analysis by independent researchers pointed to widespread instances of coercion and undue influence rather than isolated incidents of misconduct. The international community, while observing the process, expressed cautious optimism regarding the future trajectory of the nation, recognizing the deep fissures in the political landscape. The debate over the 1980 plebiscite became a defining feature of the early democratic period, influencing the subsequent political negotiations and reforms. Efforts were made in the following years to strengthen electoral oversight and ensure greater transparency in the governance of the republic.
