The project stimulated retail and residential development along the loop, but has been criticized for its adverse effects on some Black communities. In 2013, the project received a federal grant of $18 million to develop the southwest corridor. In September 2019 the James M. Cox Foundation gave $6 Million to the PATH Foundation which will connect the Silver Comet Trail to The Atlanta BeltLine which is expected to be completed by 2022. Upon completion, the total combined interconnected trail distance around Atlanta for The Atlanta BeltLine and Silver Comet Trail will be the longest paved trail surface in the U.S. totaling about . Atlanta's cultural offerings expanded during the 2000s: the High Museum of Art doubled in size; the Alliance Theatre won a Tony Award; and art galleries were established on the once-industrial Westside. The College Football Hall of Fame relocated to Atlanta and the National Center for Civil and Human Rights museum was constructed. The city of Atlanta was the subject of a massive cyberattack which began in March 2018. In December 2019, Atlanta hosted the Miss Universe 2019 pageant competition. On June 16, 2022, Atlanta was selected as a host city for the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Geography Atlanta encompasses , of which is land and is water. The city is situated in the Deep South of the southeastern United States among the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains. At above mean sea level, Atlanta has the highest elevation among major cities east of the Mississippi River. Atlanta straddles the Eastern Continental Divide. Rainwater that falls on the south and east side of the divide flows into the Atlantic Ocean, while rainwater on the north and west side of the divide flows into the Gulf of Mexico. Atlanta developed on a ridge south of the Chattahoochee River, which is part of the ACF River Basin. The river borders the far northwestern edge of the city, and much of its natural habitat has been preserved, in part by the Chattahoochee River National Recreation Area. Atlanta is 21 miles (33 km) southeast of Marietta, 27 miles (43 km) southwest of Alpharetta, 146 miles (234 km) southwest of Greenville, South Carolina, 147 miles (236 km) east of Birmingham, Alabama, and 245 miles (394 km) southwest of Charlotte, North Carolina. Its urban geography is characterized by a dense mix of historic neighborhoods and rapidly expanding suburban areas that radiate outward from the central business district. The city's infrastructure has undergone significant transformation, adapting to demographic shifts and economic growth since the mid-twentieth century. Transportation networks, including a complex system of highways and MARTA rail lines, attempt to manage the flow of commuters into and through the metropolitan area. The climate is humid subtropical, featuring hot, humid summers and mild winters, which influences both architectural styles and outdoor recreational opportunities. Topographically, the surrounding Piedmont plateau provides a gradual transition from the rolling hills of the foothills to the flatter terrain of the surrounding plains. This geological setting has historically influenced settlement patterns, with early development often clustering near reliable water sources and defensible high ground. The presence of the Chattahoochee River system is not merely geographical but is central to the city's environmental planning and public health initiatives. Water quality management remains a continuous civic concern due to the high population density. Economically, Atlanta functions as a major hub for logistics, technology, and media, often referred to as a gateway to the Southeast. The rise of the BeltLine represents a modern effort to integrate transportation corridors with recreational use, reflecting a trend seen in many older American cities seeking to revitalize former industrial or transit-dominated spaces. This revitalization effort has brought complex issues of gentrification and equitable access to public amenities to the forefront of municipal discourse. The interplay between preservation efforts, such as those protecting the Chattahoochee River National Recreation Area, and the pressures of modern urban expansion defines much of the contemporary planning debate within the municipal boundaries.

Woolworths opened the first supermarket in Hastings in 1965. Woolworths acquired the Self Help grocery chain in the early 1970s and began to rebrand these as Woolworths in 1973. Nathan, the owner of the Super Value supermarket chain, purchased Woolworths for $12 million in 1979. Nathan acquired 70 McKenzies general merchandise stores in 1980, rebranding the stores as Woolworths. The general merchandise stores were rebranded as DEKA in 1988. Nathan established the discount supermarket chain Price Chopper in 1987, and the Big Fresh supermarket chain in 1988. Dairy Farm International (1990–2002) In 1990, Hong Kong's Dairy Farm International acquired the Woolworths New Zealand business, consisting of Woolworths, Price Chopper and Big Fresh chains. Woolworths launched New Zealand's first online supermarket in 1996. Between 1990 and 2000, Woolworths trialled a network of min-supermarkets in BP petrol stations. In 2001, Woolworths began operating mini-supermarkets at 17 Gull New Zealand stores. By 2002, Woolworths New Zealand consisted of 83 supermarkets branded as Woolworths, Big Fresh and Price Chopper. It was the country's third-largest supermarket group, with a market share of about 20%. Progressive Enterprises (2002–2005) Progressive Enterprises, the owner of Foodtown, Countdown, SuperValue and FreshChoice, made a bid to purchase Woolworths New Zealand in May 2001. The merger application was cleared by the Commerce Commission but then withdrawn following court action by rival Foodstuffs. Progressive made another application for the merger in October 2001. The Commerce Commission declined the application in December 2001. Australia's Woolworths Group also expressed interest in acquiring the company. In April 2002, Progressive convinced the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council to uphold the Commerce Commission's clearance of the original merger application. Dairy Farm International agreed to the sale, and the merger proceeded later in 2002. In 2003, there were 59 full-format Woolworths stores, including 17 in Auckland. The subsequent years saw further consolidation and strategic adjustments within the retail landscape of New Zealand. Woolworths continued to refine its store formats, balancing the presence of large-format supermarkets with smaller, convenience-oriented outlets. The introduction of advanced inventory management systems aimed to improve supply chain efficiency and reduce operational costs across the various banners. Competitive pressures from established rivals necessitated continuous innovation in pricing strategies and product assortment. Recognizing shifts in consumer behavior towards digital purchasing, the online retail arm saw increased investment in platform development and logistical infrastructure. Big Fresh, in particular, was positioned to cater to a segment of the market demanding higher quality and gourmet selections. Price Chopper maintained its focus on value, appealing to budget-conscious shoppers. The integration of the acquired chains under the Dairy Farm umbrella allowed for the standardization of certain back-office functions while permitting local adaptation of merchandising and marketing efforts. This structure allowed the group to respond more flexibly to regional economic fluctuations. The expansion of the convenience store network, initially tested in petrol stations, proved to be a viable avenue for capturing incidental retail spending. Furthermore, the group explored partnerships with local producers to enhance the provenance and appeal of their fresh produce offerings. These efforts were designed to solidify Woolworths' position as a dominant force in the nation's grocery sector, challenging the entrenched market power of Foodstuffs.

USS Muskogee (PF-49), a in commission from 1944 to 1945, thus far has been the only ship of the United States Navy to be named for Muskogee, Oklahoma. She later served in the Soviet Navy as EK-19 and in the Republic of Korea Navy as ROKS Dumon (PF-61). Construction and commissioning Originally classified as a patrol gunboat, PG-157, Muskogee was reclassified as a patrol frigate, PF-49, on 15 April 1943. She was laid down on 18 September 1943, by Consolidated Steel Corporation at Wilmington, California, launched on 18 October 1943, sponsored by Mrs. Hudson, wife of the mayor of Muskogee, and commissioned on 16 March 1944. Service history US Navy, World War II, 1944-1945 After training and exercises off the California coast, Muskogee, manned by a United States Coast Guard crew, departed San Pedro, California, on 18 June 1944, for Nouméa, New Caledonia, where she arrived on 18 July 1944, for patrol and escort duty from Nouméa and, after its capture, Humboldt Bay, New Guinea. Anti-submarine patrol and screening for ships operating around New Guinea were her primary duties into October 1944. On 18 October 1944 she got underway screening the second reinforcement group bound for newly invaded Leyte in the Philippine Islands, arriving in San Pedro Bay on 24 October to screen transports and supply ships under numerous Japanese air attacks while waiting for a group of empty tank landing shipss to form up for the return passage. As her convoy retired on 26 October 1944, Japanese aircraft again attacked it, and Muskogee joined in downing several enemy aircraft. A second escort voyage to Leyte in early November 1944 was less eventful. Concluding her New Guinea patrols, Muskogee arrived in Pearl Harbor, Territory of Hawaii, on 15 December 1944, then reported at Dutch Harbor, Territory of Alaska, on 12 January 1945 for similar duty in the Aleutian Islands. Selected for transfer to the Soviet Navy in Project Hula – a secret program for the transfer of U.S. Vessel transfer The transfer of USS Muskogee to the Soviet Navy was part of a larger Lend-Lease arrangement that involved the movement of several U.S. Navy vessels to aid the Soviet war effort against Nazi Germany. Following her service in the Pacific Theater, the ship underwent necessary modifications and documentation changes to suit its new operational environment and designation within the Soviet fleet. She was renamed and assigned the hull classification symbol EK-19, reflecting her integration into the Soviet maritime structure. Subsequent to this exchange, the ship eventually passed into the service of the Republic of Korea Navy, where she was designated ROKS Dumon, receiving the hull classification symbol PF-61. This later service reflected a continuation of the global naval support structure following the conclusion of the major hostilities in the Pacific. Her service in the Republic of Korea Navy coincided with ongoing regional security concerns and stabilization efforts in East Asia after the cessation of hostilities. The vessels involved in these international transfers represented a complex logistical and diplomatic effort by the United States government during the latter stages of the Second World War.

Some of the water falls are Rongbangdare, Pelgadare, Gandrak Falls etc. Some of the streams are Rangolwari, Nokmawari, Ganol, and Dachima. Geography and climate Tura is located at . It has an average elevation of 349 metres (1145 feet). Its climate is a Humid Subtropical climate (Köppen climate classification: Cwa). Demographics The population of Tura Town is 74,858 according to the 2011 census. The indigenous Garo people form the majority of Tura's population. The population of Garo people in the town is 54,750, making up 73% of the city population. As of the 2011 Census of India, Tura had a population of 58,391. Males constitute 51% of the population and females 49%. Tura has an average literacy rate of 70%, higher than the national average of 56%: male literacy is 70%, and female literacy is 67%. In Tura, 14% of the population is under 6 years of age. Language Garo is Spoken by 54,575 people, Bengali by 12,113, Hindi by 3,563, Nepali by 1,609 and 11,911 people speaks other languages. Connectivity Tura is situated in the western part of Meghalaya which is quite close to the National Border of Bangladesh. The main mode of transport is by road, as there are no railways or any scheduled flights from nearby Baljek Airport. From Guwahati, it is 220 km, through the National Highway 217(Old NH 51). Day time Sumo and overnight bus services are available from Guwahati. There is a 3-days-a-week helicopter service available from Guwahati and Shillong, run by Pawan Hans. Society Main Residents of Tura are the Garo tribe (Native People). Christianity is the main religion, Almost 100% of the Garos are Christians. There are different Christian denominations like Baptist, Catholic, Seventh Day Adventist, Church of Jesus Christ (COJC), Christian Revival Church (CRC) etc. The Garos have a matrilineal society. Transport The nearest airport is Guwahati Airport (GAU). Although Tura has its own airport named Baljek airport situated approx. 30 km from the town but it is yet to be functional. Local administration is managed by the Tura Municipal Council, which oversees various civic amenities and local governance within the town limits. The economy of Tura relies significantly on agriculture, supplemented by trade and government employment. Rice cultivation is a primary agricultural activity in the surrounding areas, along with the growing of various vegetables and other cash crops suited to the region's climate. The proximity to the Bangladesh border also influences local commerce, facilitating cross-border trade to some extent. Tourism is an emerging sector, largely driven by the natural beauty of the area, including the waterfalls and surrounding hills, although infrastructure development in this area is still ongoing to support a larger influx of visitors. Educational institutions in Tura range from primary schools to higher secondary schools, serving the local community. Several colleges and vocational training centers cater to the educational needs of the younger generation, reflecting the moderate literacy levels reported. Healthcare facilities are present within the town, including primary health centers and some private clinics, though access to specialized medical care may necessitate travel to larger urban centers like Guwahati. The socio-cultural life of Tura is deeply intertwined with Garo traditions, despite the widespread adoption of Christianity. Festivals and cultural events often serve as focal points for community gathering and the preservation of local heritage. The matrilineal system, where lineage and inheritance are traced through the female line, remains a defining cultural characteristic of the Garo community in the region.

After the steam locomotives departed, the main shed at Gateshead was converted into a five-road straight shed, in which various diesels were stored and maintained. The conversion drastically altered the depot, as coaling stages and similar steam engine infrastructure gave way to diesel-related infrastructure, such as fuel tanks. One exception was one of the two water towers, which would remain until closure. Unlike its counterpart which vanished with the steam locomotives, and consisted of a tank on top of its own substantial brick structure in the yard to the South of the shed itself, this sat on the roof at the northwestern corner of the building and thus would have presented no obstruction to any reorganisation of the external trackwork. . Sub-Sheds in BR steam days Gateshead had several sub-sheds, some of which had sub-sheds of their own. When Sunderland (which was formerly 54A) became a sub-shed of Gateshead, it, along with its own sub-sheds, received new codes with Gateshead's 52 prefix. 52B Heaton This shed was allocated similar types of east coast main line (ECML) locomotives as Gateshead. Heaton had (and still has) extensive carriage sidings. It would also encompass South Gosforth Car Sheds, where the Tyneside electric stock was stabled, including the NER Class ES1 shunting locomotives for the steeply graded Quayside Branch. Heaton and South Gosforth are the only surviving former sub-sheds of Gateshead; all of the others listed here are now closed. Heaton carriage sidings' ability to accommodate the fixed rakes of carriages, power unit and driving van trailer of an HST played a major role in the decision to close Gateshead, whose cramped location between Askew Road and the Tyne offered limited scope for expansion. This was effectively the same reason that Darlington replaced Gateshead as the location of the NER's main works. 52C Blaydon Which, by 1955, also included Hexham and Alston. 52D Tweedmouth The northernmost extent of Gateshead's control, which included the shed at Alnmouth. 52E Percy Main Allocated locomotives for use on the former Blyth & Tyne lines in South-East Northumberland. 52F North and South Blyth Allocated locomotives mainly for use on the heavy mineral traffic in the Northumberland coalfield, North Blyth was at Cambois, and was later replaced by an entirely new diesel depot (Blyth Cambois TMD). The new depot closed in 1994. 52G Sunderland (54A until 1958) - last MPD in the region with an allocation of steam locomotives, with the last examples leaving in 1967. The operational evolution of these numerous depots reflected the broader changes occurring across British Railways as motive power shifted from steam to diesel and electric traction. The varied roles assigned to these sheds, ranging from mainline locomotive storage to the specialized stabling of electric multiple units and heavy mineral haulage units, illustrate the logistical complexity of operating the extensive routes serviced by the former North Eastern Railway network. The relocation and eventual closure of many of these smaller units signaled a rationalization of railway assets, favoring larger, more centralized facilities capable of handling modern rolling stock and maintenance requirements efficiently. The continued use of Heaton to accommodate the High Speed Train (HST) sets underscores the enduring utility of certain locations despite the decommissioning of older infrastructure. The preservation of the water tower at the Gateshead main shed, despite the obsolescence of steam operations, serves as a tangible remnant of the depot's earlier incarnation. The integration of former subsidiaries into the Gateshead coding scheme, such as Sunderland, demonstrates a hierarchical reorganization of operational control within the regional railway structure during the period of transition. The closure of the Blyth Cambois TMD marks another instance where localized, specialized infrastructure was replaced by modern, integrated depot complexes designed for the contemporary operational landscape.

Slesse Mountain, usually referred to as Mount Slesse, is a mountain just north of the US-Canada border, in the Cascade Mountains of British Columbia, near the town of Chilliwack. It is notable for its large, steep local relief. For example, its west face drops over to Slesse Creek in less than . It is also famous for its huge Northeast Buttress; see the climbing notes below. The name means "fang" in the Halkomelem language. Notable nearby mountains include Mount Rexford and Canadian Border Peak in British Columbia, and American Border Peak, Mount Shuksan, and Mount Baker, all in the US state of Washington. Geology Most of Mount Slesse is made up of granitic rocks related to the Chilliwack batholith, which intruded the region 26 to 29 million years ago after the major orogenic episodes in the region. This is part of the Pemberton Volcanic Belt, an eroded volcanic belt that formed as a result of subduction of the Farallon Plate starting 29 million years ago. The primary rock comprising Slesse is grey diorite from the batholith. However the summit ridge and the west face are composed of Darrington Phyllite, a metamorphic rock, produced by contact metamorphism with the rock of the batholith and with an intrusion of granodiorite. History Mount Slesse was first climbed on August 10, 1927, by Stan Henderson, Mills Winram, and Fred Parkes, via a route starting from Slesse Creek. The standard route today is the Southwest Route, which involves approximately of ascent, a good deal of scrambling and some sections of technical rock climbing up to class 5.6. However Slesse is most famous for the Northeast Buttress, first climbed on August 28, 1963 by Fred Beckey, Steve Marts, and Eric Bjornstad. It is a serious multi-day rock climb (Grade V) with technical difficulty of class 5.8 or 5.9. This climb is featured in Roper and Steck's Fifty Classic Climbs of North America. In July 1966 Hans Baer and Jack Bryan did the second ascent of this route, with one bivouac and a straightline exit at the top of the buttress. Climbers come to the Fraser Valley from around the world to climb the aesthetic 24 pitch granite spire, making it one of the most iconic climbs in North America. The surrounding topography features numerous smaller peaks and ridges, which contribute to the rugged and complex nature of the mountain massif. The area has seen significant geological and glacial activity over millions of years, influencing the current landscape. Glacial erosion has carved out U-shaped valleys and deposited moraines in the lower reaches of the mountain system. The presence of granitic intrusions indicates a period of significant magmatic activity within the continental crust. The weathering of these hard igneous and metamorphic rocks results in a characteristic alpine scree and talus slope accumulation at various elevations. The parkland and subalpine zones at the base contrast sharply with the barren, exposed rock faces near the summit. These ecological gradients are directly linked to elevation and the underlying geological substrate. Human interaction with Mount Slesse has evolved from early exploratory mountaineering to highly specialized technical climbing endeavors. The routes on the buttress require significant logistical planning, including approach travel, camping arrangements, and specialized climbing gear. Conservation efforts in the surrounding areas focus on preserving the unique high-altitude ecosystems and the geological integrity of the massif. The dramatic visual contrast between the dark, weathered diorite and the lighter, often fractured phyllite contributes significantly to its aesthetic appeal for both climbers and naturalists.

In terms of national politics, the city is part of Fukushima Electoral District 4 for the lower house of the Diet of Japan. Economy Aizuwakamatsu is a local commercial center. The area is traditionally noted for sake brewing and lacquerware. Modern industries include textiles, wood processing and electronics. Education Aizuwakamatsu has one prefectural university and a private junior college. The city has 19 public elementary school and 11 public junior high schools operated by the city government. In addition, there is one private elementary school and one private junior high school. The Fukushima Prefectural Board of Education operates five public high schools and one combined junior/senior high school. The prefecture also operates two special education schools. Universities and colleges University of Aizu Junior College of Aizu Senior high schools Public (prefectural) Aizu High School (会津高等学校) Aoi High School (葵高等学校) Aizu Gakuhō High School (会津学鳳高等学校) Wakamatsu Shōgyō High School (若松商業高等学校) Aizu Kōgyō High School (若松工業高等学校) Aizu Second High School (会津第二高等学校) Private Aizuwakamatsu Xaverio Gakuen High School (会津若松ザベリオ学園高等学校) Wakamatsu 1st High School (若松第一高等学校) Jinai High School (仁愛高等学校) Junior high schools Public (municipal) Aizuwakamatsu First Junior High School (会津若松市立第一中学校) Aizuwakamatsu Second Junior High School (会津若松市立第二中学校) Aizuwakamatsu Third Junior High School (会津若松市立第三中学校) Aizuwakamatsu Fourth Junior High School (会津若松市立第四中学校) Aizuwakamatsu Fifth Junior High School (会津若松市立第五中学校) Aizuwakamatsu Sixth Junior High School (会津若松市立第六中学校) Ikki Junior High School (一箕中学校) Ōto Junior High School (大戸中学校) Minato Junior High School (湊中学校) Kitaaizu Junior High School (北会津中学校) Kawahigashi Junior High School (河東中学校) Aizu Gakuhō Junior High School (会津学鳳中学校, prefectural) Note: All junior high schools are municipal except for Aizu Gakuhō Junior High School. Transportation The city is served by several railway lines, including the JR Banetsu West Line and local bus networks which connect to neighboring towns and rural areas. Air travel is accessible via nearby regional airports, although the city does not host a major international hub. Major roadways pass through Aizuwakamatsu, facilitating connection to the broader Tohoku region. Infrastructure development has focused on improving connectivity, particularly in response to seismic resilience planning. Healthcare The local medical infrastructure is supported by several general hospitals and clinics. The city's main hospital provides comprehensive care, serving as a regional referral center for specialized medical needs. Numerous smaller clinics offer primary care services across the municipal boundaries, ensuring accessibility for the resident population. Emergency medical services are managed by the municipal fire department, which maintains rapid response capabilities. Cultural Life Aizuwakamatsu maintains a rich cultural heritage, evident in its traditional festivals and historical sites. Notable cultural institutions include local museums dedicated to regional history and craftsmanship, particularly those focusing on lacquerware techniques. The city hosts several local theaters and community centers that support artistic expression. Religious life is characterized by a mix of Buddhist and Shinto traditions, with several ancient temples and shrines being points of local pilgrimage and observance. Tourism is sustained by the intersection of historical preservation and the natural beauty of the surrounding mountains. Local inns and traditional guesthouses cater to visitors interested in experiencing the regional culture firsthand. Environmental Features The geographical setting is characterized by mountainous terrain, which significantly influences local climate patterns and resource availability. The area is part of a broader ecological zone, supporting diverse flora and fauna. Water resources are primarily sourced from local rivers, which are vital for both domestic use and the traditional sake brewing industry. Agricultural land, while less extensive than in purely rural districts, remains important for producing local staples and specialty crops. Recent efforts have been made by municipal planning departments to promote sustainable land use practices, balancing economic activity with ecological preservation. The response to the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and subsequent nuclear events necessitated significant, long-term regional planning regarding land use and disaster preparedness across the entire prefectural region. These planning efforts continue to shape the urban and suburban development trajectory of Aizuwakamatsu.

However, he managed to escape from the prison and moved to German-held General Government. There he hid in Otwock and then in Warsaw, under a variety of false identities. He joined the SZP resistance organization, which was later reformed into the Association of Armed Resistance and in the end into the Home Army. As one of the high-ranking Polish officers who knew the city of Lwów - yet were not known to a wider public prior to the outbreak of World War II, Filipkowski was a perfect candidate for a chief of Polish resistance in that town. In early 1940 he returned there under a false name and started to organize the Polish resistance. Initially under Soviet occupation, he continued his work as a Home Army inspector for the area of the city after the German take-over of the area in 1941. On 1 August 1943 he was made the commander of all Home Army units in the region. In 1944 the units under his command started the Operation Tempest in the area. Filipkowski commanded the Polish forces in the Lwów Uprising, in which the Home Army, with assistance of the advancing Red Army, took control over the city from the Germans. In the same period his wife, Janina née Obiedzińska and one of his two sons Jan (b. 1922) were active members of the Home Army in Masovia. The latter was killed in the final days of the Warsaw Uprising. Soon after the German forces were pushed out of the city, Filipkowski was invited to a conference with Michał Rola-Żymierski and arrested by the Soviet NKVD in Zhytomir on 3 August 1944; at the same time most of his soldiers were also arrested and sent to Soviet prisons - or had to flee back to German-held part of Poland. Filipkowski was held in a number of Soviet prisons, including the prison in Kiev, a Smersh camp of the 1st Ukrainian Front, and NKVD camps in Kharkov, Ryazan, Dyagilev, Gryazovets and Brest. In November 1947 he was handed over to the Ministry of Public Security of Poland in Biała Podlaska, interrogated and set free. However, soon afterwards his younger son Andrzej (b. 1925), also a former soldier of the Home Army, was arrested by the Communists and was held in prisons until the destalinization thaw of 1956. His subsequent life was marked by a period of relative obscurity and political tension within the emerging Polish state. The political climate of the early Polish People's Republic made the activities of former resistance members, particularly those with deep connections to the pre-war military establishment, highly scrutinized by the communist security apparatus. Filipkowski navigated this treacherous landscape, attempting to maintain a low profile while remaining cognizant of the lingering political complexities of the post-war period. The relationship between the former insurgents and the new government was fraught with suspicion, as the regime sought to consolidate its power and eliminate any vestiges of competing authority. Despite his survival through the immediate post-war purges, the lingering shadow of Soviet influence and domestic political maneuvering continued to affect him and his family. The fate of his son Andrzej serves as a stark illustration of the pervasive repression directed at those associated with the anti-communist resistance movement. Andrzej's prolonged detention reflects the communist authorities' determination to neutralize opposition elements regardless of their past contributions to the national struggle. The period leading up to the destalinization thaw saw a general tightening of control over perceived dissent, making the plight of former Home Army members particularly precarious. His eventual release in 1956 coincided with a broader, albeit incomplete, relaxation of political restrictions across the Eastern Bloc. Following this period, Filipkowski devoted himself to private life, though the experiences of war, resistance, and political imprisonment undoubtedly shaped his later years. He remained a figure connected to the memory of the pre-war Polish military tradition, a tradition that the communist state actively sought to discredit or co-opt. The legacy of his service in the Home Army represents a significant chapter in the narrative of Polish wartime resistance against Nazi occupation, an effort that intersected with the geopolitical machinations of the Soviet Union.

Agriculture, though less dominant than in previous decades, maintains a presence, primarily involving the cultivation of vineyards and other horticultural products which align with the symbolism found in the municipal crest. The proximity to Lake Thun and the surrounding alpine landscape provides a significant base for the tourism industry, which employs a notable portion of the workforce, particularly during the warmer months. Service industries, including retail, hospitality, and local administrative functions, form the core of the daily economic activity. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) constitute the majority of the businesses operating within the municipality. Infrastructure development has focused on enhancing accessibility to the region, particularly improving road connections to larger cantonal centers and maintaining the quality of local public transport links. The municipality actively participates in regional planning initiatives aimed at sustainable development, balancing the need for economic growth with the preservation of the local natural heritage and cultural landscape. Energy consumption patterns show a steady trend towards greater efficiency, with municipal efforts promoting renewable energy sources such as solar and small-scale hydroelectric power where feasible. Water management is a critical local concern, given the dependence on the lake and surrounding catchment areas. Educational provisions cater to the needs of the resident population, with primary and secondary schooling options available within or in close proximity to the municipality. Local community life is vibrant, supported by various cultural institutions and recreational facilities that benefit from the area’s natural beauty. These communal spaces play a vital role in maintaining social cohesion among the diverse resident population. Furthermore, the municipality has implemented several local policies aimed at encouraging family formation and supporting the needs of its aging demographic, recognizing the increasing proportion of seniors in the community structure. Housing policy endeavors to manage the balance between maintaining affordable local residences and accommodating the influx of residents drawn by the region’s attractive quality of life.

Athens had to pay tribute to Crete as a term of ending the war – once every seven years seven Athenian youths and seven Athenian maidens had to be sent to Crete to be devoured by the Minotaur, a half-man, half-bull monster that lurked in a labyrinth from which escape was all but impossible. The human sacrifice of Athenians can only be ended by a hero slaying the Minotaur and defeating the Cretan warrior Tauride. The Athenian hero Teseo is on the way to Crete, resolved to do this and end his peoples' suffering, and to join with Arianna, whom he loves, and whom Minos has demanded as a hostage to ensure that the Athenian young people will be sent for sacrifice. Act 1 The Athenians embark in Crete, alongside a stone tablet with the terms of the Athenian tribute inscribed on it. King Minos agrees to Teseo's request that Arianna be freed. Among the Athenian maidens sent to be sacrificed is Carilda, whose beauty is noticed by the Cretan champion Tauride; he instantly falls in love with her. Carilda is however secretly in love with Teseo and is interested in neither Tauride or the Athenian youth Alceste, who is also in love with Carilda. Teseo tells his beloved Arianna that he is determined to slay the Minotaur, making her fear for his safety, and also tells Alceste, who wants to rescue Carilda from a cruel death, that he is more fitted for the task. In the temple of Jupiter, King Minos orders Alceste to draw the name of the first victim from an urn. Alceste is distressed when the name he draws from the vessel is that of his beloved Carilda. Teseo offers to go into the labyrinth to meet the Minotaur in her place, which Minos accepts, but makes Arianna jealous, believing Teseo must be doing this out of love for Carilda. Act 2 In a wood, Teseo ponders whether he should continue with his plan to try to kill the Minotaur, or refrain out of consideration to his beloved Arianna. He falls asleep, and has a vision of his destiny as the liberator of his people from cruel suffering. When he awakes, all indecision has been removed from his mind – he is determined to kill the monster. Alceste, like Arianna, is concerned that Teseo is acting out of love for Carilda, but Teseo assures him that he will never love anyone but Arianna and reveals to Alceste that Arianna is really the daughter of King Minos, but neither she nor the King know it. Teseo then seeks the aid of Arianna to help him devise a strategy to navigate the labyrinth and vanquish the monstrous creature. Arianna, realizing the true danger and the gravity of Teseo's quest, uses her intelligence and knowledge of the labyrinth’s structure to aid her beloved. She provides him with a thread, a simple yet ingenious tool that allows him to trace his path within the bewildering maze, ensuring his return to the surface world. The Cretan champion Tauride, having found a deeper connection with Carilda, begins to perceive the complexities of the situation, recognizing the underlying conflict between his duty and his burgeoning affection for the Athenian maiden. The narrative then shifts focus as Teseo approaches the labyrinth's entrance, the tension mounting with each step toward the beast that has haunted Athens for generations. His courage is tempered by the weight of his promise to his city and the hope of securing freedom for all Athenians. The threads of fate intertwine, bringing together the threads of love, duty, and the relentless pursuit of an end to ancient brutality. The very existence of the labyrinth itself symbolizes the inescapable nature of their predicament, a perfect metaphor for the complex entanglements of their lives and loyalties.

These resources illustrate the varied approaches to documenting and teaching the Bambara language, ranging from comprehensive academic grammars and specialized lexicons to interactive online platforms and community-driven translation databases. The availability of digital corpora, such as the Corpus Bambara de Référence, is particularly significant for linguistic study, enabling researchers to analyze authentic language use across vast quantities of text. Furthermore, the proliferation of mobile-friendly applications demonstrates a growing trend toward democratizing language acquisition, making resources accessible to learners regardless of geographical location or access to traditional academic libraries. The inclusion of multiple language pairings—English-Bambara, Bambara-French, and even Jula—in some digital tools reflects the multilingual reality of West African communication and the practical needs of modern learners and diplomats. The development of dedicated learning materials, including conversation guides and illustrated readers, caters to different proficiency levels, from complete beginners requiring foundational structures to intermediate learners seeking immersion through authentic textual exposure. The collaborative nature of projects like Maliyiri.com underscores the role of global online communities in preserving and disseminating linguistic knowledge, supplementing formal scholarly publications. The distinction between curated academic texts and dynamic, crowd-sourced online lexicons highlights a dual ecosystem for Bambara language study, where rigorous linguistic documentation coexists with rapidly evolving, user-generated resources. These diverse materials collectively support linguistic documentation efforts, pedagogical instruction, and the broader revitalization and promotion of the Bambara language in contemporary contexts.

In 1949, he moved into the ground floor of the 17th century Hôtel Lambert on the Île Saint-Louis in Paris and restored the building and its décor. He was influenced by such interior decorators as Georges Geffroy and Victor Grandpierre. Redé had become an "important influence in Paris society" by the early 1950s with his luncheons and dinners at the Hotel Lambert, which were known for their decor, luxury, and food. Well-known in Parisian high-society, Nancy Mitford called him "La Pompadour de nos jours." Redé was described as "the Eugène de Rastignac of modern Paris" by Sir Henry 'Chips' Channon and as "the best host in all Europe"; his parties were the center of le tout-Paris. Philippe Jullian described the world of Lopez-Willshaw and Redé as akin to a small 18th-century court. Members of the circle included the poet and patron of the Surrealists, Marie-Laure de Noailles (1902–70); musicians such as Henri Sauguet, Georges Auric, and Francis Poulenc; and the artist Christian Bérard. A number of his events attracted particular note, and involved designers that would later go on to become well-known. Nina Ricci designed the costumes of Redé and the Lopez-Willshaws for the famous 1951 Bal oriental given by Carlos de Beistegui at his Venetian palace, the Palazzo Labia. In 1956, at Redé's Bal des Têtes, the young Yves Saint Laurent provided many of the headdresses—the Duchess of Windsor being one of the judges—and received a boost to his career. In 1964, Redé was included on the first annual list put out by the National Society of Interior Designers for "individuals who have inspired good design". An event Redé threw at the Hotel Lambert, the Oriental Ball (Bal oriental) in December 1969, saw the hotel turned into a lavish fantasy and has been called an "apotheosis" of Redé's parties. 400 guests were invited. When Diana Vreeland heard of the plans for the event, she promptly contacted Redé and expressed her interest in having the event photographed for Vogue. The guest list was the crème de la crème of international high society. Business and later years As his partner, Redé was closely involved with managing Lopez-Willshaw's financial affairs, which he did "adroitly." In 1962, when Arturo Lopez-Willshaw died, Redé inherited half of his fortune. To manage it, he joined Prince Rupert Loewenstein in taking control of Leopold Joseph & Sons, a bank where he served as the deputy chairman. With Loewenstein, Redé was closely involved in managing the money of the Rolling Stones. Redé was also a founder of Artemis, an investment fund specializing in the purchase of fine art. After Lopez-Wilshaw's death, Rede remained involved in art collection. His patronage extended to various forms of artistic endeavors, although his social prominence remained his most visible pursuit. The Hotel Lambert, under his stewardship, became more than a venue; it functioned as a temporary, exquisitely curated stage upon which the elite of postwar European culture performed their social roles. The gatherings facilitated a unique cross-pollination between the worlds of high fashion, avant-garde art, classical music, and international finance. His ability to assemble such disparate yet equally influential figures speaks to a profound social acumen rather than merely superficial hosting ability. These events provided a crucial nexus where cultural trends were often initiated or solidified before gaining mainstream recognition. The sheer extravagance of the décor and the impeccable quality of the entertainment served as a powerful statement of his status and taste. His influence subtly shaped the trajectory of several careers in the creative industries, offering them exposure to the most discerning patrons. The continuation of his social calendar after the death of his partner saw him navigate the transition from pure social impresario to significant financial player, leveraging his accumulated social capital into substantial business interests. This dual role allowed him to maintain a degree of visibility even as the focus of his life shifted toward more conservative financial management.

After the war, Hanthawaddy entered its golden age whereas its rival Ava gradually went into decline. From the 1420s to the 1530s, Hanthawaddy was the most powerful and prosperous kingdom of all post-Pagan kingdoms. Under a string of especially gifted monarchs—Binnya Ran I, Shin Sawbu, Dhammazedi and Binnya Ran II—the kingdom enjoyed a long golden age, profiting from foreign commerce. Its merchants traded with traders from across the Indian Ocean, filling the king's treasury with gold and silver, silk and spices, and all the other stuff of early modern trade. The kingdom also became a famous centre of Theravada Buddhism. It established strong ties with Ceylon, and encouraged reforms that later spread throughout the country. The powerful kingdom's end came abruptly. Due to the inexperience of King Takayutpi, the kingdom was captured by a smaller kingdom to the north, Kingdom of Toungoo in 1539 led by King Tabinshwehti and his deputy Gen. Toungoo captured the Irrawaddy delta and Pegu in 1538–1539, and Martaban in 1541. The kingdom was briefly revived in 1550 after Tabinshwehti was assassinated. But Bayinnaung quickly defeated the rebellion in 1552. Restored Hanthawaddy (1740–1757) Though Toungoo kings would rule all of Lower Burma well into the mid-18th century, the golden age of Hanthawaddy was fondly remembered by the Mon. In 1740, they rose up against a weak Toungoo Dynasty on its last legs, and succeeded in restoring the fallen Hanthawaddy Kingdom. Supported by the French, the upstart kingdom quickly carved out a space for itself in Lower Burma, and continued its push northward. On 23 March 1752, its forces captured Ava, and ended the 266-year-old Toungoo dynasty. A new dynasty called Konbaung led by King Alaungpaya rose in Upper Burma to challenge the southern forces, and went on to conquer all of Upper Burma by January 1754. After Hanthawaddy's second invasion of Upper Burma failed in May 1754, the kingdom's leadership in self-defeating measures killed off the Toungoo royal family, and persecuted ethnic Burmans in the south, both of which only strengthened Alaungpaya's hand. In 1755, Alaungpaya invaded Lower Burma. This invasion marked the beginning of the final phase of the Burmese civil wars, a protracted period of conflict that reshaped the political landscape of the region. Alaungpaya's campaign against the restored Hanthawaddy state was marked by military prowess and strategic acumen, allowing the Konbaung forces to gradually consolidate control over the peninsula. The ensuing struggles were not merely dynastic power plays but also involved significant shifts in regional trade routes and the balance of power between the various ethnic groups inhabiting the Burmese territories. The Mon population, who had initially fueled the resurgence of Hanthawaddy, found themselves caught between the ambitions of the southern Mon-influenced rulers and the rapidly expanding power of the Burman Konbaung dynasty from the north. This period saw the introduction of new administrative structures and military organization by the Konbaung regime, contrasting sharply with the more decentralized nature of the earlier Mon-dominated polities. The political instability that characterized the mid-18th century set the stage for a more centralized, though often militarized, imperial structure under the Konbaung monarchs. Their successful campaigns against the fragmented powers in the south demonstrated a capacity for sustained military mobilization that had been less evident in the preceding centuries of intermittent regional dominance. This consolidation of power eventually led to a period of relative internal stability, albeit one maintained through rigorous military control and the incorporation of diverse populations into a larger administrative whole.

In 1963 Taranaki regained the Ranfurly Shield once again off Wellington with a win at Athletic Park. Their third tenure would be its most successful one. The first challenge came from Wanganui who were making their second challenge of the season, having lost earlier to Auckland. Wanganui later would suffer a further defeat in 1964. Taranaki lost to Auckland in their last defence in 1965 and would not reclaim the shield again until 1996 when they edged Auckland 42-39. North Harbour lost narrowly in a tight contest before Taranaki was beaten by 20 points against Waikato. Professional era In August 2011 Taranaki defeated Southland 15-12 in Invercargill to begin a fifth tenure of the shield. This ended in October 2012 when Waikato won the last challenge of the season. In 2013 Taranaki RFU assembled a women's professional team although it was later disbanded the following year. They claimed the national title for the first time in their history with a win over Tasman in the 2014 ITM Cup. Referees Taranaki has a proud history of producing top level referees. Brian Duffy was the region's first test match referee and controlled six internationals, including one test between the British and Irish Lions and All Blacks in 1977. Paul Williams followed with his test debut coming in 2017. Cam Stone and Will Johnston are in the National Panel and take charge of domestic competition matches. Richard Kelly featured in the panel for 12 years, including a successful sevens career, where he was the world's most capped sevens referee when he retired in March 2021. He controlled 280 matches over 52 tournaments, including the Gold Coast Commonwealth Games in 2018, 2018 World Rugby 7s World Cup and 2016 Rio Olympics, in which he refereed one semi-final. Other Taranaki referees have been involved in the national scene in the past, these are; Dee Luckin, Darryl Heibner, Chris Pollock, Brian MacDonald, Paul Macfie, Stuart Beissell, Ross Whitmore, Paul Honiss, Russell Hodge and Murray Dombroski. Affiliated clubs There are 29 registered clubs incorporated and secondary schools affiliated with the Taranaki RFU, most of which have teams at both senior and junior levels. The Taranaki Rugby Referees' Association is also an affiliated member of the Taranaki RFU. The structure of the Taranaki Rugby Football Union reflects a deep commitment to both the elite levels of the sport and the foundational development within the province. The breadth of affiliation ensures a pipeline of talent from grassroots participation right through to the senior representative teams. The involvement of secondary schools is particularly significant, as it provides a structured environment for young athletes to develop fundamental skills and an understanding of the culture surrounding rugby union. This early exposure is crucial for maintaining the high standards of play seen at the provincial and national levels. Furthermore, the governance structure allows for close coordination between the various stakeholders, including clubs, schools, and the referees' association. The Taranaki Rugby Referees' Association plays a vital supporting role, ensuring that the officiating quality across all levels of competition remains consistently high and adheres to modern standards of play. This symbiotic relationship between the participating clubs and the governing body is a cornerstone of the region's sporting identity. The financial sustainability of these affiliated entities is often bolstered through local sponsorship and community engagement initiatives driven by the RFU. These efforts help to keep rugby accessible to a broad cross-section of the Taranaki community, reinforcing the sport's role as a unifying cultural force. The continuous investment in infrastructure, both training grounds and administrative capabilities, supports the ambition of the regional teams to compete effectively against more established provincial rivals. The integration of professional structures, while relatively recent, demonstrates the union's adaptability to the evolving landscape of professional rugby in New Zealand.

The group's musical evolution reflects broader shifts within the Korean popular music scene while maintaining a distinct, energetic core. Early in their career, NRG established a reputation for high-octane performances that fused polished pop structures with aggressive electronic undertones. This combination allowed them to appeal to a broad audience, securing them a foundational place in the history of contemporary Korean music. The incorporation of elaborate stagecraft, including the integration of acrobatics, set them apart from many of their contemporaries, turning their concerts into spectacles as much as musical events. The subsequent hiatuses and periods of activity have seen the members engage in various solo projects and collaborations, demonstrating sustained creative output even when the collective unit was not fully operational. The reunion period of 2017 and 2018 was particularly significant as it provided a platform for the members to address the past and reconnect with their fanbase after a substantial period of separation. This comeback effort was notable not only for its commercial success with the album 20th Century but also for its emotional weight, particularly in their public acknowledgements regarding the loss of founding member Kim Hwan-sung. NRG's influence extends beyond mere charting success; their stylistic choices and pioneering integration of performance art into pop music continue to serve as a reference point for subsequent generations of K-pop artists interested in dynamic, theatrically driven musical presentations.

Her first publication, Selections from the Dramas of Goethe and Schiller appeared in 1843. The selections included Goethe's Torquato Tasso and Iphigenia in Tauris, and Schiller's Maid of Orleans. In 1850, she released a volume of translations from Goethe containing the first part of Faust, Egmont, and the two plays of the former volume. The translations are in blank verse. In 1878, she published the second part of Faust; the two parts with Moritz Retzsch's illustrations appeared together in one volume the same year. Miss Swanwick's Faust passed through many editions and was included in Bohn's series of translations from foreign classics. Her English version is accurate and spirited, and is regarded as one of the best in existence. About 1850, Bunsen advised her to try her hand at translating from the Greek, with the result that in 1865 she published a blank-verse translation of the Trilogy of Aeschylus, and in 1873 of the whole of his dramas. The choruses are in rhymed metres. Her translation has passed through many editions and ranks high among English versions. It keeps fairly close to the original. Miss Swanwick did not confine herself to literary work. She took a keen interest in many social issues of the day, especially women's education, and in raising the moral and intellectual tone of the working classes. She was a member of the councils both of Queen's College and Bedford College, London, and was for some time president of the latter. She assisted in the founding of Girton College, Cambridge, and Somerville Hall, Oxford, and in extending the King's College lectures to women. To all these institutions she subscribed liberally. She was associated with Anthony John Mundella and Sir Joshua Girling Fitch in carrying out the provisions of the will of Mrs. Emily Jane Pfeiffer, who left in 1890 large sums of money for the promotion of the higher education of women. She strongly advocated the study of English literature in the universities, and herself lectured privately on the subject to young working men and women. Miss Swanwick's life was thus divided between literary pursuits and active philanthropy. She never sought publicity, but her example and influence had an important and invigorating effect on women's education and on their position in the community. She signed John Stuart Mill's petition to parliament in 1865 for the political enfranchisement of women. Her commitment to progressive ideals extended to broader social reform movements of the Victorian era. She frequently wrote articles for periodicals and journals addressing subjects ranging from temperance to suffrage, demonstrating a commitment to intellectual engagement beyond the realm of pure translation or academic administration. These writings reflected her belief that societal improvement required a confluence of enlightened thought and diligent action among all social strata. Although she maintained a relatively low profile in the press, her intellectual contributions provided substantial ballast to the burgeoning feminist discourse of the time. Her dedication to establishing institutions that provided rigorous education for women mirrored her belief that intellectual equality was the fundamental prerequisite for social equality. The challenges faced by women seeking higher education in the nineteenth century were manifold, encompassing not only institutional resistance but also prevailing cultural biases regarding female intellectual capacity. Swanwick's direct involvement in founding and supporting colleges served as a practical refutation of these limiting assumptions. Furthermore, her advocacy for the study of English literature emphasized the importance of cultural literacy as a key component of a well-rounded and capable citizenry, regardless of gender. Her influence extended beyond the physical structures of the colleges to the very curriculum and the expectations placed upon female scholars. This multifaceted dedication solidified her position not merely as a literary scholar, but as a significant cultural architect of Victorian intellectual life.
