Sliosberg (a Jewish lawyer in Russia) Pavel Milyukov Witnesses who participated in the First Zionist Congress at Basel (1897) Mayer Ebner, Cernauti/Romania (1872–1955) Marcus Ehrenpreis, Stockholm (chief rabbi) David Farbstein, Zurich (1868–1953) Max Bodenheimer, Amsterdam (1865–1940) Franz Sieber (shorthand writer) Hermann Dietrich (shorthand writer) Otto Zoller (editor at the "Basler Nachrichten 1897) Witnesses about Freemasonry Theodor Tobler, Berne (founder of well-known Toblerone) Eduard Welti, Berne Only witness of the defendants Alfred Zander (Swiss frontlist who wrote articles in the "Eiserner Besen"/the iron broom)(1905–1997) Witnesses cited, but not appearing before the court Philip Graves, London (gave written testimony to the judge) , Vienna/Jerusalem (cited, but not able to come) Alberto Meyer, Zurich (author of the incriminated antiSemite article "Schweizermädchen..." in "Der Eidgenosse") Main Court Session, April 29 – May 13, 1935: Three experts In the Main Session 1935 three experts intervened: (1) C. The first expert, Professor Adolf Mercktell, a legal scholar, examined the documentary evidence presented, focusing particularly on the internal consistency and the linguistic characteristics of the document in question. His testimony addressed the methodology employed in the alleged creation of the Protocols, suggesting that the document displayed characteristics more aligned with political satire than with genuine clandestine correspondence. The second expert, Dr. Fritz Stadelmann, a historian specializing in late Imperial Russian political movements, provided context regarding the intense anti-Semitic sentiment prevalent in the Russian Empire during the period cited. Stadelmann discussed the systematic use of scapegoating in state propaganda, noting that the Tsarist regime frequently employed fabricated narratives to justify oppressive measures against Jewish populations. The third expert, Dr. Erwin Weiss, a specialist in comparative religious texts, analyzed the structure and thematic content of the Protocols against known tropes in medieval and modern anti-Jewish polemics. His findings indicated a heavy reliance on established, centuries-old anti-Semitic stereotypes, suggesting that the document might be a compilation rather than a singular, original work of conspiracy. The court proceedings were highly publicized in various European media outlets, attracting considerable attention from both Jewish and non-Jewish intellectuals, as well as various political factions. The presentation of evidence regarding the alleged connection between Jewish interests and global finance received significant scrutiny, with numerous financial experts being consulted by the parties involved to verify the purported claims within the Protocols. The defense's reliance on Alfred Zander was considered weak by many observers, as his writings were viewed by the prosecution as self-serving attempts to bolster a pre-existing anti-Semitic framework rather than objective historical analysis. The sheer number of witnesses presented, many of whom were prominent figures in Zionist or European intellectual circles, lent an air of legitimacy to the proceedings, even if the ultimate conclusions remained contested by various quarters. The final judgment, delivered after weeks of intense deliberation, addressed the credibility of the documentary evidence and the testimony provided by the experts regarding the document's authenticity and origin. The legal conclusion ultimately favored the position that the Protocols were not an authentic record of a Jewish conspiracy, thereby undermining the foundational claims upon which the Nazi ideology had been partially built.

Slayton saves Grifter, but was unable to save Diaz as well, forced to leave him for dead again. When they left the island by helicopter, Lynch contacts his boss, Miles Craven, for an update, but Craven ordered the destruction of Caballito Island, using a special satellite. Grifter blames Backlash for Diaz' apparent death. Despite the island being almost completely destroyed, Bloodmoon and the Kindred would later turn up alive, partly because they had been on parts of the island that weren't hit by Craven's satellite, partly because there were Kindred on nearby islands as well. The Kindred II (2002) Backlash and his friend, Dingo, also a Kindred, are sent to Griffis Air Force base to investigate multiple murders and theft. Dingo quickly concludes that the attackers were Kindred. Grifter catches a news report about the attack on the Air Force base and decides to investigate as well. Grifter and Backlash start arguing and Dingo leaves them alone. As he does, the two are attacked by reptilian Kindred, but saved and taken by mammalian Kindred. The mammalian Kindred reveal the ability to turn into humans (though their eyes are still inhuman) and tell Grifter and Backlash that the reptilian Kindred stole more Gen-serum and neural inhibitors from I.O.-bases, so they could create their own army of Kindred. They also explain that the different Kindred-tribes have started warring and some have moved to different islands: Avian Kindred are isolationists, Reptillians are aggressive and the Mammals are peaceful. Grifter and Backlash help the mammals against the Reptilian, with the Kindred Silver becoming quite attracted to Grifter, much to the amusement of Backlash. During their fight with Reptilian leader Kronos, Grifter is turned into a Kindred as well. Backlash manages to stir Grifter's memory and he turns against Kronos, destroying the devices that allow Kronos to control the other Kindred. Kronos escapes and Grifter's already active Gen-Factor reverts him to human. Taboo and Dingo arrive to take them back and Backlash asks Dingo to stay with the Kindred and give them leadership. At the end Grifter and Backlash end their long-running feud and become friends again. Other appearances of Kindred The Kindred, including Bloodmoon, made various appearances in Backlash's solo-series and one Kindred, Dingo, became a recurrent supporting character. In Backlash's own book, they would team up to confront Uni-Com, a company threatening the Kindred. They also confront Gramalkin, a human-Kindred hybrid who was not in control of his own actions. The conflict between the various Kindred factions intensified following the skirmishes on the islands, leading to increased territorial disputes and covert operations across the archipelago. Avian Kindred, maintaining their self-imposed isolation, occasionally intervened in mainland affairs only when their specific ancestral grounds were threatened. The Mammals, valuing diplomacy and communal living, found themselves increasingly caught between the militaristic Reptilians and the unpredictable nature of the other tribes. Grifter's transformation into a Kindred introduced a volatile new element into the group dynamics, as his struggle with his newfound nature provided a focal point for the tribe's internal tensions. Backlash's role as a mediator became crucial, often requiring him to navigate the treacherous social landscape of the nocturnal society. The growing influence of Uni-Com, a corporate entity with deep ties to illicit genetic research, provided a common external threat that momentarily unified several disparate Kindred groups against a shared commercial and existential danger. Gramalkin's condition, a result of an unstable merging of human and Kindred biology, served as a potent warning about the dangers of unregulated hybridization and uncontrolled genetic alteration. These events solidified the fragile alliances that began to form, suggesting a temporary truce dictated by mutual survival against overwhelming external pressures.

The monument to the battle was constructed in 1951 and in 1971 it was protected as a registered cultural heritage site. After the integration of the region under the central government rule in the late 1990s the monument to the battle was devastated in 1999 and 2000. The municipality initiated reconstruction efforts in 2002 and the work was not completed until 2013 when the Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Croatia provided funds for this purpose. The monument is allegedly target of intentional desecration with illegal waste disposal. Modern day Municipality of Jagodnjak was established in 1998 with the support of the United Nations representatives in the final stage of the UNTAES transitional administration over the region of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Syrmia. It was created in order to ensure adequate Serb local self-government through the creation of municipalities in Eastern Slavonia in which the group constitute ethnic majority. Today Jagodnjak is only municipality in Croatian part of Baranya with an ethnic Serb majority. Together with other municipalities with Serb majority in Eastern Croatia it constitutes the Joint Council of Municipalities. Demographics Population There are 2,537 inhabitants in the municipality (2001 census), including: Serbs (64.72%) Croats (26.65%) Hungarians (2.88%) Romani (1.18%) Before World War II there was a substantial Danube Swabian minority here but they were all expelled by the Communist regime of Josip Broz Tito after 1945. Languages Due to the local minority population, the Jagodnjak municipality prescribe the use of not only Croatian as the official language, but the Serbian language and Serbian Cyrillic alphabet as well. Religion Politics Joint Council of Municipalities The Municipality of Jagodnjak is one of seven Serb majority member municipalities within the Joint Council of Municipalities, inter-municipal sui generis organization of ethnic Serb community in eastern Croatia established on the basis of Erdut Agreement. As Serb community constitute majority of the population of the municipality it is represented by 2 delegated Councillors at the Assembly of the Joint Council of Municipalities, double the number of Councilors to the number from Serb minority municipalities in Eastern Croatia. Minority councils Directly elected minority councils and representatives are tasked with consulting tasks for the local or regional authorities in which they are advocating for minority rights and interests, integration into public life and participation in the management of local affairs. The cultural landscape of Jagodnjak reflects the complex historical and ethnic dynamics of the region. The persistence of distinct cultural practices alongside official state mandates illustrates the ongoing negotiation between national identity and local communal heritage. Economic activities within the municipality are primarily centered on agriculture, capitalizing on the fertile lands along the Danube River. Traditional farming methods remain prevalent, although modernization efforts are gradually being adopted to improve yields and market access. Tourism, though nascent, represents a growing potential sector, capitalizing on the area's natural beauty and historical sites, provided that infrastructure development continues to keep pace with regional growth. Infrastructure challenges, particularly concerning road maintenance and utility provision in more remote settlements, remain a persistent concern for local administration. The Joint Council of Municipalities serves not only as a political body but also as a vital conduit for regional development initiatives, coordinating efforts that transcend the administrative boundaries of individual municipalities. These cooperative structures are crucial for addressing shared socioeconomic issues that individual smaller entities might struggle to resolve independently. Further integration into broader Croatian economic frameworks is a subject of continuous deliberation within the Council.

Each of the Gnessin sisters had studied piano and graduated with distinction from the Moscow Conservatory. Construction of the modern building began in 1937, interrupted during the war and resumed in 1943. The main part of the academy was built in 1946. The college quickly became, and remains, an elite music school, considered second only to the Moscow Conservatory. Founders The Gnessin sisters were born in Rostov-on-Don, the children of Rostov Rabbi Fabian Osipovich Gnessin. The entire family appears to have possessed musical talent. Their brother, Mikhail Fabianovich Gnessin, was a celebrated composer and teacher who later served (1945–1957) as head of Gnessin State Musical College. He was influenced by Taoists, Laozi and Zhuangzi, and although we are told he enjoyed Lao Tzu’s Daodejing (Tao-te ching, Dotokyu-kyo), he was overjoyed when he discovered the Vimalakirti Sutra. This encounter transformed his life and he became a Buddhist. He was known as being among the ablest of the disciples of Kumārajīva. Sengzhao was recognized as both a scholar of high skill and someone of profound understanding relating to religious matters. He was involved in translating Indian treatises, which formed the only source of study for early Chinese Mādhyamika Buddhism. He also authored a small number of texts, but is famous for the book Zhaolun. Its chapters are as follows: Things Do Not Shift, Non-Absolute Emptiness, Prajna Is Without Dichotomizing Knowledge, and Nirvana Is Without Conceptualization. He is mentioned in the Memoirs of Eminent Monks. Sengzhao criticized earlier Chinese Buddhist schools for believing in being or non-being. He concluded that all dharmas are empty. Contribution He composed a series of treatises published under the title Chao Lun or Zhao Lun, which was first translated (1948) into English as The Book of Chao by Walter Liebenthal, and later (1968) republished in a revised edition with the revised title of Chao Lun, the Treatises of Seng-chao. . Later References A number of other accounts exist concerning the life of Sengzhao, though they rarely shed any new light on his work or activities. The Weishou accords Sengzhao preeminence among the eight hundred or so scholars gathered at Chang’an: “Daorong and his fellows were of knowledge and learning all-pervasive, and Sengzhao was the greatest of them. When Kumrajva made a translation, Sengzhao would always take pen in hand and define the meanings of words. He annotated the Vimalakrtinirdesha Stra and also published several treatises. They all have subtle meaning, and scholars venerate them.” (Hurvitz 54) While adding nothing substantively new, this version highlights Sengzhao's importance as a liaison between the Indian Kumarajiva and the Chinese language. All indications point to the foreign master's reliance on Sengzhao's ability to “translate” the Indian terminology into stylistically acceptable Chinese. His role extended beyond mere linguistic mediation; he was an intellectual conduit through which complex Indian philosophical concepts were rendered intelligible within the burgeoning Chinese scholastic landscape. The Mādhyamika doctrine, characterized by its radical critique of inherent existence, required a nuanced vocabulary and conceptual framework that native Chinese Buddhist terminology struggled to accommodate fully. Sengzhao’s interpretive skill allowed for a bridging of these metaphysical gulfs. The emphasis on emptiness, or shunyata, was not presented as a simple denial of reality, but rather as the absence of self-nature or fixed essence within phenomena, a subtlety that his commentaries helped to preserve and propagate. This doctrinal rigor positioned his work at the forefront of early Chinese Mahayana thought, setting a high standard for subsequent scholastic endeavors. His critiques of earlier dogmatic assertions regarding ultimate reality demonstrated a mature engagement with the core tenets of Nagarjuna’s school of thought. By asserting that all dharmas lack independent being, he reinforced the anti-essentialist stance central to Mādhyamika philosophy. The transmission of this particular lineage of Buddhist thought was pivotal, influencing later developments in Chinese dialectical philosophy as well as other Buddhist traditions. While the extant material is fragmentary, the consensus among Sinologists regards him as a foundational figure whose translation and exposition ensured the survival and flourishing of a sophisticated philosophical tradition in China. His commitment to precision, evidenced in the Weishou account, speaks to a disciplined scholarly practice that valued conceptual accuracy over purely devotional exposition. The preservation of his insights through the Chao Lun has provided scholars with a primary window into the practical application of sophisticated Indian logic within the early Chinese religious milieu.

The first four tracks are brand new and as strong as any of the more familiar stuff to come." musicOMH editor Neil Jones found that "Blige is undoubtedly one of the fascinating figures of modern pop culture, so even though there's more than a suspicion of Christmas cash-in here, and omissions are made, Reflections (A Retrospective) amply represents every extreme of her ouvre. AllMusic's senior editor Stephen Thomas Erlewine wrote that the album "remains a completely enjoyable (if not completely satisfying) listen", going on to say that "Unfortunately, Reflections (A Retrospective) is nowhere close to being that straightforward. A mere handful of the top ten hits are included; while obvious picks are present, a casual fan could rattle off just as many well-known songs that are not." Similarly, Sal Cinquemani from Slant Magazine noted that "the tracks previously unavailable on a Mary album make this a valuable purchase for diehard collectors, but it will be useless to more casual fans. The fact that Reflections might be one of the worst excuses for a greatest hits collection ever is a testament to the longevity and consistency of Mary's career." Commercial performance Reflections (A Retrospective) debuted at number nine on the Billboard 200 Albums Chart, selling about 171,000 units in its first week. The album achieved moderate success in physical sales, though its long-term sales figures varied depending on the market and promotional efforts surrounding its release. The critical reception, however, was more varied, reflecting the nature of the compilation itself. Critics often praised the inclusion of deeper cuts and lesser-known material, which offered a more comprehensive look at the artist's evolution than a standard collection of biggest hits would allow. Conversely, reviewers who expected a definitive collection of her most radio-friendly anthems found the selection too esoteric or too sparse to justify the purchase for the casual listener. Mary J. Blige's career trajectory has been marked by a successful navigation of mainstream pop accessibility while maintaining a distinct artistic core rooted in R&B and hip hop. Her early work established her as a powerful voice within the burgeoning sound of 90s urban music, characterized by its raw emotion and fusion of soulful vocals with hard-hitting beats. As the musical landscape shifted throughout the 2000s and beyond, Blige continued to adapt, incorporating elements of electronic music, contemporary pop production, and varied stylistic influences without entirely abandoning her foundational sound. This adaptability is a key element often cited by music analysts when discussing her sustained relevance in a highly competitive industry. The compilation, Reflections (A Retrospective), serves as a sonic map of this evolution, presenting moments of intense commercial peak alongside more introspective or genre-bending experimentation. The tracklist itself is not presented chronologically, which forces the listener to piece together the narrative of her career through curated sonic snapshots. This deliberate arrangement often sparks discussion among dedicated fans regarding the intent behind the selection process, questioning whether the compilation prioritizes artistic breadth over popular recognition. Market positioning for retrospective albums such as this is inherently complex. They must appeal both to the established fanbase who seek archival material and to newer listeners who are unfamiliar with the breadth of the artist's catalog. For Blige, whose discography spans several decades and numerous stylistic shifts, this dual requirement presents a significant curatorial challenge. The fact that the album received praise for its depth suggests a successful targeting of the dedicated collector demographic, a group willing to invest in artifacts that offer deeper context to an artist's legacy. Beyond the sales figures and critical assessments, the release prompted further analysis regarding the changing nature of "greatest hits" albums in the digital age. In an era where streaming platforms allow for near-instantaneous access to every recorded track, the traditional physical greatest hits compilation faces an existential challenge. Such compilations now often serve a more niche, archival function, catering to those who value physical media, liner notes, and a curated, single-packaged presentation of an artist's work, rather than simply enjoying a playlist of their most popular songs. Reflections (A Retrospective) fits squarely into this latter category, functioning more as an artifact of her journey than a simple jukebox.

The most confident of the four characters, Margot, seems to be patiently waiting for Gaspard to find himself and discover her love. The filming is mostly on the tourist beaches, except when Margot extracts Gaspard for excursions out of his comfort zone. We do not see Gaspard's relationships with Solène or Léna as extending past the beach, the water, and other places commonly frequented by tourists. In contrast, Margot and Gaspard's long walks and conversations lead them outside of the tourist areas and into the countryside. All characters seem to be in constant motion, restlessly wandering, hiking, or simply pacing the room, in reference to the impatience and spontaneity of youth. Gaspard is conscious of his own isolation, and confides his dislike of groups to Margot, and yet the viewer can see that his isolation is of his own making. Indeed, the first ten minutes of the film follow Gaspard's solitary wanderings on his first day in town, and he sometimes makes up excuses to be by himself throughout the film. Gaspard sees this as a protest against superficiality, but deeper analysis shows it may just be a way for him to protect his ego. Rohmer's use of clothing appears to be a metaphor for the personalities which Gaspard has to choose from. After the first scene at the beach, Gaspard does not see Margot in swimwear again. Her attire is loose, casual and she even appears in pajamas in a later scene. Her skirts are often short, and she appears to use her legs to flirt with the oblivious Gaspard. Léna and Solène's personalities seem to drift with the clothing choices. Léna is accepting, sexual and embracing in her bikini, but cold, uptight and angry in her street clothes. In a similar fashion, the provocative Solène is more hot-headed and quicker to anger when she appears in street clothes. Time plays an important role in the film: title-cards show the date each day from 17 July to 6 August. Gaspard tracks how many days late Léna is, while walking with Margot and scanning the beaches for her. Characteristically of Rohmer's films, time is shown highly linearly. Gaspard is shown to be extremely conscious of time constraints: he has a date on which he must leave for his new life as a teacher and is upset at Léna for going on an unplanned trip to Jersey with her cousins, on the grounds that it leaves them with too little time to visit Ouessant together. The relationship between Gaspard and Léna is further complicated by these temporal pressures, as his plans for the future clash with the unpredictable nature of their summer romance. His attempts to structure their time, evident in his counting of days and his anxieties about missed opportunities, contrast sharply with the fluid, improvisational nature of Margot's pursuit. Solène, meanwhile, embodies a more immediate, passionate engagement with the present moment, seemingly less burdened by the weight of future commitments that plague Gaspard. The scenery itself often shifts from the sun-drenched, communal spaces of the seaside to the more intimate, isolated landscapes of the regional roads, mirroring the varying levels of connection between the characters. These transitions are not merely geographical; they represent shifts in the emotional register of the narrative. The countryside sequences, where Margot and Gaspard are most engaged, feel expansive and open, suggesting the potential for genuine connection, whereas the confines of the small rented apartments often serve as arenas for awkwardness and unspoken tension. The film thus becomes a meditation on the precarious balance between desire, societal expectation, and the relentless passage of time during a fleeting period of youthful liberty. The subtle shifts in the characters' wardrobe serve not merely as aesthetic choices but as visual signifiers of their internal conflicts and evolving levels of self-presentation.

Early life Coupland was born in Leeds, West Riding of Yorkshire in 1928, the only child of Elsie (née Beck) and Denis Coupland. She originally wanted to be a ballet dancer but could not fulfil this ambition, owing to a horse-riding accident. Her music career began when she was 15; Barney Colehan, a BBC producer, heard her sing and invited her onto one of his radio shows. By the time she reached the age of 18, she was singing full-time at the Mecca Locarno in Leeds, and the following year, moved to London with her parents, where she became a resident singer at Mecca's Tottenham Court Road ballroom. Coupland became a leading singer of the 1940s and 1950s, working at the Dorchester Hotel and the Savoy Hotel. Career Coupland serenades the opening scene of the film Flannelfoot (1953) in which she featured as a nightclub singer. In 1959, she was unexpectedly cast by Joan Littlewood as Sally in the Theatre Workshop musical Make Me An Offer, and soon appeared in West End shows such as Gigi and Not Now, Darling. She made her television debut in a 1961 episode of Emergency – Ward 10. Her other early roles were in Dixon of Dock Green, The Wednesday Play, Softly, Softly and Z-Cars. After playing a mother in Please Sir! and the Siberian wife in Mel Brooks's film The Twelve Chairs (1970), she was cast as Jean Abbott, the long-suffering wife of Sid James's character, in Bless This House, which began its run in February 1971. She reprised the role in the 1972 feature film, and continued in the role until James died in 1976. She appeared in several other films, including The Millionairess (1960), The Family Way (1966), Charlie Bubbles (1967), Spring and Port Wine (1970), The Rise and Rise of Michael Rimmer (1970), The Best Pair of Legs in the Business (1972) and Operation Daybreak (1975). She also dubbed the singing voices of actresses who could not sing, including Lana Turner in Betrayed, and was the playback singer for Ursula Andress's dubbed performance of the song "Underneath the Mango Tree" in the first James Bond film Dr. Her filmography continued with appearances in classics such as The Pink Panther (1963) and a later, more prominent role as the wife of a policeman in the series Inspector Jack Frost. In the 1980s, Coupland maintained a presence in stage productions, often appearing in revues and musical comedies, demonstrating a consistent engagement with live performance despite the increasing prominence of television and film in the industry. Her television work spanned several decades, including guest appearances on various anthology series and light entertainment programs of the era. Despite the varying nature of her roles, her career trajectory reflected the evolving landscape of British entertainment, transitioning from nightclub performer to acclaimed stage and screen actress. She was recognized for her versatility, capable of portraying characters ranging from glamorous nightclub chanteuses to more domestic and emotionally complex figures. Throughout her career, Coupland maintained a connection to theatrical traditions, which underpinned her early successes. Later in life, she also took on mentoring roles, sharing her extensive industry knowledge with younger performers. Her enduring presence in British culture is evidenced by the longevity and breadth of her professional engagements across multiple mediums.

His evolution reflects a growing incorporation of international musical styles while maintaining a strong regional identity. Early recordings were heavily rooted in the folk traditions of his home area, particularly the characteristic sounds associated with Alentejo. As his career progressed, the influence of urban popular music and various other genres became more pronounced, leading to a richer and more diverse sonic tapestry in his later works. This willingness to experiment and absorb external influences without sacrificing his cultural moorings has been a defining feature of his artistry. Critics have often noted the unique tension in his music, a delicate balance between the melancholic, deeply rooted narratives of the countryside and the more dynamic, contemporary rhythms of city life. This duality allows his music to resonate with a broad audience, spanning both traditionalists and younger listeners attracted to modern musical explorations. The instrumentation employed varies considerably across his albums, shifting from traditional acoustic ensembles to arrangements featuring modern percussion and keyboard sounds in subsequent decades. His vocal delivery itself demonstrates a remarkable range, shifting seamlessly from the raw, impassioned cries typical of traditional Cante Alentejano to the more polished, nuanced phrasing required by mainstream popular song structures. Collaborations with other musicians have further enriched his sound palette, introducing new instrumental textures and compositional approaches to his established repertoire. These collaborations have often been crucial in bridging the gap between his historical sound and contemporary musical trends, ensuring his continued relevance within the Portuguese musical landscape. The thematic content of his songs remains largely consistent, often touching upon themes of social life, rural struggle, unrequited love, and the changing face of Portuguese society, providing a cultural commentary through his musical lens.

Old Indic adhi-pá- 'protector, ruler, master, king'). Biography Early history In 57 BC Julius Caesar conquered parts of Gaul and also Belgica (Belgium, modern-day Northern France, Luxembourg, part of present-day Netherlands below the Rhine River; and the north-western portion of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany). There were several tribes in the country who fought against each other frequently. The Eburones were ruled by Ambiorix and Catuvolcus. In 54 BC Caesar's troops urgently needed more food, and so the local tribes were forced to give up part of their harvest, which had not been good that year. Understandably the starving Eburones were reluctant to do so and Caesar ordered that camps be built near the Eburones' villages. Each centurion was ordered to make sure the food supplies were delivered to the Roman soldiers. This created resentment among the Eburones. Although Julius Caesar had freed him from paying tribute to the Atuatuci, Ambiorix joined Catuvolcus in the winter of 54 BC in an uprising against the Roman forces under Quintus Titurius Sabinus and Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta. Resisting the Romans Because a drought had disrupted his grain supply, Caesar was forced to winter his legions among the rebellious Belgic tribes. Roman troops led by Sabinus and Cotta were wintering among the Eburones when they were attacked by them, led by Ambiorix and Cativolcus. Ambiorix deceived the Romans, telling them the attack was made without his consent, and further advised them to flee as a large Germanic force was preparing to cross the Rhine. Trusting Ambiorix, Sabinus and Cotta's troops left the next morning. A short distance from their camp, the Roman troops were ambushed by the Eburones and massacred. Elsewhere, another Roman force under Quintus Tullius Cicero, younger brother of the orator Marcus, were wintering amongst the Nervii. Leading a coalition of rebellious Belgic tribes, Ambiorix surrounded Cicero's camp. After a long while, a Roman messenger was finally able to slip through the Belgic lines and get word of the uprising to Caesar. Mobilizing his legions, Caesar immediately marched to Cicero's aid. As they approached the besieged Roman camp, the Belgae moved to engage Caesar's troops. The engagement between Caesar's forces and the allied Belgic tribes proved to be a prolonged and fierce affair. Caesar's military machine, renowned for its discipline and tactical flexibility, faced a unified and determined enemy. The initial skirmishes saw the tribal warriors employing hit-and-run tactics, utilizing the dense terrain to their advantage, a common feature of Gallic warfare. Caesar responded by employing his disciplined legions in set-piece battles, relying on the coordinated strength of the manipular formation. The ensuing conflict was not a swift rout but a grinding campaign that tested the limits of Roman resolve against the fierce indigenous resistance. Ambiorix and Catuvolcus continued to play crucial roles as military leaders, uniting disparate tribal groups under a shared banner of defiance against Roman hegemony. Their ability to forge alliances across different tribes, despite longstanding intertribal rivalries, was a significant factor in the early successes against the invading legions. Caesar, aware of the strategic danger posed by this coordinated rebellion, devoted substantial resources to pacifying the region. His response involved a calculated combination of overwhelming force, strategic siege warfare, and the use of diplomacy where possible, though the Eburones and their allies proved remarkably resistant to simple appeasement. The outcome of this early phase of the Gallic Wars set a precedent for the nature of the conflict to follow, demonstrating that conquest would not be achieved through mere punitive expeditions but required a sustained and exhaustive military commitment from Rome.

He later appeared as Lois Lane's father in the 1978 Superman film. Alyn had Alzheimer's disease later in his life and died in 1999 at the age of 88. Lee Quigley Lee Quigley, who played the infant Superman in the 1978 film, came from an unstable home and suffered schoolyard bullying. He died in 1991 at age 14 from inhalant abuse. George Reeves George Reeves played Superman in the 1951 film Superman and the Mole Men and the ensuing television series Adventures of Superman. Like Alyn, he was too closely associated with the role to find further work. On June 16, 1959, days before he was to be married, Reeves was found dead of a gunshot wound at his home with his Luger pistol near him. The death was ruled a suicide, but controversy surrounds the death, as Reeves's fingerprints were never found on the gun, and he had been having an affair with the wife of MGM exec Eddie Mannix. It was Reeves's death that inspired the conspiracy theories and the urban legend of a curse associated with the character. Christopher Reeve Christopher Reeve played Clark Kent / Superman in the 1978–87 Superman film series: Superman: The Movie (1978), Superman II (1980), Superman III (1983), and Superman IV: The Quest for Peace (1987). Subsequently, he was subject to typecasting and found difficulty acquiring roles, being relegated to Superman sequels and supporting roles. Reeve was paralyzed from the neck down after being thrown from his horse in a cross-country equestrian riding event on May 27, 1995. He died on October 10, 2004 15 days after his 52nd birthday. No official autopsy was performed, but both Reeve's wife Dana and his doctor John McDonald believed that an adverse reaction to a drug caused Reeve's death. In one of his last roles, Reeve portrayed supporting character Dr. Virgil Swann on the WB/CW television series Smallville. Other alleged victims Marlon Brando Marlon Brando, who played Jor-El in the 1978 film, is cited for the misfortune he suffered in his private life, such as his son Christian's shooting of his half-sister Cheyenne's boyfriend in 1990 and subsequent five-year imprisonment, Brando's own admission in court that he had failed his son and daughter, his daughter's 1995 suicide and his later reclusiveness. The character of Jor-El, the Kryptonian father of Superman, has been portrayed by various actors throughout the franchise, each bringing a distinct interpretation to the iconic figure. The depiction of Kryptonian life and the tragic destruction of the planet Krypton have been central themes in numerous adaptations, often serving as the mythological backdrop for Superman's arrival on Earth. Early portrayals often focused heavily on the sci-fi aspects of Krypton, presenting it as a highly advanced, yet ultimately doomed, civilization. As the narratives evolved, the focus shifted toward the moral and philosophical implications of Krypton's demise, using it to explore themes of destiny, alien identity, and the responsibility of immense power. Later iterations have seen Jor-El's character developed beyond a mere expositional figure, providing deeper insight into Kryptonian societal structure and its internal conflicts. These portrayals often link Jor-El's wisdom and foresight directly to Clark Kent's development as Superman, suggesting that his legacy is not simply genetic but also ideological. The various interpretations of Jor-El reflect the broader shifts in the comic book medium itself, moving from pulp adventure toward more complex, character-driven science fiction drama. The impact of these portrayals extends beyond the cinematic scope, influencing the understanding of Superman's origin across different media formats, including animation and literature. The concept of a dying world sending a hopeful remnant to a new planet resonates with various human existential concerns. Furthermore, the lineage of Jor-El often serves as a point of comparison with other powerful, parental figures in mythology, placing Superman within a broader pantheon of savior archetypes. The evolution of the Kryptonian lore has provided material for extensive fan analysis and scholarly discussion regarding narrative tropes in superhero fiction. Discussions frequently center on the balance between the alien nature of Superman and his terrestrial humanity, a balance heavily informed by the stories of his adoptive parents and his Kryptonian heritage, personified by Jor-El. These debates continue to shape how modern creators approach the foundational elements of the Superman mythos.

The molecule viewer BALLView, also developed by the BALL project team, is a C++ application of BALL using Qt, and OpenGL with the real-time ray tracer RTFact as render back-ends. For both, BALLView offers three-dimensional and stereoscopic visualizing in several different modes, and applying directly the algorithms of the BALL library via its graphical user interface. The BALL project is developed and maintained by groups at Saarland University, Mainz University, and University of Tübingen. Both the library and the viewer are used for education and research. BALL packages have been made available in the Debian project. Key features Interactive molecular drawing and conformational editing Reading and writing of molecular file formats (PDB, MOL2, MOL, HIN, XYZ, KCF, SD, AC) Reading secondary data sources e.g. (DCD, DSN6, GAMESS, JCAMP, SCWRL, TRR) Generating molecules from and matching of SMILES- and SMARTS expressions to molecules Geometry optimization Minimizer and molecular dynamics classes Support for force fields (MMFF94, AMBER, CHARMM) for scoring and energy minimization Python interface and scripting functionality Plugin infrastructure (3D Space-Navigator) Molecular graphics (3D, stereoscopic viewing) comprehensive documentation (Wiki, code snippets, online class documentation, bug tracker) comprehensive regression tests BALL project format for presentations and collaborative data exchange NMR editable shortcuts BALL library BALL is a development framework for structural bioinformatics. Using BALL as a programming toolbox allows greatly reducing application development times and helps ensure stability and correctness by avoiding often error-prone reimplementation of complex algorithms and replacing them with calls into a library that has been tested by many developers. File import-export BALL supports molecular file formats including PDB, MOL2, MOL, HIN, XYZ, KCF, SD, AC, and secondary data sources like DCD, DSN6, GAMESS, JCAMP, SCWRL, and TRR. Molecules can also be created using BALL's peptide builder, or based on SMILES expressions. General structure analysis Further preparation and structure validation is enabled by, e.g., Kekuliser-, Aromaticity-, Bondorder-, HBond-, and Secondary Structure processors. A Fragment Library automatically infers missing information, e.g., a protein's hydrogens or bonds. A Rotamer Library allows determining, assigning, and switching between a protein's most likely side chain conformations. BALL's Transformation processors guide generation of valid 3D structures. Its selection mechanism enables to specify parts of a molecule by simple expressions (SMILES, SMARTS, element types). This selection can be used by all modeling classes like the processors or force fields. Molecular mechanics Implementations of the popular force fields CHARMM, Amber, and MMFF94 can be combined with BALL's minimizer and simulation classes (steepest descent, conjugate gradient, L-BFGS, and shifted L-VMM). Python interface SIP is used to automatically create Python classes for all relevant C++ classes in the BALL library to allow for the same class interfaces. The application of these integrated features allows researchers to move seamlessly from raw data import to detailed structural analysis and dynamic simulation within a unified environment. For instance, a user can import a protein structure from a PDB file, automatically add necessary hydrogen atoms and assign correct bond orders using the Fragment Library, then utilize the Rotamer Library to select energetically favorable side-chain conformations. Subsequently, the structure can be subjected to energy minimization employing the MMFF94 force field and a conjugate gradient algorithm available in the library. The resultant optimized structure can then be visualized in BALLView, where stereoscopic viewing options permit the user to inspect the molecular geometry in three dimensions. The comprehensive plugin infrastructure facilitates the extension of the framework, allowing developers to incorporate specialized analysis tools or novel visualization techniques tailored to specific research needs without modifying the core library code. The availability of the Python interface, managed by the SIP tool, significantly lowers the barrier to entry for computational chemists and biologists already proficient in Python, enabling rapid prototyping and integration of BALL functionalities into broader scripting workflows. The commitment to regression testing ensures that as new features are added or underlying algorithms are updated, the established behavior of the library remains consistent across different use cases. This robust foundation makes BALL a valuable resource not only for advanced academic research but also for industrial applications requiring reliable molecular modeling and structural bioinformatics tools.

The surname is common in the British Isles, as well as locations associated with settlement by the people of these regions. The name has two main sources of origin. The first is of Norman origin, coming from the region of La Houssaye in Northern France. In Old French, the name relates to holly ('hous' in Old French). Hussey also has an Irish origin, stemming from the Ó hEodhasa family. The variations in spelling and pronunciation of the name reflect the linguistic transitions and regional dialects across the areas where it has taken root. The Norman derivation suggests an association with flora, a common motif in place names across medieval Europe. Conversely, the Gaelic origins point toward ancient lineage and localized kinship structures within Ireland. Genealogical research into the different branches of the name often requires careful consideration of historical documentation, as common surnames can obscure distinct family lines over several centuries. In the context of British society, the surname often appeared among the landed gentry, particularly during periods of expansion and political realignment in the early modern era. Immigration patterns subsequently disseminated the name globally, attaching it to communities in North America, Australia, and other parts of the Commonwealth. Biographical data concerning individuals bearing the name reveals a broad spectrum of professions, from academia and the arts to sports and political service, illustrating the varied trajectories of those who have carried this designation through history. The prevalence of the name in historical records allows for a complex mapping of migration routes and social mobility across different epochs.

The themes prevalent in the works of Némirovsky often explore the precarious nature of human existence amidst societal upheaval. Her narratives frequently juxtapose moments of profound personal intimacy with the broader currents of political and historical instability. The intricate psychological landscapes inhabited by her characters reflect a deep engagement with the fragility of individual identity when confronted by overwhelming external forces. Her prose, characterized by its lyrical quality and sharp observational power, manages to render the internal struggles of her subjects with both delicate nuance and unflinching realism. Critics have often noted the masterful way she constructs tension, allowing moments of quiet reflection to carry as much narrative weight as dramatic confrontations. The exploration of relationships, particularly those under duress, forms a significant pillar of her literary output. Furthermore, her examination of moral ambiguity invites readers to reconsider established notions of heroism and victimhood. The impact of the historical context on her characters is rarely merely a backdrop; it is an active, shaping agent within the fabric of her storytelling. This pervasive sense of historical weight gives her fiction a distinctive resonance that continues to draw academic and popular attention. The translation efforts noted above underscore the international recognition of her literary achievements across various linguistic communities. Her writing demands a reader attentive to the subtext, recognizing the unspoken anxieties that permeate her carefully constructed worlds.

However, the primary branch H2 (P96) seems to have been found in sparse levels primarily in Europe and West Asia since prehistory. Pre-Pottery Neolithic B (PPNB) is part of the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, a Neolithic culture centered in upper Mesopotamia and the Levant, dating to years ago has been found in remains also the later Linear Pottery culture and Neolithic Iberia. H2 likely entered Europe during the Neolithic with the spread of agriculture. Its present distribution is made up of various individual cases spread out throughout Europe and West Asia today. Structure H-L901/M2939 is a direct descendant of Haplogroup GHIJK. There are, in turn, three direct descendants of H-L901/M2939 – their defining SNPs are as follows: H1 (L902/M3061) H1a previously haplogroup H1 (M69/Page45, M370) H1b B108, Z34961, Z34962, Z34963, Z34964 H2 previously haplogroup F3, (P96, L279, L281, L284, L285, L286, M282) H2a FGC29299/Z19067 H2b Z41290 H2c Y21618, Z19080 H3 (Z5857) H3a (Z5866) H3b (Z13871) Ancient distribution H-L901/M2939 is believed to have split from HIJK 48,500 years before present. Its probable site of introduction is South Asia, since it is highly concentrated there. H1a With limited ancient DNA testing in South Asia, accordingly there is a limited amount of ancient samples for H1a, despite it being a populous and well distributed haplogroup today. The first set of ancient DNA from South Asia was published in March 2018. 65 samples were collected from the Swat Valley of northern Pakistan, 2 of which belonged to H1a. H2 The earliest sample of H2 is found in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic B culture of the Levant 10,000 years ago. From ancient samples, it is clear that H2 also has a strong association with the spread of agriculture from Anatolia into Europe, and is commonly found with haplogroup G2a. H2 was found in Neolithic Anatolia, as well as in multiple later Neolithic cultures of Europe, such as the Vinča culture in Serbia, and the Megalith culture of Western Europe. The 2021 study "Using Y-chromosome capture enrichment to resolve haplogroup H2 shows new evidence for a two-path Neolithic expansion to Western Europe" found that while H2 is less than 0.2% in modern-day western European populations it was more common during the Neolithic, between 1.5 and 9%. They identified two major clades H2m and H2d. With respect to the current ISOGG nomenclature, H2m appears to be defined by a mix of H2, H2a, H2a1 and H2c1a SNPs while H2d appears to be defined by two H2b1 SNPs, and four additional SNPs which were previously undetected. They estimated TMRCA for H2d and H2m was ~15.4 kya with H2m and H2d estimated TMRCAs of ~11.8 and ~11.9 kya respectively. The presence of H2 across disparate Neolithic cultures suggests a complex migratory pattern rather than a single, straightforward dispersal event. Genetic analyses further indicate that the Neolithic expansion into Europe was not monolithic but involved multiple waves or distinct genetic introductions. The differentiation observed between H2m and H2d provides molecular evidence for these separate evolutionary trajectories within the haplogroup. Furthermore, the genetic relationship between H2 and G2a reinforces the connection between these haplogroups and the Neolithic demographic shifts associated with farming practices. The continued investigation of ancient genomes from diverse geographic regions is crucial for refining the timeline and mechanisms of this ancient population movement. Differences in the frequency and genetic substructure of H2 across various Neolithic sites may reflect local adaptation, genetic drift, or the assimilation of distinct incoming populations. Future studies aim to integrate these Y-chromosome data with autosomal and mitochondrial DNA studies to construct a more comprehensive picture of Neolithic European ancestry. The specific mechanisms by which H2 became established in various cultural landscapes, from the Levant to the Vinča sites, remain subjects of ongoing debate within population genetics.

Trønderfly started an air ambulance service in the early 1970s. Widerøe introduced the de Havilland Canada Dash 7 in 1982, resulting in the terminal being expanded. Offshore helicopter services began the following year. The runway was expanded to in 1987. Offshore helicopter operations commenced out of Brønnøysund Airport in 1981, when Helikopter Service was contracted to fly to the exploration field on Trænabanken. A combined fixed-wing and helicopter hangar was completed in 1983. The contract changed to Lufttransport in 1984. Operations remained limited and in 1989 the airport only saw 34 helicopter flights. The exploration resulted in a positive finding on the Norne field, which started production in 1997. Norsk Helikopter, later renamed Bristow Norway, established a helicopter base at Brønnøysund Airport in 2002 and took over flights to the Skarv Oil Field. NATO showed interest in upgrading Brønnøysund Airport in 1991. Specifically, they intended to spend NOK 125 million in expanding the runway to and building a fuel depot. The airport was planned used as a relief military airbase without any permanently stationed aircraft. The plans were canceled in 1993 following cutbacks in NATO. Widerøe introduced Dash 8 aircraft in 1992, gradually replacing the Dash 7. In 1996, Brønnøysund and 25 other regional airports were taken over by the state and the Civil Aviation Administration (later renamed Avinor). The runway was extended to in 1999; including the safety zone at each end. While allowing for a direct service to Oslo, the service was terminated the following year. The same year a new control tower was opened and the old tower was taken over by a motorcycle club. Airport security was introduced on 1 January 2005. This put a large strain on the terminal capacity and the terminal had to be expanded. Makeshift solutions were used, such as plywood boards to allocate people through the security check. In late 2004, the airport started planning an all-new terminal building, as the old terminal was deemed both too small and out of date. Construction of the NOK-115-million terminal started on 24 October 2006. As the first airport in the world, Brønnøysund received SCAT-I, a satellite-based landing system, on 29 October 2007. The new terminal opened on 26 May 2008, which allowed the a restaurant to open at the airport, all vehicles to be stored indoors and included a new helicopter terminal. The introduction of the modern terminal facility significantly improved passenger flow and operational efficiency at the airport. Subsequent upgrades focused on enhancing air traffic control capabilities and improving cargo handling infrastructure to meet the growing demands of regional and specialized aviation. The integration of advanced navigational aids further solidified Brønnøysund's role as a critical hub in the North Sea operations. The airport continued to support the evolving needs of the petroleum industry, facilitating logistics for offshore installations throughout the region. Widerøe continued its operations, adapting its fleet to newer, more fuel-efficient models as environmental regulations tightened across the aviation sector. The state ownership structure ensured continued investment in infrastructure maintenance and technological modernization, preventing the decline seen at some smaller, privately managed regional airfields. Furthermore, the airport served as a vital connection point for local communities, linking them with larger national networks via air travel, even as its primary commercial focus remained tied to the energy sector. Environmental considerations became increasingly important in the airport's long-term planning, leading to initiatives aimed at reducing noise pollution and carbon emissions from aircraft operations. This commitment to sustainability reflected broader national trends in infrastructure development and environmental governance within the Scandinavian region.

Chopra conceived the film after his low-budget suspense thriller (1985) failed to find a distributor for a theatrical release. This motivated him to make a more mainstream film with well-known actors. received critical acclaim when released. It is considered by several critics and scholars to be the turning point in the introduction of realism in Hindi cinema. won two National Film Awards and five Filmfare Awards, and was India's official selection for the 1990 Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, but it was not nominated. In 2015, Chopra remade as a Hollywood film titled Broken Horses. Plot Kishan and Karan are orphaned brothers who grew up on the streets of Bombay. To provide Karan with a better upbringing and education, Kishan works for Anna Seth, a gangster who owns an oil factory as a front for his illegal activities. Unaware of his brother's affiliation with a gang, Karan returns to Bombay after completing his studies in the United States. Inspector Prakash, Karan's friend, knows Anna is a gangster, but he is unable to arrest him due to lack of evidence. Anna plans to have Prakash killed during his reunion with Karan. Attempting to prevent this, Kishan books an earlier flight for Karan, but it is delayed and Anna's henchmen shoot Prakash, who dies in Karan's arms. Paro, Prakash's sister and Karan's childhood friend, believes Karan is responsible for her brother's death. Karan learns from Anna's former messenger Iqbal that Anna is Kishan's boss and that Anna orchestrated Prakash's murder. He is also told that Anna burnt his wife and developed pyrophobia. Karan tells Paro that Anna and Kishan killed Prakash; they fall in love with each other. A few days later, Abdul is arrested and Karan recognises him as one of Prakash's killers. Kishan warns Karan against testifying, and is wounded when Anna's henchmen shoot at Karan. When Karan is summoned to identify the assailants at police headquarters, Abdul extorts his silence, threatening that Kishan will be killed by his home nurse if Karan testifies. Karan decides not to testify, and instead joins Anna's gang to get close to the crime boss. Anna tests Karan's resolve by ordering him to shoot Iqbal, who shoots himself so Karan can continue his plan without guilt. The narrative subsequently develops the complexities of Karan's entanglement with Anna's operations, moving beyond the initial premise of simple revenge. His infiltration allows him to gather crucial information regarding Anna's wider criminal network and the extent of his influence over the city's underbelly. Paro, witnessing Karan's increasing proximity to danger and his conflicted loyalties, becomes a pivotal figure, often serving as the moral compass in the escalating violence. The film explores themes of fractured family loyalty, the corrupting influence of organized crime, and the difficulty of seeking justice within a system compromised by power and influence. Chopra utilized the gritty urban landscape of Bombay not merely as a backdrop but as an active participant in the drama, reflecting the moral decay prevalent in the environment. The pacing shifts from suspenseful cat-and-mouse encounters to intense sequences of confrontation, highlighting the personal toll the criminal enterprises exact on the protagonists. Karan's decision to participate in the gang structure represents a descent into the very world he sought to dismantle, forcing him to compromise his own ethical boundaries. This period of immersion allows for a deeper character study of Kishan, whose conflicted position—being both a victim and a functional participant in the criminal structure—adds layers of tragic irony to the plot. The film masterfully balances the stylized action typical of genre cinema with moments of raw, unflinching human vulnerability, solidifying its reputation as a significant piece of modern Indian cinematic realism.

The broad duties of a Forensic Odontologist include forensic identification of individuals, including in multi-casualty events, age estimation in living and deceased persons, interpreting injuries in the oral and perioral regions, bite mark analysis and comparison, and assisting forensic pathologists in determining the cause of death if there is a possible contributing dental condition. Dental evidence is useful in establishing human identity by comparing the dental features of a deceased person with antemortem dental records. Forensic pathology Forensic pathology is a subfield in forensics where experts examine persons (bodies) who die suddenly, unexpectedly or violently, and thus determine the cause of death. The function of a forensic autopsy is to provide information through a postmortem examination of the body and analysis of the fluids to determine the cause of death, manner of death, and mechanism of injury. A forensic pathologist is a medical doctor who is an expert in both trauma and disease and is responsible for performing autopsies. He/she applies their extensive knowledge of the human body and possible internal and external inflections as he/she performs an autopsy, to ascertain the manner and cause of death hopefully. Information derived from the autopsy often greatly assists investigative efforts and scene reconstruction. Forensic toxicology Forensic toxicology is the use of toxicology and other disciplines such as analytical chemistry, pharmacology and clinical chemistry to aid medical or legal investigation of death, poisoning, and drug use. The primary concern for forensic toxicology is not the legal outcome of the toxicological investigation or the technology utilized but rather the obtainment and interpretation of results. Forensic microbiology With recent advances in massive parallel sequencing (MPS), or next-generation sequencing (NGS), forensic microbiology has become an increasingly promising area of research. "Initial applications in circumstances of biocrime, bioterrorism and epidemiology use microorganisms for the following reasons: (i) as ancillary evidence in criminal cases; (ii) to clarify causes of death (e.g., drownings, toxicology, hospital-acquired infections, sudden infant death and shaken baby syndromes); (iii) to assist human identification (skin, hair and body fluid microbiomes); (iv) for geolocation (soil microbiome or microbiome of bodies of water); and (v) to estimate postmortem interval (PMI) via thanatomicrobiome and epinecrotic microbial community". In fact, scientists estimate the time elapsed since death or the PMI by analyzing the stage of decay from bacterial decomposition or the bacterial succession patterns. The analysis of microbial communities present on a body or in its surrounding environment provides unique temporal and geographic information. The microbial succession observed during decomposition is highly dependent on environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, and the presence of scavengers, which necessitates careful contextualization of microbial data. Furthermore, the study of the microbiome offers potential avenues for tracing an individual's movements or exposure history, thereby supplementing traditional forensic methodologies. Integrating data from different forensic disciplines, such as odontological records, toxicological screens, and microbial signatures, allows investigators to build a more comprehensive and robust profile of events leading to death or injury. This multi-faceted approach moves beyond single-point evidence analysis towards a holistic forensic reconstruction. DNA analysis, a cornerstone of modern forensic science, is another vital component, employed through techniques like DNA profiling, short tandem repeat (STR) analysis, and mitochondrial DNA analysis. These methods permit the identification of individuals from biological samples collected at a crime scene or from the deceased, offering high levels of discriminatory power. Challenges in forensic science often revolve around sample degradation, contamination, and the need for standardized protocols across diverse laboratory settings. Advances in automation and bioinformatics are continually improving the sensitivity and throughput of these analytical techniques, thereby enhancing the reliability of forensic conclusions. The integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning is also beginning to impact these fields, promising greater efficiency in pattern recognition, particularly in large-scale data sets such as mass spectrometry outputs or genomic sequencing reads.

Gene dosage is the number of copies of a particular gene present in a genome. Gene dosage is related to the amount of gene product (proteins or functional RNAs) the cell is able to express. Since a gene acts as a template, the number of templates in the cell contributes to the amount of gene product able to be produced. However, the amount of gene product produced in a cell is more commonly dependent on regulation of gene expression. The normal gene dosage is dependent on the species; humans generally have two doses -- one copy from the mother and one from the father. Changes in gene dosage can be a result of copy number variation (gene insertions or gene deletions), or aneuploidy (chromosome number abnormalities). These changes can have significant phenotypic consequences. Ploidy Ploidy refers to the number of complete sets of chromosomes in a cell. Humans typically have a gene dosage of two. Because they are diploid, they have two sets of 23 different chromosomes. The number of copies of chromosomes generally correlates to the number of copies of a gene present in the genome. For example, the gene that codes for the beta-subunit of hemoglobin (HBB) is located on chromosome 11. Humans have 2 copies of chromosome 11, so they have 2 copies of the HBB gene. Because humans are diploid -- getting one copy of each chromosome from either their mother or father -- different alleles can be inherited. Gene dosage can be affected if you present with two different alleles. Such as carriers for sickles cell anemia, who carry one disease allele and one normal allele for hemoglobin. As a result they only produce half normal hemoglobin, and the other half is diseased. Aneuploidy If an individual has an abnormal number of chromosomes, then it is called aneuploidy. Aneuploidy is very common in humans, with around 20-40% of all conceptions making a embryo displaying aneuploidy. Most aneuploidy events are fatal and lead to miscarriage. However, there are a few exceptions, including Down Syndrome and intersex conditions. Down Syndrome is caused by trisomy 21, which means having three copies of chromosome 21. Thus gene dosage is increased by 50% for the genes on that chromosome. Though not fully understood, it is thought that the increased expression of genes on chromosome 21 is the cause of some of the characteristic traits of Down syndrome. Other forms of aneuploidy result in different clinical presentations. For instance, Turner syndrome, characterized by monosomy X (45,X), involves the absence of one sex chromosome, leading to a reduced dosage of genes located on the X chromosome. Conversely, Klinefelter syndrome, resulting from the presence of an extra X chromosome (47,XXY), involves an increased dosage of X-linked genes. The physiological impact of these dosage imbalances is highly complex and context-dependent, involving intricate networks of gene regulation and protein-protein interactions. Beyond large-scale chromosomal changes, submicroscopic variations that alter gene dosage are also significant. Copy number variations (CNVs) encompass duplications or deletions of segments of DNA that are too small to be detected by standard karyotyping but large enough to affect gene function. These CNVs can range in size from a few kilobases to several megabases and are implicated in a wide array of disorders, including autism spectrum disorders and schizophrenia. The precise mechanism by which an altered gene dosage manifests as a specific phenotype remains an active area of genetic research. Some genes exhibit haploinsufficiency, meaning that having only one functional copy is insufficient to produce enough protein for normal function, leading to disease. In contrast, some conditions may result from gene triplosensitivity, where having three copies results in a toxic overexpression of the gene product. Therefore, the consequence of a gene dosage change is not always a simple linear relationship between copy number and phenotype. Research into the regulatory pathways controlling gene expression, such as epigenetic modifications and transcription factor binding affinity, is crucial for fully elucidating the pathogenic effects of dosage alterations.

HBCD has been classified as a category 2 for reproductive toxicity. Since August 2010 hexabromocyclododecanes are included in the EPA's List of Chemicals of Concern. In May 2013 the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) decided to include HBCD in the convention's Annex A for elimination, with specific exemptions for expanded and extruded polystyrene in buildings needed to give countries time to phase-in safer substitutes. HBCD is listed for elimination, but with a specific exemption for expanded polystyrene (EPS) and extruded polystyrene (XPS) in buildings. Countries may choose to use this exemption for up to five years after the request for exemption is submitted. Japan was the first country to implement a ban on the import and production of HBCD effective in May 2014. Because HBCD has 16 possible stereo-isomers with different biological activities, the substance poses a difficult problem for manufacture and regulation. The HBCD commercial mixture is composed of three main diastereomers denoted as alpha (α-HBCD), beta (β-HBCD) and gamma (γ-HBCD) with traces of others. A series of four published in vivo mice studies were conducted between several federal and academic institutions to characterize the toxicokinetic profiles of individual HBCD stereoisomers. The predominant diastereomer in the HBCD mixture, γ-HBCD, undergoes rapid hepatic metabolism, fecal and urinary elimination, and biological conversion to other diastereomers with a short biological half-life of 1–4 days. After oral exposure to the γ-HBCD diastereomer, β-HBCD was detected in the liver and brain, and α-HBCD and β-HBCD was detected in the fat and feces with multiple novel metabolites identified - monohydroxy-pentabromocyclododecane, monohydroxy-pentabromocyclododecene, dihydroxy-pentabromocyclododecene, and dihydroxy-pentabromocyclododecadiene. In contrast, α-HBCD is more biologically persistent, resistant to metabolism, bioaccumulates in lipid-rich tissues after a 10-day repeated exposure study, and has a longer biological half-life of up to 21 days; only α-HBCD was detected in the liver, brain, fat and feces with no stereoisomerization to γ-HBCD or β-HBCD and low trace levels of four different hydroxylated metabolites were identified. Developing mice had higher HBCD tissue levels than adult mice after exposure to either α-HBCD or γ-HBCD indicating the potential for increased susceptibility of the developing young to HBCD effects. The reported toxicokinetic differences of individual HBCD diastereoisomers have important implications for the extrapolation of toxicological studies of the commercial HBCD mixture to the assessment of human risk. The differing metabolic rates and bioaccumulation potentials among the isomers suggest that a single hazard classification for the commercial mixture may not adequately represent the risks posed by its constituent parts. Regulatory efforts, therefore, have increasingly focused on stereospecific assessment to better inform risk management strategies. Research into the environmental fate of HBCD also highlights concerns regarding its persistence in various environmental compartments, including soil and aquatic systems, despite the global regulatory push for its elimination. The degradation pathways identified in laboratory settings are crucial for predicting its long-term environmental behavior and potential for transformation into other harmful compounds. Furthermore, the potential for cross-contamination between different products containing various HBCD isomers presents a complex challenge for waste management and recycling industries. Industrial processes must implement stringent controls to prevent the release of these persistent chemicals into the environment during manufacturing, use, and disposal. The ongoing scientific investigation aims not only to characterize the precise toxicological endpoints of each isomer but also to develop reliable analytical methods capable of quantifying these specific forms in complex matrices such as biological samples and environmental media. This detailed understanding is vital for ensuring public health and environmental safety as the global phase-out of HBCD progresses under international treaty obligations.

Name The municipality (originally the parish) is named after the old Bruvik farm () since the first Bruvik Church was built there. The first element is which means "mountain ridge" or "rim". The last element is the genitive case of the word which means "bay", "cove" or "inlet". Thus it means the bay by the mountain ridge. Coat of arms The coat of arms was granted on 14 December 1960. The blazon was "Azure, a chevron over a cogwheel argent". This means the arms have a blue field (background) and the charge is a cogwheel with a chevron ordinary above it. The charge has a tincture of argent which means it is commonly colored white, but if it is made out of metal, then silver is used. The design was chosen to symbolize the importance of industry in the municipality. In 1964 when Bruvik municipality was dissolved, the new municipality of Vaksdal (which included the majority of the old Bruvik municipality) chose to continue using the old arms of Bruvik. Later that evening, Hays (although still a brigadier general and junior in rank to Caldwell), was assigned to command the II Corps. He led the corps throughout the summer until permanent command was given to Maj. In November, Hays was appointed provost marshal of the southern district of New York, and was also promoted to major in the regular army. At the expiration of his term in February 1865, Hays rejoined the Army of the Potomac at Petersburg and served again in the II Corps, this time commanding the 2nd Division. He was appointed a brevet brigadier general in the regular army on March 13, 1865, for gallant conduct, but on April 6 he was relieved of command for sleeping on duty and thus failing to prepare his troops for departure as they pursued Confederate forces. His brevets were revoked and Brig. Barlow was assigned to lead the division. The church was declared a Grade I listed building in 1966. Currently the Church accepts monetary donations for its maintenance and preservation. History The Church of Saint Michael, Framlingham, has been built, rebuilt and added to down the ages. A surviving feature, the capitals of the chancel arch, date from the twelfth century, but the majority of the church was built in the Perpendicular style between 1350 and 1555. The roof is especially glorious with intricate fan tracery which conceal hammer beams. The roof itself dates from about 1521. Framlingham was a major seat of the Earls and Dukes of Norfolk. Vast estates of the Norman Bigods were forfeited to Edward I and Framlingham came to Thomas of Brotherton, eldest son of Edward and Margaret of France. After many other changes of inheritance, in about 1635 Sir Robert Hitcham bequeathed the Framlingham estate to Pembroke College, Cambridge, who remain Lords of the Manor to this day. The church contains many fine tombs including that of Thomas Howard, 3rd Duke of Norfolk. Bells The church has a ring of 8 bells from a mixture of founders and date from between the 15th and 20th centuries. The ring was augmented to 8 with addition of 2 new trebles in 1718 cast by John Stephens of Norwich. The bells hang in oak frame made by George Day of Eye, Suffolk dating from 1892. The bells were overhauled by John Taylor & Co of Loughborough in 1990. The 1708 Thamar Organ One of the most noted features of the church is the world-famous Thamar organ. Only eight large-scale organs in total survived the English Civil War, and only three of those are Thamars. The other examples being in Gloucester Cathedral and St Nicholas's church in the hamlet of Stanford upon Avon, Northamptonshire. The painted front pipes belong to the Thamar organ first built for the church's patrons, Pembroke College, Cambridge, by Thomas Thamar in 1674 just after the Restoration (celebrated by the hatchment on the south wall); the only other painted pipes of this style are to be found in Gloucester Cathedral. The case is believed to date back to before 1630 (maybe much earlier – 1580 has been mentioned) and some of the pipework may at least pre-date the Commonwealth. In 1707 the college decided it would like a larger and more up to date organ by Father Smith for their Wren chapel; the Thamar organ came to St. The organ was eventually returned to the church in 1711, a process that involved considerable effort and expense. The instrument, despite its age, remains a significant artifact of English musical history, renowned for its complex tonal qualities and historical provenance. The architectural setting of the church provides an acoustically resonant backdrop for the organ's performance. Beyond the ecclesiastical significance, the building itself offers valuable insight into the evolving architectural tastes and social hierarchies of the English gentry and nobility across several centuries. The Perpendicular style, characterized by its emphasis on vertical lines and large window openings, is particularly evident in the nave and aisles, contrasting with earlier Norman elements. The careful preservation efforts undertaken by the current custodians ensure that these layers of history remain accessible for study and appreciation. The maintenance of such a large and complex structure requires constant vigilance against environmental degradation, including moisture ingress and structural fatigue. Local historical societies and architectural bodies frequently document the minor alterations and repairs that have occurred over the centuries, providing a continuous narrative of the building's life. The collection of tombs and memorials further illustrates the changing funerary practices and the social standing of the families connected to Framlingham. The intricate detail in the fan tracery, for example, demonstrates a high level of craftsmanship characteristic of the late medieval period in English ecclesiastical architecture. The longevity of the Thamar organ is remarkable, surviving periods of intense religious and political upheaval that saw many other such instruments destroyed or dismantled.
