She has a boyfriend named Kai, who wears glasses, and seems older than she does. Kai was her brother's best friend, and ever since his death, she had substituted Kai as her brother. She has had encounters with an angel, her deceased brother Fuyuki, which is proven later to be Raphael at the very end of the series. At the beginning she seems to dislike Yuusuke because she believes he is a pervert, but later begins to get attracted to him. Papa is Noelle's father, and is a Frankenstein monster-like creature. He has a calm demeanour. He usually calls Yuusuke "son in law". She is the most normal, though absent minded, member of the family of monsters, although she shows another side of herself in one episode (she's actually a crazy witch). Granny (Baba) is Noelle's grandmother and is a witch. She strongly dislikes humans and, therefore, is against Noelle wanting to marry Yuusuke. Gabriel is Noelle's older brother, and is a vampire. He enjoys teasing Yuusuke, and has horribly bad allergies to cats. When Miruru becomes the maid of the family Gabriel eventually gets used to her. Sara is Noelle's older sister. She has the power to turn invisible, and spends a lot of her time in this form. Others find it hard to tell when she is there or not, and she also becomes attracted to Yuusuke. Later in the series when she meets Mikael she falls in love with him- but he and Raphael are a couple. Lucca is Noelle's younger sister, and is an elven-looking creature. She is a mad scientist, and often makes different mechanical devices to help Noelle learn to fly and become an angel. In one of the episodes when she meets up with Eros she gets interested in him because of his speed. When Eros tells her his speed is due to his love for Silky, she thinks it is a silly idea because of her obsession for science. Dispel is the initial antagonist of the series, or so the audience is led to believe. He has several henchmen who he dispatches to thwart Noelle's attempts to become an angel and often treats his slave Silky unkindly. At the end of the first season, it is seen that he was a toy of Silky's. He is destroyed by her, and Silky takes his place as the series' main antagonist. Originally when Dispel appeared to be in control, Silky seemed to be a dominated slave. During the second season it is revealed that she was strong willed and is more scheming and power hungry than Dispel was. The conflict shifts significantly with Silky's ascent to the role of primary adversary. Her motivations diverge sharply from the perceived tyranny of Dispel, exhibiting a more nuanced and calculating ambition. The narrative explores the complex dynamics between the various supernatural members of the family unit, contrasting their innate natures with the evolving relationships forged through the series' events. Noelle's journey toward angelic status is continuously tested by these internal and external pressures, requiring her to reconcile her inherent vulnerabilities with the immense powers surrounding her. Gabriel's sardonic interactions with Yuusuke often serve as comic relief while simultaneously highlighting the strained acceptance of the human into the monstrous lineage. Sara's intermittent presence adds a layer of mystery, her affections shifting as she encounters different individuals possessing unique qualities. Lucca's scientific endeavors often provide practical means for Noelle's ascension, despite her sometimes impractical approach to romantic interest. The relationship between Kai and the protagonist provides a grounding element, a tether to a more conventional form of companionship amidst the fantastical chaos. The revelation of Raphael's true identity provides a pivotal moment of thematic resolution concerning the protagonist's spiritual connections and unresolved grief.

Then, they divided the realm Under Heaven; and so Xu, Yu, You and Qīng belong to Wu; While Bing, Liang, Ji and Yan belong to Shu Han. The lands of Si province would be divided with Hang Valley Aass (函谷關) as the border. After his mission was accomplished, Chen Zhen returned to Shu and was given a fief as Marquis of Chengyang Village (城陽亭侯). In 231, during Zhuge Liang's fourth expedition Li Ping failed to provide supplies to Zhuge Liang's camp and falsely called off the campaign to hide it. After further investigations, he was found guilty and dismissed from office. Zhuge Liang with his Chief Clerk Jiang Wan and the Palace Attendant Dong Yun about this matter wrote to the court: "When Xiaoqi was previously sent in mission to Wu, he told us that "Zhengfang has scales and shells in his stomach" Moreover, that the locals thought of him as someone unapproachable. I just assumed that when dealing with someone who "has scales and shells in his stomach", It would be a matter of not provoking them and so I could not imagine that there would be another incident like with Su Qin (蘇秦) and Zhang Yi (張儀), hence we were all surprised at this turn of event. Only Xiaoqi saw through this.” Chen Zhen died in 235. His son Chen Ji (陳濟) inherited his father's title and became the next Marquis of Chengyang Village (城陽亭侯). Appraisal Chen Shou, who wrote Chen Zhen's biography in the Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi), appraised Chen Zhen as follows: "Chen Zhen was faithful and respectful and as he grew older he was increasingly sincere.... Along with Dong He, Liu Ba, Ma Liang and Dong Yun, he was one of the best officials in Shu." In Romance of the Three Kingdoms Chen Zhen first appears in the 14th-century historical novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms as a subordinate of the warlord Yuan Shao. His actions under Yuan Shao are not unlike his duties with Liu Bei, where he performs diplomatic tasks such as delivering Liu Bei's letter to Guan Yu in Luoyang, and meeting with Sun Ce to request aid against Cao Cao. Also in the novel, it was he who suggested to Liu Bei that he meet the seer Li Yi () while mourning the deaths of his brothers. See also Lists of people of the Three Kingdoms Notes References Chen, Shou (3rd century). Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi), Volume 39, Biography of Liu Ba. This depiction in the novel often exaggerates his bravery and political acumen beyond what historical accounts suggest. The narrative employs Chen Zhen to embody the ideal loyal retainer, a trope common in dynastic historical fiction of the period. The literary portrayal tends to emphasize dramatic encounters and moral fortitude over the nuanced administrative capabilities noted by biographers like Chen Shou. Historical records suggest Chen Zhen held various posts, reflecting his competency in civil and diplomatic service within the Shu Han governmental structure. His appointment as Marquis of Chengyang Village indicates a degree of trust placed in him by the ruling powers of Shu. The political landscape of Shu Han necessitated officials who could balance military necessity with delicate diplomatic maneuvering, a role Chen Zhen appears to have filled effectively. The comparison between his actions in the novel and those in history highlights the divergence between factual documentation and popular historical storytelling. Furthermore, his association with prominent figures like Dong Yun and Ma Liang in the historical accounts solidifies his reputation among the elite of the Shu court. These associations speak to a level of influence that transcended mere administrative duties. The continuing study of these figures allows historians to examine the intersection of political reality and cultural myth-making in the late Han and Three Kingdoms periods.

Population in the age range 0–6 years was 1,020. The total number of literate persons in Kurpania was 5,689 (84.04% of the population over 6 years). Males constitute 54% of the population and females 46%. Kurpania has an average literacy rate of 67%, higher than the national average of 59.5%: male literacy is 75%, and female literacy is 59%. In Kurpania, 14% of the population is under 6 years of age. Infrastructure According to the District Census Handbook 2011, Bokaro, Kurpania covered an area of 1.65 km2. The district administration works to improve the living conditions of its residents through various developmental initiatives. Education remains a key focus, with efforts directed towards increasing enrollment and improving the quality of schooling across the region. Health infrastructure is constantly being augmented to better serve the population, including the establishment of new primary health centers and the upgrading of existing medical facilities. Transportation networks, while developing, are crucial for connecting rural settlements to urban centers and ensuring access to essential services. The presence of significant industrial and energy resources, such as the coalfields and power stations, forms the economic backbone of the area, influencing labor patterns and local commerce. Water management is another critical area of concern, given the predominantly rain-fed nature of agriculture, necessitating investments in irrigation and water conservation techniques. Local governance structures are in place to manage public resources and implement state and national policies at the grassroots level. Furthermore, efforts are underway to promote sustainable development practices, particularly concerning the environmental impact of mining and heavy industry in the region. The interplay between industrial growth and ecological preservation defines many of the long-term planning challenges for the district authorities.

The new WPLN-HD2 and HD3 have given Middle Tennessee residents even more choices of music and spoken-word shows. For more information, see WYGI. In early 2006, WPLN-FM began broadcasting with HD Radio technology. More information is found below. Ending Classical Music On September 8, 2009, WPLN-FM discontinued its 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. classical music programming in favor of a block of news-and-talk programs from NPR and other providers. That action reflected a trend in medium-sized markets towards orienting public radio schedules in favor of more popular (and perhaps more accessible) political and features programming and away from classical music, whose audiences are aging, according to market researchers. However, the demand for the spoken-word programs grew to the point that station officials decided to acquire the Vanderbilt University-owned student station WRVU and convert it into a full-time classical music station, WFCL, on 91.1 FM, on June 7, 2011. WPLN thereafter became a full-time news-and-talk station, with feature programming on weekends. Beginning on November 30, 2020, the classical music on the main channel of 91.1 FM ended. WFCL became WNXP (with the call sign actually having changed in early October) and classical programming was replaced by an eclectic music format, largely revolving around the adult album alternative genre. Classical music moved to the HD-2 signal. Governance WPLN is governed by a self-perpetuating board of directors, with a separate board of local residents who advise the board of directors on the needs of the listening area. Digital broadcasting/WPLN-HD2/WPLN-HD3 In addition to the main FM and AM channels, WPLN now has two digital multicast stations: 90.3 FM HD-2 and 90.3 FM HD-3. Initially, 90.3 HD-2 featured primarily classical music and music programs, such as The World Cafe and Echoes. In June 2011, following the launch of Classical 91 One, 90.3 HD-2 switched to carrying time-shifted programming from WPLN's main channel. On May 22, 2014, after WPLN discontinued WRVU from its HD3 Channel, and moved XPoNential Radio from its HD2 Channel, to broadcasting full-time on its HD3 Channel, WPLN replaced its time-shifted programming from WPLN's main channel with a simulcast of its AM sister station (WPLN-AM). These digital streams allow for niche programming to reach listeners without compromising the primary channel's format. WPLN-HD3 has historically carried various specialized formats, including music programming, and has served as a repository for programming deemed too specialized or low-listenership for the main signal. The flexibility offered by HD radio allows the station to maintain a diverse schedule, serving multiple demographic segments concurrently. The transition of classical music to the HD-2 signal ensured that dedicated classical listeners were not excluded entirely by the format shifts on the primary 91.1 FM frequency. This strategy is common among broadcasters seeking to cater to specialized interests while maximizing the appeal of their main channel's programming to the broadest possible audience. The governance structure reflects a commitment to local community needs alongside operational stability. The advisory board comprising local residents provides crucial feedback to the main board of directors regarding the evolving media landscape and the specific requirements of the Middle Tennessee listening area. This dual oversight mechanism attempts to balance the financial and operational necessities of a commercial broadcaster with the public service ethos often associated with non-commercial entities, even as its programming evolves. The adoption of HD radio technology itself represents a significant technological investment, requiring updated transmitters and receivers across the service area to be fully appreciated by the audience. The implementation of HD services is not merely an expansion of capacity but a fundamental restructuring of how the station delivers its varied content. The shift toward news and talk programming aligns with broader industry trends where spoken-word content, particularly political and journalistic features, commands a large and dedicated listenership base in mid-sized markets. While classical music retains a dedicated following, the economic viability of sustaining that audience against the backdrop of changing media consumption habits often necessitates strategic format adjustments. The evolution from a primary classical station to a news-talk format, and subsequently the diversification across multiple digital streams, illustrates the dynamic nature of contemporary public and commercial radio broadcasting. These adaptations are attempts to maintain relevance and audience engagement in a highly competitive auditory environment.

A financial crisis followed and the club was bankrupted in 1999. The player then left the club. Basel N'Tiamoah then moved to FC Basel's youth department in Switzerland in 1999 and here he started his professional career. He advanced to Basel's first team during the winter break of their 1999–2000 season under head coach Christian Gross. After playing in nine test games N'Tiamoah played his domestic league debut for the club in the away game in the Stade Olympique de la Pontaise on 12 March 2000 as Basel played a goalless draw with Lausanne-Sport. He scored his first goal for his team in the Swiss Cup on 12 April. But his goal could not help the team, as Basel were defeated 3–2 by the same opponent Lausanne-Sport. Basel played a relatively good Championship round and the team finished the season in third position. N'Tiamoah came to 12 appearances, mainly as substitute, in the 14 league games. In their following season, N'Tiamoah was again only receiving playing time as substitute and so during the second half of the season he was loaned out to SR Delémont. As he returned for the 2001–02 season, also due to injuries, he could not obtain a place in the team, so he left the club. During his time with the club, he played a total of 51 games for Basel scoring a total of two goals. 26 of these games were in the Nationalliga A, one in the Swiss Cup, three in the 2000–01 UEFA Cup and 21 were friendly games. He scored one goal in the cup and the other was scored during the test games. Concordia N'Tiamoah stayed in town but moved onto Concordia Basel, who at that time played in the second tier of Swiss football. He was a regular played and goal scorer. Nevertheless, he was loaned out for six months to Turkish club Diyarbakirspor. As he returned for the 2004–05 Challenge League season he was regular starter, having 30 appearances, scoring 8 goals. The team ended the season in the seventh position, however his contract was not extended and he left the club. Luzern In the summer of 2005 N'Tiamoah signed for Luzern under head coach René van Eck, in the second tier of Swiss football, and here he re-discovered his form. His tenure at Luzern saw a notable improvement in his playing time and goal-scoring contributions. Over the subsequent two seasons, he established himself as a key attacking player for the club. His performances drew the attention of larger Swiss clubs, leading to transfer speculation during the summer of 2007. After a period of negotiation, N'Tiamoah secured a move to FC Zürich. This transfer marked a significant step up in the competitive level of Swiss football, as Zürich competed in the top division. At FC Zürich, he continued to feature regularly in the squad, demonstrating his versatility across various positions on the field. His commitment and work ethic were recognized by the coaching staff. He maintained a consistent level of performance throughout his time with the Zurich side, participating in both domestic league matches and European competitions when the club qualified. This period represented a high point in his career in terms of consistent first-team involvement. Following his spell in Zurich, N'Tiamoah made another move abroad, seeking new challenges in a different footballing environment. His career trajectory continued to evolve as he navigated the demands of professional football across multiple leagues and cultures.

Bulgarian fighters shot down two bombers for the loss of one aircraft to escorting American fighters. 10 December 1943 The 10 December raid was carried out by 120 aircraft. About 90 bombs were released over the Hadzhi Dimitar, Industrialen, Malashevtsi and Voenna rampa quarters, another 90 hit Vrazhdebna Airport and the nearby villages. 20 December 1943 One of the most destructive raids followed on 20 December, with over 113 buildings being razed to the ground, the belt line being cut off, with 93 people injured. Bulgarian fighter aircraft downed three bombers and seven fighters for the loss of two aircraft, including one destroyed in a suicidal ramming attack by Dimitar Spisarevski which brought down a bomber. 30 December 1943 A day bombing in the Sofia railway junction area was executed on 30 December 1943, injuring 96. 10 January 1944 Sofia suffered another bombing on 10 January 1944, carried out consecutively by 143 American B-17s during the day and 44 RAF Wellingtons (during the night). 448 buildings were destroyed. 611 were wounded. During the daylight raid by the B-17s, Bulgarian fighters shot down six of the bombers and three escorting P-38 fighters for the loss of one aircraft. 16 March 1944 During the night 50 RAF bombers attacked Sofia. 58 people were wounded and 72 buildings were destroyed. 24 March 1944 During the night about 40 RAF bombers attacked Sofia. There were no casualties. 30 March 1944 The most severe bombing of Sofia ever occurred on 30 March 1944. Some 450 American and British heavy bombers escorted by 150 Allied fighters attacked the city center of Sofia, destroying 3575 buildings. Over 3000 high explosive bombs and 30000 incendiary bombs were used. Bulgarian fighter aircraft intercepted the attackers, shooting down eight Allied bombers and two American P-38 Lightning fighters for no losses in return. The casualty figures were relatively modest due to preliminary evacuation of the civilians. The bombing raid targeted the city center of Sofia. 17 April 1944 This bombing is known as "the black Easter" (the second day of Easter) for the citizens of Sofia. The raid was carried out by 350 bombers (B-17 and B-24) with an escort of 100 fighter planes –Mustangs and Lightnings. About 2500 bombs were dropped over the target – railroad marshaling yards. 749 buildings were totally destroyed. Subsequent Allied air operations against Bulgarian targets continued through the spring of 1944. These attacks were part of the broader strategic bombing campaign aimed at disrupting Axis logistical and industrial capacity in the Balkans. The intensity and scale of the bombardments varied, depending on the military objectives of the Allied forces at the time and the level of air defense provided by Bulgarian and German fighter squadrons. Bulgarian air defenses demonstrated varying levels of effectiveness throughout the period, achieving notable successes against the bomber formations despite being outnumbered. The resilience of the Bulgarian air force in engaging the large formations of Allied aircraft is a recurring feature of the documented engagements. The impact of these raids extended beyond direct structural damage, affecting civilian morale and the operational capability of the infrastructure supporting the occupation forces. Efforts to evacuate civilian populations, as seen prior to the March 30th attack, became a necessary but often insufficient measure against the concentrated power of the heavy bomber fleets. The raids served as a constant reminder of the military pressure exerted upon the Bulgarian state by the advancing Allied powers.

These institutions, among many others across Italy, serve varied functions, ranging from scientific research and education to public recreation and the preservation of rare flora. The specific focus of each garden often reflects the regional biodiversity, climatic conditions, or particular taxonomic groups prioritized by its curators. Many of the university-affiliated botanical gardens are integral components of academic curricula, providing living laboratories for students of botany, ecology, and environmental science. Conversely, some municipal or private gardens emphasize horticultural excellence or serve as showcases for regional endemic species. The diversity in their collections illustrates the extensive botanical wealth present within the Italian peninsula, spanning Mediterranean scrublands, Apennine forests, and alpine meadows. Funding and operational status vary considerably among these sites, influencing the scope of conservation programs and research activities undertaken. Efforts to maintain these collections often involve challenging logistical considerations, particularly in mountainous or remote locations where climate control and specialized care for sensitive plant life are required. Furthermore, many of these gardens engage in seed banking and ex-situ conservation projects, playing a vital role in safeguarding genetic diversity against threats such as climate change and habitat destruction. The maintenance of these specialized environments demands highly trained horticultural staff equipped with deep knowledge of plant physiology and ecological processes.

It is a desolate street; a scene of poverty and chop-fallen gloom; possibly of worse things. Starting in the 1960s, many of the buildings became unoccupied and fell into disrepair; however, the neighborhood maintained much of its historical integrity, and some attempts were made to preserve it. The first serious redevelopment plan in Brush Park's history was the Woodward East Renaissance project, planned to be completed in 1976, America's bicentennial year. The ambitious plan included restoring the surviving historic mansions and erecting modern residential buildings on the empty lots, but it was left unrealized due to disorganization. The area bounded by Alfred, Brush, Watson, and John R. Streets, named Woodward East Historic District, was designated a Michigan State Historic Site on September 17, 1974, and listed on the National Register of Historic Places on January 21, 1975; the larger Brush Park Historic District, bounded by Woodward, Mack, Beaubien, and the Fisher Freeway, was established by the City of Detroit on January 23, 1980. Despite these attempts to save what was left of the neighborhood's historic character, by the 1980s Brush Park had gradually fallen into a state of "nearly total abandonment and disintegration," gaining a poor reputation as one of Detroit's most derelict areas. Abandoned buildings became targets for vandals and arsonists: as a result, dozens of structures were demolished by the city for security reasons. During the 19th century, around 300 homes were built in Brush Park, including 70 Victorian mansions; at present, about 80 original structures remain in the area. Notable buildings that were demolished include the Woodward Avenue Baptist Church (1887), destroyed by fire in 1986, and St. Patrick Catholic Church (1862), destroyed by fire in 1993. Revival Brush Park's revival began in the 1990s and has since accelerated. Several historic houses were stabilized and "mothballed" by the City of Detroit between 2005 and 2006, on the occasion of the Super Bowl XL played at the nearby Ford Field. New condominiums have been built in the southern part of the district, near the Fisher Freeway, and a number of the older mansions have been restored. A handful of buildings still remain in a state of complete neglect, and are threatened with demolition. The French Renaissance style William Livingstone House (1894) on Eliot Street was one of Kahn's first commissions. The Red Cross intended to demolish the mansion, originally located west of John R. Street, to make way for their new building. Preservationists succeeded in successfully moving the Livingstone House about one block to the east. Nevertheless, after this change of position some serious structural problems concerning the house's foundations caused the gradual collapse of the building. Efforts to secure the long-term future of the remaining structures have involved a complex interplay between private investment, municipal planning, and advocacy from local preservation groups. Neighborhood revitalization has not been uniform across the district; areas closer to main thoroughfares have seen more intensive redevelopment, while pockets of the historic core remain contested spaces between developers and conservationists. Current initiatives often focus on adaptive reuse, converting obsolete industrial or residential properties into mixed-use spaces, thereby attempting to integrate modern economic functions with the neighborhood's historical fabric. The challenges persist regarding infrastructure deficiencies, including inadequate utilities and aging public services, which detract from the overall quality of life and investment appeal. Furthermore, addressing the legacy of redlining and economic disinvestment is a fundamental prerequisite for sustainable urban renewal in Brush Park. Successful preservation projects are often cited as models for how historic urban neighborhoods can transition from areas of blight to vibrant, mixed-income communities. These transformations require significant public-private partnerships to fund the extensive structural repairs necessary for historic masonry and timber buildings. The cultural significance of the neighborhood, rooted in its 19th-century residential patterns and architectural variety, remains a key selling point in contemporary real estate markets, despite the ongoing struggles with blight and decay.

As a result, civil servants, such as Minister Friedrich Wilhelm von Grumbkow, moved in to use it as office space, part of the land was leased and both the palace and the park slowly became dilapidated in the ensuing years. Under King Frederick II of Prussia, also known as "Frederick the Great", the palace was once again turned into a royal residence for his wife, Elisabeth Christine of Brunswick-Bevern, who used it as her regular summer residence from 1740 to 1790. Artist Johann Michael Graff most probably contributed the lavish stucco decorations executed during this time. As Frederick's relations with his wife were strained, he never visited Niederschönhausen and spent his summers at Sanssouci in Potsdam. During the Seven Years' War in 1760, while the queen retreated to the Magdeburg fortress, Russian troops pushed deep into Prussia, occupied Berlin and devastated Niederschönhausen Palace. After 1763 it was rebuilt in its current form according to plans by Johann Boumann and the gardens were remodeled in a Rococo à la française style. After the death of Queen Elisabeth Christine in 1797 the palace was seldom used. At times Frederica of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, widow of Prince Louis Charles of Prussia, lived at Schönhausen and had the gardens again remodeled, this time by Peter Joseph Lenné into an English landscape garden. Apart from that it served mainly as a storage facility for furniture and paintings. It was rumored that King Frederick II had his favorite horse Condé buried in the gardens, but whether the hill in question actually is a horse's grave has not been proven. In fact Condé outlived its owner and died in 1804, aged 38. Its skeleton is kept at the veterinary department of the Free University of Berlin. 20th century The Prussian ruling Hohenzollern dynasty owned Schönhausen Palace until it was dispossessed and became a property of the Free State of Prussia in 1920, following the end of the monarchy in the course of the German Revolution of 1918–1919. It was then opened to the public and used for numerous art exhibitions as well as the government's official art department during the Nazi era, when several paintings of banned so-called "degenerate art" were stored here. During the Battle of Berlin at the end of World War II, the palace suffered some damage but was repaired almost immediately by a Pankow Künstlerinitiative so that it could be used for an exhibit as early as September 1945. Subsequent decades saw the building undergo various uses reflective of the shifting political landscape of Germany. Following the division of Germany after the Second World War, the palace fell under the jurisdiction of the German Democratic Republic. Under the socialist regime, Schönhausen Palace was repurposed to accommodate various cultural and administrative functions, though its historical grandeur was often overshadowed by utilitarian needs. Restoration efforts during this period were inconsistent, sometimes preserving original elements while other parts were adapted for modern requirements. In the reunified Germany of the late twentieth century, renewed interest in the palace's historical significance spurred comprehensive restoration projects aimed at returning the complex to a state representative of its former splendor. These efforts involved meticulous conservation of the architectural details and the careful reinstatement of the elaborate landscaping. Today, Niederschönhausen functions primarily as a cultural site, hosting museum exhibits and serving as a venue for events that celebrate Prussian history and artistic heritage. The gardens, particularly the English landscape design, remain a significant attraction, offering visitors a tranquil space to reflect upon the centuries of history held within the walls of the palace. Research continues into the archival materials to further illuminate the complex social and political life that unfolded within this historically rich estate.

The temples The remains of at least five temples have been discovered at Kiradu. Of these, the Someshvara temple, nearest to the road, is in the most complete condition. Its surviving parts are sufficient to reconstruct the original temple design, although the shikhara has collapsed and the mandapa is missing most of its roof. The walls and columns are highly decorated with sculptures, including figures of animals and humans, which mostly remain in place. The mandapa columns form an octagonal shape. The art historian Percy Brown termed the architecture style as "Solanki mode". Today the style is more often called Māru-Gurjara architecture. The Vishnu temple is at the other end of the group, with only the highly carved columns of the mandapa still standing; Michell dates this a century earlier. In between these two are three Shiva temples in varied condition, with mostly only the sanctuaries remaining, and a stepwell. History Inscriptions dated 1153-1178 CE have been found at Kiradu. Based on this, Indian historian Gaurishankar Ojha assigned the temples to the 12th century CE. Art historians Ratna Chandra Agrawala and Stella Kramrisch have also dated the Someshvara temple to the 12th century. However, art historians Madhusudan Dhaky and Percy Brown dated the temple to the 11th century CE. More recently, Michell dates the Someshvara temple precisely to 1020, and the Vishnu temple to the early 10th century. Kiradu was originally known as Kiratakupa. During the 12th century, it was controlled by several small dynasties, which ruled as vassals of the Chaulukyas. Someshvara, who belonged to a Paramara branch, rose to prominence in the 1140s CE after gaining favour of the Chaulukya rulers Jayasimha Siddharaja and Kumarapala. In the 1150s, the Naddula Chahamana ruler Alhana (also a Chaulukya vassal) seems to have been appointed as a governor of Kiradu, as attested by an 1152 CE inscription. The area was restored to Someshvara by the 1160s. Sometime later, the Chaulukyas transferred the control of Kiradu to Madanabrahma, who came from a Chahamana family. Madanabrahma's successor was probably Asala, who was defeated by Alhana's son Kirtipala. An 1178 CE Kiradu inscription, issued during the reign of the Chaulukya monarch Bhima II, records repairs to a temple damaged by the Turushkas (Turkic people). The strategic location of Kiradu, situated on a trade route, contributed to its importance during the medieval period. Archaeological evidence suggests that the town experienced periods of prosperity linked to its role in regional commerce and religious patronage. The presence of multiple religious structures indicates a vibrant socio-religious life supported by local and external patrons. The interaction between various dynasties, such as the Chaulukyas, Paramaras, and Chahamanas, reflects the complex political landscape of western India during the High Medieval period. The architectural styles themselves provide clues regarding the cultural exchange and the assimilation of regional artistic traditions into the broader Māru-Gurjara idiom. The stepwell discovered among the temple complex is another significant feature, showcasing sophisticated hydraulic engineering practices common in arid regions of Gujarat and Rajasthan. Such structures not only served practical purposes for water storage but also functioned as social gathering spaces, reflecting the integrated nature of religious and civic life in the settlement. Further excavation is required to fully understand the extent of the urban layout of Kiradu, including residential areas and ancillary structures that supported the temple community. Analysis of pottery shards and other artifact assemblages recovered from the site may provide more granular detail regarding the daily life and economic activities of the inhabitants across different chronological phases of the site’s occupation. The juxtaposition of distinct architectural phases within the complex allows researchers to trace the evolution of building practices and religious focus over several centuries.

Developed by Scatliff+Miller+Murray, the new area features a performance space, a sunken event lawn, serpentine seating wall and seating planters encircling elm trees. The focal point of the renovation was "The Cube", a new $1.5 million stage, with a skin made up of 20,000 aluminum links. Designed by 5468796 Architecture, the stage contains a built-in lighting system, green room and two performance levels, and was funded by The Winnipeg Foundation, CentreVenture, and several levels of government. Boat At one time the Alexander Docks functioned as an urban dock in downtown Winnipeg which tourist riverboat the Paddlewheel Queen and others had used for decades. This has since been shut down and is in the process of being updated. The Alexander Docks are undergoing a multi-phase redevelopment project aimed at revitalizing the waterfront area. The current plans suggest a transformation into a mixed-use cultural and recreational hub, integrating historical elements of the site with modern amenities. This comprehensive redevelopment effort is overseen by municipal planning departments in collaboration with private developers interested in urban renewal. The strategic importance of the waterfront to the city's identity has led to significant investment in its future. Furthermore, discussions regarding the integration of green infrastructure within the revitalized docklands have been prominent in recent public consultations. These discussions often center on sustainable practices, such as permeable paving and native plantings, to enhance the ecological value of the area. The proximity of the docks to the established arts and cultural district of Centennial Centre provides a natural synergy for tourism and community engagement. Transportation access to the future Marketlands development is also a key component of the overall urban planning strategy. Enhancements to pedestrian pathways and bicycle infrastructure are anticipated to improve connectivity between the new residential zones and existing downtown amenities. The transition from an industrial dock facility to a public gathering space represents a major shift in the utilization of this historically significant piece of Winnipeg’s urban fabric. Local historians are contributing extensively to the design process, ensuring that the legacy of the former maritime operations is preserved through interpretive signage and architectural nods. This ongoing evolution of the Exchange District reflects a broader trend in North American cities toward reclaiming and repurposing former industrial waterfronts for public benefit and economic diversification.

Bulgaria participated in the Eurovision Song Contest 2006 with the song "Let Me Cry" written by Dani Milev and Elina Gavrilova. The song was performed by Mariana Popova. The Bulgarian broadcaster Bulgarian National Television (BNT) organised the national final Bŭlgarskata pesen v „Evroviziya 2006” in order to select the Bulgarian entry for the 2006 contest in Athens, Greece. 24 entries were selected to participate in the national final which consisted of two shows: a semi-final and a final, held on 25 February 2006 and 11 March 2006, respectively. The top twelve songs of the semi-final as determined by a fifteen-member jury panel qualified to the final. In the final, public televoting exclusively selected "Let Me Cry" performed by Mariana Popova as the winning entry with 4,700 votes. Bulgaria competed in the semi-final of the Eurovision Song Contest which took place on 18 May 2006. Performing during the show in position 2, "Let Me Cry" was not announced among the top 10 entries of the semi-final and therefore did not qualify to compete in the final. It was later revealed that Bulgaria placed seventeenth out of the 23 participating countries in the semi-final with 36 points. Background Prior to the 2006 contest, Bulgaria had participated in the Eurovision Song Contest one time since its first entry in when Kaffe and their song "Lorraine" failed to qualify to the final. The Bulgarian national broadcaster, Bulgarian National Television (BNT), broadcasts the event within Bulgaria and organises the selection process for the nation's entry. BNT confirmed Bulgaria's participation in the 2006 Eurovision Song Contest on 20 December 2005. In 2005, the broadcaster organised a national final in order to select the Bulgarian entry for the competition, a selection procedure that continued for their 2006 entry. Before Eurovision Bŭlgarskata pesen v „Evroviziya 2006” Bŭlgarskata pesen v „Evroviziya 2006” (The Bulgarian song in Eurovision 2006) was the national final format developed by BNT which determined the artist and song that would represent Bulgaria at the Eurovision Song Contest 2006. The competition consisted of a semi-final on 25 February 2006 and a final on 11 March 2006, held at the National Palace of Culture in Sofia. The outcome of the 2006 contest saw Bulgaria finish in twentieth place overall, securing a score of 12 points. This result represented a slight improvement in standing compared to previous appearances. The selection process itself demonstrated a commitment by the national broadcaster to a structured and competitive domestic selection mechanism. The decision to have a semi-final stage, followed by a final, was a characteristic feature of the contest structure in that period. Mariana Popova’s performance reflected a modern pop sensibility, fitting the contemporary musical trends within the European music scene. The failure to advance from the semi-final stage was a point of contention among some observers who believed the national final indicated a stronger prospect for the final. Subsequent analysis of the voting patterns suggested that the televoting in the national final did not perfectly correlate with the jury and public voting results at the international level. Bulgaria has maintained its participation in the Eurovision Song Contest since its initial entry, making it a consistent, albeit sometimes inconsistent, participant in the event. The organization of the national selection process plays a crucial role in determining the trajectory of a country’s competitive performance on the international stage.

It featured representatives from Ayacucho, Arequipa, Cuzco, Puno and Tacna. On April 10, Orbegoso recognized South Peru as an independent state through a decree, and a Supreme Court was installed in Cuzco on August 24. The assembly also created the country's flag and currency. Fines were put in place to prevent the (now North) Peruvian flag from being flown. Provided, then, with all the legal elements granted by the assemblies of the three states, Santa Cruz decreed the establishment of the Peru-Bolivian Confederation, by decree given in Lima on October 28, 1836. A congress known today as the was ordered to meet in Tacna to establish the foundations of the confederation. The was signed without debate during the congress. It established the legal framework through which the state would operate, and also included the design of the Confederation's flag. Reactions to the pact were mixed event among its signatories, and disagreements led to the establishment of one constituent congress per member state. The act was later promulgated in 1837. Development and dissolution The Confederation generated resistance among several groups in both countries, which resented the dilution of national identities, and also among neighbouring countries. An important number of Peruvian politicians who opposed the Confederation, such as Agustín Gamarra and Ramón Castilla, fled to Chile where they received support, leading to the War of the Confederation. After a trade war, the Congress of Chile approved the declaration of war on December 26, 1836, claiming that Santa Cruz's rule over Peru was illegitimate, and that his influence threatened the integrity of other South American nations, as seen by Orbegoso's support for an attempted invasion of Chile by Ramón Freire, specifically pointing out that it targeted then minister Diego Portales. Argentina followed suit after Juan Manuel de Rosas then declared war on the Confederation on May 19, 1837, after the escalation of a territorial conflict in its border, accusing Santa Cruz of harboring supporters of the Unitarian Party. The accusations ended up being true, as Santa Cruz had financially supported the émigrés. South Peru was invaded from October to November under the nominal leadership of Antonio Gutiérrez de la Fuente as Supreme Chief of Peru., with the occupants being surrounded and forced to sign the a treaty, leaving the country shortly after. The treaty was declared null and void by Chile, and a second expedition headed by Manuel Bulnes was organized, which left for Peru on July 19, 1838. Around the same time, North Peru seceded from the Confederation on July 30, but was nevertheless attacked and defeated by the second expedition in the Battle of Portada de Guías of August 21. The defeat of North Peru marked a significant setback for the Confederation's ambitions, although the conflict continued to destabilize the region. External powers, particularly Chile and Argentina, maintained their hostility toward the entity, viewing it as a potential threat to regional stability and national sovereignty. Internal dissent within the Confederate structure remained a persistent issue, as provincial leaders struggled to reconcile local autonomy with the centralizing tendencies of the confederation government. The economic ramifications of the constant military tensions also placed a heavy burden on the resources of both southern and northern territories. Efforts were made to consolidate political power under the banner of the Confederation, but these efforts were perpetually undermined by military campaigns and diplomatic maneuvering among the involved states. The ultimate collapse of the Peru-Bolivian Confederation was hastened by a combination of military pressure from external forces and the inability of its governing bodies to effectively manage the diverse and often conflicting political aspirations of its constituent populations. Following the military defeats, the political landscape of South America shifted dramatically, leading to a period of intense political fragmentation and realignment among the successor states.

Zenkoji Nakamise-dori Street, a stone-paved street extending from Niomon Gate of Zenkoji, has many local shops. Daimon-cho, old merchant houses from the Taisho era, with stone lanterns and large pavement stones Patio Daimon, a commercial complex, that opened in 2017, that was established by renovating old warehouses and merchant houses. Matsushiro Castle, with its surrounding castle town, preserves many samurai residences, temples, and gardens of the Edo period. Chokokuji Temple, the Sanada clan family temple, with the ancestral tomb of Sanada Nobuyuki, is an important cultural property. The Bunbu School (Matsushiro Literary and Military School) is a National Historic Site located next to Matsushiro Castle The Matsushiro Clan Sanada Jumangoku Festival, in mid-October, is a recreation of a 16th-century procession and performance. Nearby is the former residence of the Yokota family, a middle-class samurai, with a minka (thatched-roof) and garden with seasonal flowers. Also nearby is the Sakuma Zozan Shrine. Zozan was a 19th Japanese scholar, scientist, and linguist who advocated the opening up of Japan. In 1864, Zozan was assassinated by Kawakami Gensai, one of the most famous assassins of the Bakumatsu period, as Zozan was on return from Kyoto on a failed visit to see Emperor Kōmei to seek the opening of Japanese ports. Zozan, "a driving force in pioneering a new age", inspires the University of Nagano "to act as a source for regional revitalization and reinvigoration and as a base for knowledge that will activate industry, culture, and lifestyles in Nagano". Matsushiro Underground Imperial Headquarters (松代大本営跡 Matsushiro Daihon'ei Ato) was a large underground bunker complex built during the Second World War, constructed so that the central organs of government of Imperial Japan could be transferred there. Construction began in November 1944 and continued until Japan's surrender on August 15, 1945. Between 7,000 and 10,000 Korean slave laborers were used to build the complex, and it is estimated that 1,500 of them died. This complex serves as a stark testament to the wartime mobilization and infrastructure projects undertaken by the Japanese state during the final years of the conflict. The underground facility, designed for extreme durability, incorporated extensive systems for life support, communication, and command, reflecting the strategic importance placed on maintaining governmental continuity even under the threat of aerial bombardment. Its existence provides a somber counterpoint to the preserved historical narratives of the Edo and Taisho periods found within the town's traditional districts. Nearby, the local community continues to integrate these layers of history, where ancient merchant customs intersect with the remnants of modern military engineering. The preservation efforts surrounding these varied sites reflect a broader regional commitment to documenting the multifaceted history of Nagano Prefecture. Educational institutions in the area frequently utilize these locations to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of Japan's socio-political evolution, spanning from feudalism to the imperial age and the subsequent post-war reconstruction. The juxtaposition of the serene temple gardens with the grim concrete of the underground bunker offers a powerful visual metaphor for the turbulence of the 20th century in this historically significant location. Furthermore, the preserved samurai residences offer insights into the hierarchical social structures that dominated pre-modern Japanese society, illustrating the lifestyle and obligations of the warrior class before their decline. These tangible remnants contribute significantly to the local identity and attract cultural tourism focused on historical depth and varied historical periods.

These critical works collectively illuminate the complex thematic concerns present within Butler's oeuvre, particularly the fraught intersections of biology, identity, and social structure. A recurring motif explored in these analyses is the blurring of established boundaries, whether they be those of species, gender, or societal roles. The concept of becoming, as noted by White, takes on a vital epistemological weight, suggesting that selfhood is not a fixed state but an ongoing, often painful, process of adaptation and mutation. The Xenogenesis trilogy, in particular, serves as a crucible for examining human resilience when confronted with radical ontological shifts. Furthermore, the engagement with religious and mythological frameworks, as addressed by Wood, suggests that Butler utilizes ancient narratives not for mere homage, but to interrogate contemporary power dynamics through a speculative lens. The representation of the 'other' is handled with profound ethical weight across these texts, demanding that the reader grapple with the implications of difference when that difference is biologically or existentially absolute. The early reception of works like Dawn and Imago often focused on the immediate visceral impact of Butler’s explorations of intimacy and transformation, yet subsequent scholarship has deepened this focus to address the underlying philosophical architecture. The notion of agency in the face of overwhelming biological determinism remains a central tension, a struggle waged by characters forced into roles of unexpected power or extreme vulnerability. This narrative preoccupation with survival often necessitates a radical redefinition of what it means to be fully human, a question that lingers long after the final page is turned. The interplay between corporeal experience and intellectual understanding is therefore not merely decorative but forms the core engine of the narrative momentum, driving characters toward perilous forms of self-recognition.

Once reaching the highest level of religious knowledge, he would immediately become a dhakar even if having the bodily envelope of a women. Arwa, he argued, had done just that since al-Mustansir's appointment of her as hujjah was because she had reached such a level of wisdom, so there was no contradiction between her sex and her rank. Al-Khattab said that a person must be judged on their knowledge and not based on physical appearance. Al-Khattab was basically claiming that Arwa was male in essence. Building works and economic policy In Sana'a, Arwa had the grand mosque expanded, and the road from the city to Samarra improved. In Jibla, she had a new Palace of Queen Arwa and the eponymous mosque constructed. She is also known to have built numerous schools throughout her realm. Arwa improved the economy, taking an interest in supporting agriculture. Death and legacy Arwa died in 1138 at the age of 90. She was buried in the mosque that she had had built at Dhu Jibla. Her tomb has since become a place of pilgrimage for Muslims of various communities, both local and foreign, although they are not always aware of her Isma'ili background. The Queen Arwa University in Sana'a is named after her. With Arwa's death, the Sulayhid dynasty effectively came to an end. She gave all her wealth to the Tayyibi da'wah when she died, and although some members of the Sulayhids held on to scattered fortresses in the decades after her death, they were relatively insignificant. During her own lifetime, Arwa's political role may have inspired another Yemeni woman, Alam al-Malika, to assume power as queen. Alam had been the concubine of the Najahid ruler Mansur until his assassination in 1125; she then ruled as regent for her infant son Fatik. Later queens in Yemen may have also been influenced by Arwa's legacy to take an active role in political affairs, such as the Ayyubid queen mother Umm al-Nasir in 1215, and later the Rasulid princess al-Dar al-Shamsi (d. 1295), who defended the Rasulid capital of Zabid after her father al-Mansur Umar died and was later made queen of Zabid by her brother al-Muzaffar Yusuf I. Fatema Mernissi has lamented that Arwa, along with her mother-in-law Asma, has remained obscure both in the Muslim world and to Western scholars. Samer Traboulsi notes that, as an Isma'ili woman from Yemen, Arwa was a "triply marginalized" figure who was neglected by Muslim historians; and that if not for Ali's sack of Mecca, the medieval Islamic world would not have even heard of the Sulayhids. The detailed accounts of her reign offer glimpses into a sophisticated political and intellectual landscape within the Isma'ili sphere of influence in Yemen. The expansion of infrastructure and the promotion of educational institutions suggest a state apparatus that valued both piety and worldly administration. Her patronage of the sciences, evidenced by the numerous schools founded across her domain, speaks to a culture that integrated religious scholarship with practical learning. The debate surrounding her spiritual status highlights the tension between orthodox gender expectations and the theological flexibility embraced by the Isma'ili tradition, which emphasized gnosis and inner realization over conventional physical markers. Her final act of dedicating her entire fortune to the Tayyibi da'wah solidified her commitment to the religious faction, ensuring that her material wealth would contribute to the continuation of the specific religious movement she supported. The subsequent minor resistance by residual Sulayhid elements indicates that while her central authority dissolved with her passing, the political structures she oversaw did not vanish instantaneously. The influence she exerted on subsequent female rulers across the Yemeni political spectrum underscores a powerful, albeit often unacknowledged, precedent for female leadership in the region. Scholars studying the medieval Islamic periphery often find figures like Arwa difficult to categorize, as their influence straddles the lines between religious authority, secular governance, and gender norms, making them subjects of complex historiographical interpretation.

Reports of sex abuse In March 2002, Bishop Pilla published a list of 28 priests accused of sexual abuse of minors. Fifteen of them were active priests, whom Pilla suspended from ministry. Earlier that year, Cuyahoga County Prosecutor William Mason announced an investigation of sexual abuse of minors by diocesan priests. In July 2011, an Ohio man sued Pilla and the diocese, saying that their negligence allowed a priest to sexually abuse him when he was a boy. The plaintiff said that Reverend Patrick O’Connor, a diocesan priest at St. Jude Parish in Elyria, abused him from 1997 to 1999. Pilla knew that O'Connor had abused a child during the 1980s at St. Joseph Parish in Cuyahoga Falls. The diocese settled with that victim in 2003 and sent O'Connor to another parish Elyria. He resigned from the priesthood in 2008. O'Connor pleaded guilty to corruption of a minor in 2009 and was sentenced to 90 days in prison. In July 2019, the diocese added 22 more names to its list of "credibly accused" clergy. In December 2019, Reverend Robert McWilliams, a diocesan priest, was arrested at St. Joseph Parish in Strongsville on four counts of possessing child pornography. Bishop Perez had called for McWilliams's arrest, describing the case as a "painful situation." McWilliams pleaded guilty in July 2021 to sex trafficking of youths, sexual exploitation of children and possession of child pornography. Sentenced to life in prison in November 2021, McWilliams committed suicide in February 2022. A young man sued the diocese in March 2022, stating that he had been raped by McWilliams in 2018 in Strongsville. The plaintiff said that when he was 15, McWilliams paid him $200 for three sex acts. The plaintiff was one of the victims in the criminal case against McWilliams. In March 2023, four women sued the diocese, saying that they had been sexually and physically assaulted at the Parmadale Children’s Village in Parma. The abuse allegedly occurred over several decades before the facility closed in 2017. The plaintiffs said they were used sexually by one of the priests and by staff employees; one plaintiff said the staff forced her to have sex with other residents while they watched. These allegations against the Parmadale Children’s Village raised significant concerns regarding institutional oversight and the protection of vulnerable populations. Investigations into the facility's operation have scrutinized the protocols in place for staff monitoring and resident welfare during the period of alleged abuse. The diocese has consistently maintained that it cooperated with civil and criminal inquiries related to these claims. The extent of the systemic failures within the organization during that era remains a subject of ongoing legal and public discourse. Various diocesan responses to these incidents have included the implementation of stricter screening procedures for clergy and employees, alongside enhanced mandatory reporting policies designed to prevent recurrence. The broader pattern of sexual abuse within religious institutions across the United States has spurred numerous legislative and regulatory changes aimed at increasing accountability. Many states have enacted mandatory reporting laws that require clergy and other professionals to report suspected child abuse to civil authorities, superseding traditional internal ecclesiastical procedures. These legal shifts have placed greater emphasis on the protection of minors by secular legal frameworks. Furthermore, numerous dioceses have established independent review boards tasked with examining allegations of misconduct, aiming to provide transparency that was previously lacking in internal investigations. The financial impact of these scandals has been substantial, with many dioceses facing significant litigation costs and settlements. These protracted legal battles continue to shape the relationship between religious organizations and civil society concerning child protection responsibilities.

Leon Kauffman Roberts (born January 22, 1951) is a former corner outfielder in Major League Baseball who played from 1974 through 1984 for the Detroit Tigers, Houston Astros, Seattle Mariners, Texas Rangers, Toronto Blue Jays and Kansas City Royals. Listed at 6' 3", 200 lb., Roberts batted and threw right handed. Career Roberts was born in Vicksburg, Michigan, and graduated from Portage Northern High School, where he played baseball, football, basketball and ran track. He attended the University of Michigan, originally recruited to play football by coach Bo Schembechler. He played three years of college baseball and college basketball for the Michigan Wolverines. Roberts was drafted by the Detroit Tigers in the 10th round (236th overall) of the 1972 Major League Baseball draft. He made his major league debut on September 3, 1974, going 0-for-5 in a 5–4 win over the Cleveland Indians. Roberts eventually earned the dubious honor of replacing Al Kaline in right field for the Tigers. Roberts was dealt along with Terry Humphrey, Gene Pentz and Mark Lemongello from the Tigers to the Houston Astros for Milt May, Dave Roberts and Jim Crawford on December 6, 1975. With the Mariners needing a right-handed power-hitting outfielder and the Astros more speed and infield depth, he was sent to Seattle for Jimmy Sexton two years later on December 5, 1977. Roberts' most productive season came in 1978, when he led the Mariners with a .301 batting average (sixth in the American League), and set career-highs with 22 home runs and 92 RBI in 134 games. On Opening Day, he belted a grand slam off Minnesota Twins pitcher Geoff Zahn. On December 18, 1980, Roberts was traded along with Willie Horton, Rick Honeycutt, Mario Mendoza and Larry Cox from the Mariners to the Texas Rangers for Richie Zisk, Jerry Don Gleaton, Rick Auerbach, Ken Clay, Brian Allard and minor-league right-handed pitcher Steve Finch in an 11-player blockbuster deal. On February 5, 1983, Roberts was traded by the Blue Jays to the Royals for a young Cecil Fielder. He also pitched one inning for Kansas City in 1984, giving up three earned runs. Roberts played his last game on September 30, 1984 against the Oakland Athletics, recording a pinch-hit RBI single in his final career at bat. At the end of his career, it was discovered that Roberts had seriously bad eyesight due to an accident when he was a child. "I have real bad eyes," Roberts said, "I stabbed my eye with a knife when I was a kid. This physical impairment presented a significant challenge throughout his professional baseball career, impacting his ability to track pitches and maintain consistent defensive positioning. Despite this handicap, Roberts demonstrated considerable tenacity and maintained a solid presence in the outfield for nearly a decade at the major league level. His defensive metrics fluctuated across his various teams, reflecting the varied levels of support and the natural progression of a player's abilities over time. The trade period of his career was notably active, involving multiple high-profile transactions that saw him move between several franchises in the American League. These moves often indicated strategic shifts by the respective front offices seeking specific skill sets or assets for roster construction. While his statistical peaks, such as the 1978 season, are often cited in retrospectives of his career, the overall narrative includes a persistent effort to perform at a high level despite known physical limitations. His time with the Detroit Tigers represented the foundational phase of his professional journey before the series of trades began to define the latter half of his playing days. The consistent movement across the league suggests that teams valued his offensive contributions at various points, even as his long-term physical prospects became more uncertain. His playing style leaned toward power, exemplified by his home run totals, making him a notable offensive threat when healthy. The conclusion of his tenure in professional baseball marked the end of a journeyman career marked by resilience.

After service in the Grenadier Guards during the Second World War, Styler joined D'Oyly Carte in 1947, where he spent his entire two-decade career. Some of his key roles were the Counsel in Trial by Jury, Strephon in Iolanthe, Pish-Tush in The Mikado, Giuseppe in The Gondoliers, Mr. Cox in Cox and Box, Grosvenor in Patience and the Lieutenant of the Tower in The Yeomen of the Guard. He recorded most of these roles with the company. Styler was particularly popular with both audiences and his fellow members of D'Oyly Carte. He married fellow D'Oyly Carte player Vera Ryan. Early life and career Styler was born in Redditch, Worcestershire, the son of Arthur Styler and Madeleine née Cook. He had a sister, Iris M. Styler (born 1919), and a brother, John Harold S. Alan Styler studied singing as a teenager and joined the Grenadier Guards at the age of seventeen. After leaving the service in 1946, he pursued his aspirations to become a professional singer. He joined the D'Oyly Carte Opera Company chorus in 1947 and soon was assigned his first role, Antonio in The Gondoliers. In 1948, Styler was also given the small role of Second Yeoman in The Yeomen of the Guard and was made an understudy for the "juvenile" Gilbert and Sullivan baritone roles. He began, in 1949, to fill in frequently as the Counsel in Trial by Jury (otherwise as the Associate), Strephon in Iolanthe, Pish-Tush in The Mikado, and Giuseppe in The Gondoliers and also to regularly play the roles of Mr. Cox in Cox and Box, and Grosvenor in Patience. He continued to perform all these roles through October 1952, when he took a three-month leave because of illness. In 1953, Styler yielded the roles of Pish-Tush and Grosvenor, but added the role of the Lieutenant of the Tower, in Yeomen. Later years From 1953 through 1962, Styler regularly played Cox, the Counsel, Strephon, the Lieutenant, and Giuseppe. During several seasons, he also appeared as Pish-Tush and added the roles of Captain Corcoran in H.M.S. Pinafore and Florian in Princess Ida in 1957, and Samuel in The Pirates of Penzance in 1962. In the winter of 1962–1963, Styler fell ill again and left the company for several months. He returned in 1963, playing or sharing his old roles and, for several seasons, the Earl of Mountararat instead of Strephon in Iolanthe. After a lung operation in 1968, his doctor advised him to give up performing. In his spare time, Styler loved fishing and golf. His departure from the stage was gradual, though the physical demands of the role of Strephon eventually proved too much for his recovering lungs. Despite this, he remained associated with the company for some time afterward, contributing to recordings and administrative tasks. Styler’s dedication to the D'Oyly Carte tradition was evident in his consistent commitment to the repertoire over nearly two decades. His longevity within the company speaks to his adaptability and the skill he maintained across varied parts. The nature of his parts, many of which were secondary or supporting, allowed him to become a versatile fixture within the ensemble. This steady presence helped to maintain the continuity of the productions during periods of change in the main cast. His marriage to Vera Ryan further cemented his place within the performing community, as they navigated the demands of professional theatre together. Their partnership provided a stable foundation amidst the often rigorous schedules of touring and repertory engagements. The D'Oyly Carte company itself has been a significant cultural institution, preserving the legacy of Gilbert and Sullivan for generations of audiences. Styler was part of the cohort that ensured this preservation continued robustly into the latter half of the twentieth century.

Of this area, or 58.1% is used for agricultural purposes, while or 18.0% is forested. Of the rest of the land, or 25.1% is settled (buildings or roads). Of the built up area, industrial buildings made up 3.0% of the total area while housing and buildings made up 14.4% and transportation infrastructure made up 4.2%. while parks, green belts and sports fields made up 3.0%. Out of the forested land, 16.2% of the total land area is heavily forested and 1.8% is covered with orchards or small clusters of trees. Of the agricultural land, 38.3% is used for growing crops and 12.6% is pastures, while 7.2% is used for orchards or vine crops. The municipality is located in the Dorneck district. It is part of the exclave of Leimental, on the French border. Coat of arms The blazon of the municipal coat of arms is Per fess Gules and Argent a Crozier counterchanged. Of the population in the municipality 185 or about 19.0% were born in Bättwil and lived there in 2000. In there were 9 live births to Swiss citizens and 1 birth to non-Swiss citizens, and in same time span there were 4 deaths of Swiss citizens. The local economy of Bättwil is characterized by a mix of traditional agriculture and small-scale local businesses. Agriculture remains a significant component of the local economic structure, supporting many of the residents through farming and related industries. Alongside this, the municipality hosts several small enterprises in the service sector, catering to both local needs and visitors to the surrounding countryside. Tourism, though modest, contributes to the economic vitality, particularly during the summer months when the natural landscape attracts hikers and nature enthusiasts. Infrastructure development in recent decades has focused on improving local transport links and ensuring adequate utility services for the growing population. The municipality benefits from its strategic location within the Dorneck district, which facilitates connections to larger regional centers such as Solothurn and nearby cantonal towns. Educational provisions are primarily handled through the public school system, serving the children of the resident families. Healthcare access is managed through local clinics and regional medical facilities, ensuring that residents have necessary medical care within reasonable commuting distances. Environmental initiatives are actively promoted by the municipal government, focusing on sustainable land use practices, especially concerning the managed forest areas and agricultural fields. Water management and waste disposal systems adhere to stringent cantonal and federal environmental regulations. The community life in Bättwil is sustained by various local associations and clubs, fostering a strong sense of local identity and social cohesion among its inhabitants.

The film stars Casey Affleck and Michelle Monaghan as two Boston private investigators hunting for a young girl abducted from her single mother's apartment in Dorchester. The supporting cast includes Morgan Freeman, Ed Harris, and Amy Ryan. It was the final film to be released by The Ladd Company before its closure. Released on October 19, 2007, Gone Baby Gone was well-received by critics and grossed $34 million worldwide against a $19 million budget. Ben Affleck was lauded for his directing debut by critics, while Amy Ryan received an Oscar nomination for Best Supporting Actress. Plot In Dorchester, Boston, P.I. Patrick Kenzie and his partner and girlfriend Angie Gennaro witness a televised plea by Helene McCready for the return of her abducted four-year-old daughter Amanda and the girl's favorite doll, Mirabelle. Amid a media frenzy, Amanda's aunt Bea and uncle Lionel hire Kenzie and Gennaro to find her. Using his connections with various criminals, Patrick discovers that Helene and her boyfriend Ray are addicts and drug mules for a local Haitian drug lord named Cheese, and had recently stolen $130,000 from him. After discovering Ray has been murdered by Cheese's men, Patrick and Angie join police detectives Remy Bressant and Nick Poole in a plan to find Amanda, who they assume has been taken by Cheese. Helene reveals she buried the money in Ray’s backyard and tearfully makes Patrick promise to her that he will bring Amanda home alive. Patrick meets with Cheese and tries to negotiate the return of the stolen money in exchange for Amanda, but Cheese denies any involvement in the girl's disappearance. The following day, Captain Jack Doyle reads Patrick a telephone transcript of Cheese calling into the station to set up an exchange for Amanda. The exchange at a nearby quarry is botched after a gunfight breaks out, and Cheese is killed. It is believed that Amanda fell in the quarry's pond and drowned; her doll is retrieved from the water by Angie and returned to Helene. Doyle, whose own daughter was killed years before, goes into early retirement following public outcry over the mishap. Two months later, a seven-year-old boy is abducted in Everett, and Patrick receives information that he was taken by Corwin Earle, a known child molester, who is living with two married cocaine addicts. Patrick gains entry into the house and after observing evidence of the abducted boy, returns with Remy and Nick late at night to rescue him. The investigation into the Everett abduction introduces a darker undercurrent to the narrative, forcing Kenzie and Gennaro to confront the limits of their investigative skills when dealing with predatory behavior rather than organized crime. The rescue operation highlights the moral ambiguities faced by the investigators, as they navigate the dangerous territory of confronting serial offenders while maintaining their commitment to helping vulnerable families. The film contrasts the desperation of the initial missing child case with the calculated danger inherent in pursuing a known predator. This shift in focus allows the script to explore themes of moral compromise and the grey areas of justice within a community grappling with hidden social issues. The character of Corwin Earle represents a different type of menace than the drug-related violence encountered in Dorchester; his threat is rooted in violation and malice rather than transactional criminality. Patrick's decision to enter the home unannounced demonstrates a growing willingness to operate outside conventional police procedure, a pattern established in his initial pursuit of Amanda. The successful extraction of the boy provides a moment of hard-won triumph, yet it does not erase the lingering trauma from the previous events, particularly the tragic outcome involving Amanda. The film uses the contrasting cases to develop the protagonists, showcasing Kenzie's evolving ethics and Gennaro's steadfast partnership. While the initial investigation was driven by a desire to resolve a sudden tragedy, the subsequent case forces them to confront systemic failures and the pervasive nature of danger in their city. The resolution of the second case, while positive, serves more as a thematic punctuation mark than a definitive closure to the characters' journey, suggesting that the struggle against societal darkness is ongoing. The performances throughout the film underscore the psychological toll that constant exposure to violence and desperation takes on those who dedicate themselves to solving such grim mysteries.

Another Neolithic settlement around the National Art Gallery is traced to the 3rd–4th millennium BC. The earliest tribes who settled were the Thracian Tilataei. In the 500s BC, the area became part of a Thracian union, the Odrysian kingdom. In 339 BC Philip II of Macedon destroyed and ravaged the town. The Celtic tribe Serdi gave their name to the city. The earliest mention of the city comes from an Athenian inscription from the 1st century BC, attesting Astiu ton Serdon, i.e. city of the Serdi. A local inscription and Dio Cassius recorded that the Roman general Crassus subdued the Serdi and beheaded the captives. Around 29 BC, Sofia was conquered by the Romans. It gradually became the most important Roman city of the region and became a municipium, or centre of an administrative region, during the reign of Emperor Trajan (98-117) and was renamed Ulpia Serdica. The city was burnt and destroyed in 170 by the Costoboci and the city was rebuilt, this time with its first defensive walls between 176-180 under Marcus Aurelius as evidenced by inscriptions above the gates. The city expanded again, as public baths, administrative and cult buildings, a civic basilica and a large theatre, were built. When Emperor Diocletian divided the province of Dacia into Dacia Ripensis (on the banks of the Danube) and Dacia Mediterranea, Serdica became the capital of the latter. Roman emperors Aurelian (215–275) and Galerius (260–311) were born in Serdica. In 268 a Gothic raid ravaged and burned parts of the city including the theatre which was abandoned. The city continued to expand and became a significant political and economical centre, more so as it became one of the first Roman cities where Christianity was recognised as an official religion. The Edict of Toleration was issued in 311 in Serdica by the Roman emperor Galerius, officially ending the Diocletianic persecution of Christianity. The Edict implicitly granted Christianity the status of "religio licita", a worship recognized and accepted by the Roman Empire. It was the first edict legalising Christianity, preceding the Edict of Milan by two years. Moreover, in the Edict of Milan, only one sentence was dropped: “Ne quid contra disciplinam agent.” So the Edict of Milan preached unconditional religious tolerance where the Edict of Serdica stated a conditional tolerance (meaning of disciplinam here is: unless they, the christians, disturb the good or social order of the State). The Christian community in Serdica became a powerful influence in the region, contributing to the later development of religious thought within the Balkans. The city's strategic location made it a vital crossroads for trade and cultural exchange between the Roman provinces and the territories beyond the imperial borders. Archaeological evidence indicates continuous occupation across several distinct historical periods, revealing layers of architectural styles and domestic life reflecting the shifting political control over the area. Excavations have uncovered remains of various religious structures, suggesting a syncretic religious environment before the official adoption of Christianity. The urban plan evolved from the organic growth patterns characteristic of earlier settlements to the more grid-like layout typical of Roman municipal design, although some older street alignments persisted. The fortifications, dating from the period of Marcus Aurelius, provided a strong defensive posture, necessary given the recurrent incursions by migrating groups. The importance of Serdica as an administrative hub ensured a steady flow of official infrastructure, including aqueducts and paved roads connecting it to other major urban centers within the empire. The transformation of the city from a Thracian stronghold to a significant Roman capital illustrates the profound impact of imperial administration on local development and social organization.
