Their circulation patterns and editorial stances often reflect broader regional trends while simultaneously documenting unique local events. Early editions frequently contained lengthy local advertisements detailing agricultural sales, real estate transactions, and services provided by local merchants. Furthermore, obituaries and marriage announcements offered a tangible record of community membership and demographic shifts over time. The evolution of these newspapers mirrors the modernization of Kansas itself, transitioning from purely agrarian reporting to incorporating more national and international news coverage as transportation and communication networks improved. Some later publications began to adopt a more overtly partisan tone, aligning themselves closely with specific political factions, which necessitated careful source evaluation when conducting historical research. The advent of mass printing technology significantly increased the production capacity of these papers, allowing for greater coverage depth and wider distribution across the state. Digital archives and modern journalistic practices have subsequently altered how this vital local information is accessed and preserved, but the foundational records remain invaluable for social historians studying the development of Kansas society.

A small amount of the distillery's output is exported to Belgium, the Netherlands, France, Great Britain, Germany, Italy, and the United States. History The distillery in Łańcut was founded by Duchess Lubomirska on the vast estate of the Lubomirski family. An original document attesting to the distillery's existence in 1784 can be found in its museum. Primarily the Łańcut estate produced regular, anise flavoured and sweetened vodkas. Count Alfred Wojciech Potocki, a grandson and heir of the Duchess, started to run the Łańcut and Lwów Lubomirski estates in 1823. He modernised the management of these properties, and implemented the Schwartz distillation equipment. The production of premium vodkas, liqueurs, creams and ratafias was started, in addition to regular and anise flavoured vodkas. The estate ran two company outlets in Lwów and Vienna. In 1882 Alfred Józef Potocki created a network of agents to promote sales in Galicia and Austria-Hungary. Trains of the Viennese rail lines passing through the town of Łańcut used to make longer stops to allow travellers to buy the distilleries' famous products. In 1900, Count Alfred Potocki's Distillery won a gold medal at the International Exposition in Paris for his array of products. Between 1911–1912 Roman Potocki moved the plant to a newly equipped building. Some of the buildings were destroyed with the eruption of World War I. The difficulties were helped by establishing a stock company in 1917. In 1924 the State alcohol monopoly was funded in Warsaw. Łańcut distillery managed to hold its position among the best companies in the country thanks to investments in equipment and innovations. The plant survived the outbreak of World War II largely intact, but it suffered major destruction in 1944 from the withdrawing German armies and advancing Russian units. In 1951 a state enterprise called Łańcut Spirits Industries was created out of the Łańcut Spirits Stock Company and Count Alfred Potocki's Privileged Distillery of Liqueurs, Rosoglios and Rum in Łańcut. In 1969 the plant was producing fifteen kinds of unflavoured and flavoured vodkas, about 200,000 bottles a day. Modernization efforts continued throughout the later decades of the twentieth century, focusing on increasing production capacity and diversifying the product portfolio beyond traditional vodka offerings. The distillery adapted to evolving market demands, incorporating new technologies while maintaining a commitment to traditional Polish distillation methods. The post-war period necessitated significant reconstruction and reorganization to meet the needs of the national economy. Throughout the communist era, the state maintained control over the facility, integrating it into the larger centralized plan for alcohol production within the Polish People's Republic. Despite periods of political and economic turbulence, the brand name maintained a degree of recognition within the domestic market. Following the political transition at the end of the twentieth century, the distillery underwent privatization, allowing for a shift towards a more market-oriented operational structure. This change enabled the company to explore new distribution channels and compete in both domestic and international markets more vigorously than in previous decades. Contemporary production emphasizes quality control, adherence to EU standards, and the preservation of historical recipes while introducing modern flavor profiles to cater to diverse consumer preferences. The estate remains a significant cultural touchstone, balancing industrial production with heritage preservation.

These records highlight the depth and diverse experiences of professional baseball players during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Many of these individuals navigated periods of significant organizational instability, moving between multiple teams across various leagues as the sport itself was in a state of rapid professional evolution. The varying career lengths and the transition between the National League, American Association, and other short-lived professional circuits underscore the competitive and sometimes volatile nature of early baseball careers. The achievements noted, such as firsts in fielding or offensive milestones, represent important markers in the historical record of the game. The longevity of some players, like Candy Nelson, demonstrates remarkable durability in a sport with demanding physical requirements. Conversely, the single-game appearances of others suggest the fluidity of rosters and the difficulty in securing long-term spots in major league clubs during that era. The development of base-running achievements, as seen with Dan McGann's remarkable feat, reflects the increasing strategic sophistication of the sport as teams began to exploit every advantage available on the field. These entries collectively paint a picture of a professional baseball landscape far different from contemporary standards, rich with pioneering figures who shaped the sport's foundational lore.

All the water in the municipality is flowing water. Of the unproductive areas, 2.8% is unproductive vegetation and 1.5% is too rocky for vegetation. The municipality is located in the Sierre district. The original haufendorf village (an irregular, unplanned and quite closely packed village, built around a central square) was located on the left side of the Lienne and along the right side of the Rhone valley. By the middle of the 20th Century, it had spread out into the valley floor. Coat of arms The blazon of the municipal coat of arms is Azure, issuant from Coupeaux Vert a Pine tree of the same trunked proper between in chief two Mullets of Five Or. Demographics Saint-Léonard has a population () of . , 13.6% of the population are resident foreign nationals. Over the last 10 years (2000–2010 ) the population has changed at a rate of 10.7%. It has changed at a rate of 8% due to migration and at a rate of 2.7% due to births and deaths. Most of the population () speaks French (1,741 or 93.0%) as their first language, German is the second most common (53 or 2.8%) and Portuguese is the third (38 or 2.0%). There are 20 people who speak Italian and 1 person who speaks Romansh. , the population was 48.7% male and 51.3% female. The population was made up of 864 Swiss men (41.3% of the population) and 155 (7.4%) non-Swiss men. There were 912 Swiss women (43.6%) and 163 (7.8%) non-Swiss women. Of the population in the municipality, 987 or about 52.7% were born in Saint-Léonard and lived there in 2000. There were 531 or 28.4% who were born in the same canton, while 117 or 6.3% were born somewhere else in Switzerland, and 191 or 10.2% were born outside of Switzerland. , children and teenagers (0–19 years old) make up 24.5% of the population, while adults (20–64 years old) make up 60.5% and seniors (over 64 years old) make up 15%. , there were 718 people who were single and never married in the municipality. There were 973 married individuals, 103 widows or widowers and 78 individuals who are divorced. , there were 712 private households in the municipality, and an average of 2.5 persons per household. There were 169 households that consist of only one person and 54 households with five or more people. , a total of 680 apartments (91.9% of the total) were permanently occupied, while 51 apartments (6.9%) were seasonally occupied and 9 apartments (1.2%) were empty. , the construction rate of new housing units was 2.9 new units per 1000 residents. The local economy is characterized by a diverse mix of agricultural activities, small-scale industry, and a growing service sector. Agriculture remains significant, with vineyards and fruit orchards being prominent features of the surrounding landscape, benefiting from the favorable microclimate provided by the Rhone valley. Industrial activities are concentrated in several small manufacturing units specializing in wood processing and light metalworking, providing stable employment for a portion of the workforce. The service sector has expanded notably in recent years, driven by the municipality's location and proximity to larger urban centers. Tourism represents another vital component of the local commerce, particularly during the warmer months, attracting visitors interested in the natural beauty of the region and its cultural heritage. Infrastructure development has focused heavily on improving local road networks to facilitate both agricultural transport and tourist access. Public services, including healthcare and education, are managed at the municipal level, though specialized services are coordinated with cantonal authorities. Environmental policies place a strong emphasis on sustainable resource management, particularly concerning water usage and agricultural runoff, reflecting the area's sensitivity to ecological balance. Future economic planning aims to further diversify employment opportunities while maintaining the character of the traditional village structure. Energy consumption within the municipality shows a gradual trend toward greater renewable energy integration, with several new residential and commercial buildings incorporating solar power installations. The municipal administration works closely with local stakeholders to ensure that development aligns with conservation goals.

The turbidites of the upper volcanic unit are made of a siliceous rock type and have sandstones and conglomerate tops. Next is the lower volcanic unit, which is mostly pillow lava, breccia, and intrusive rocks. Metasediments of mostly mafic and intermediate tuffaceous composition are cut by dikes (intrusive rock). Below the lower volcanic unit is the dike complex. The dike complex has dacite and rhyolite dikes that cut into the rocks of the lower volcanic unit. At the base is the plutonic suite that are made up of gabbro, diorite, and other plutonic rocks that are intruded by dikes as well as granitic plutons from the Nevadan Orogeny. See also References Additional Reading Assembling California, John McPhee, 1993. Farrar, Straus and Giroux, New York. Tuminas. "Structure and tectonics of the northern Sierra Nevada." Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 87.B3 (1982): 1803–24. Orogenic gold formation and tectonic evolution of the Grass Valley gold district and temporal correlations of gold deposits in California. The progression of these rock units reflects a complex history of magmatism, tectonic activity, and subsequent deformation within the region. The intrusive granitic plutons, associated with the Nevadan Orogeny, represent a major magmatic event linked to the continental collision processes that formed the Sierra Nevada batholith. These plutonic bodies were emplaced during periods of significant crustal thickening and thermal uplift. The presence of dikes cutting through the lower volcanic unit demonstrates subsequent brittle fracturing and magma intrusion into already solidified and emplaced rock sequences. Pillow lavas indicate effusive underwater volcanism, suggesting periods when the tectonic setting involved subduction or island arc activity beneath an oceanic or shallow marine environment. Breccias, in this context, point toward intense fracturing and subsequent cementation, often associated with faulting or explosive volcanic events. The metasediments, derived from tuffaceous material, further document the presence of volcanic ash deposits that were subsequently subjected to regional metamorphism due to burial and tectonic stress. The overall stratigraphic succession, from the basement plutons upward through the lower and upper volcanic units, illustrates a polygenetic sequence encompassing oceanic crustal material, arc magmatism, and later continental involvement. The chemical and mineralogical characteristics of these rocks provide crucial constraints for models attempting to reconstruct the paleo-tectonic environment of the area, particularly the transition from an island arc to a continental margin setting. Further geological mapping and geochemical analysis are necessary to fully delineate the spatial extent and chronological relationships among these diverse lithologies.

Lycoris hyacinthina - Griffinia hyacinthina Lycoris radiata - Ungernia trisphaera Lycoris severzowii - Ungernia severzowii Hybrids Lycoris × chejuensis chejuensis K.H.Tae & S.C.Ko - Korea Cultivation and uses Lycoris are extensively cultivated as ornamental plants in China and Japan, and also in other warm temperate regions of the world. In Japan, they are widely used at the edges of rice paddy fields to provide a strip of bright flowers in the summer, and over 230 cultivars have been selected for garden use. They are locally naturalised in the southeastern United States, where they are often called hurricane flowers, due to their blooming period coinciding with the peak of hurricane season. In China, people often use them as decorations in festivals or celebrations. Legends Since these scarlet flowers usually bloom near cemeteries around the autumnal equinox, they are described in Chinese and Japanese translations of the Lotus Sutra as ominous flowers that grow in Diyu (also known as Hell), or Huángquán (), and guide the dead into the next reincarnation. These cultural associations have led to varying interpretations and superstitions regarding the species. In some East Asian cultures, the fiery coloration of certain spider lilies is believed to carry spiritual significance, marking transitions between life states. The specific blooming time, often coinciding with the late summer or early autumn months, further contributes to this perception of liminality. Beyond funerary symbolism, some traditions incorporate the plant into seasonal rites or medicinal preparations, although scientific validation of these uses varies considerably. The adaptability of many Lycoris species allows them to thrive in diverse soil types, ranging from damp, rich loam to drier, more alkaline substrates, which aids their widespread cultivation across various climates. Propagation is typically achieved through division of the rhizomes or by seed, though the latter can be less reliable for maintaining specific ornamental traits. Modern horticulture has led to the development of numerous hybrids, which exhibit novel combinations of flower colors, sizes, and bloom times, expanding the ornamental appeal of the genus. Research continues into the ecological roles of these plants, particularly their interaction with local insect populations during their brief flowering period.

Lyrita began releasing LPs in October 1959 as Lyrita Recorded Edition for sale by mail order subscription. The founder of the company, Richard Itter (5 April 1928 - 1 March 2014) of Burnham, Buckinghamshire, was a businessman and record collector. Having heard many poor records, he determined to make only good ones. Lyrita concentrated on the work of United Kingdom composers. At first, this consisted of the piano music of Arnold Bax, Gordon Jacob, E.J. Moeran , and Michael Tippett amongst others. The earliest recordings were made in the music room of Itter's home. Itter was responsible for the engineering, production, and editing of the recordings. If he managed to sell 100 copies Itter was able to break even. RCS.2 was the first catalog number, and Gordon Jacob wrote a composition specifically for this album, "Elegy for Piano and Cello", to fill out the program on the disc. In time, the bulk of Lyrita's catalogue became orchestral and symphonic works, including otherwise-neglected composers at that time, including William Alwyn, Malcolm Arnold, Arnold Bax, Havergal Brian, Frank Bridge, Arnold Cooke, Gerald Finzi, John Foulds, George Lloyd, Edmund Rubbra, Humphrey Searle and Cyril Rootham. Many Lyrita LPs became regarded as demonstration discs, suitable for showcasing the sonic qualities of high-end hi-fi equipment. Nearly all of Lyrita's recordings were produced by Decca Records and pressed by either Decca or Nimbus Records. When Decca joined PolyGram in 1980, the relationship with Lyrita ended. The only non-British music to be recorded and issued on Lyrita was Brazilian piano music performed by Elizabeth Powell on RCS.22. Works by Paul Hindemith, Edward MacDowell , and Francis Poulenc were also recorded but not issued. Lyrita issued monaural records in the RCS series, and stereophonic records in the SRCS series beginning at SRCS.31 (which corresponded with monaural RCS.31). The stereo series ran to SRCS.131. Lyrita issues compact discs (CDs) in the SRCD series beginning with SRCD.200 and running through SRCD.332. Lyrita's stereophonic LPs from the SRCS series were also issued in the U.S. by the Musical Heritage Society (1972–1977) and HNH (1978–1979). Lyrita began exporting their records to the U.S. in 1980. The first digital productions were made in June 1982, and LP production was discontinued in 1988. The continued focus on neglected British composers allowed Lyrita to establish a niche market catering to serious classical music enthusiasts and audiophiles alike. The early commitment to high-fidelity sound quality, originating from Itter's meticulous involvement in the technical aspects of the recordings, was a defining characteristic of the label's output. This dedication positioned Lyrita not merely as a record producer but as a preserver of musical heritage, often presenting performances that offered fresh interpretations of established repertoire. Despite the limited initial production runs, the critical reception to the recordings was largely positive, leading to growing recognition within specialist circles. The transition from early monaural pressings to stereo material marked a technological evolution for the label, mirroring the broader advancements in consumer audio technology during the 1960s and 1970s. The ongoing collaboration with Decca provided access to professional studio facilities and distribution networks, which were crucial for the viability of the small, dedicated operation. The subsequent shift to digital formats signaled the label's adaptation to the changing landscape of music consumption, ensuring the continuation of their archival mission into the late twentieth century. Following the cessation of LP manufacturing, the focus remained on maintaining the catalogue through the CD format, thereby extending the lifespans of the recordings initially captured in Itter's home environment.

Vézelay Abbey was also a major starting point for pilgrims on the Way of St. James to Santiago de Compostela. This was crucially important in attracting pilgrims and the wealth they brought to the town. Bernard of Clairvaux preached the Second Crusade at the Council of Vézelay in 1146 with King Louis VII of France. The crowd was so large that a large platform was erected on a hill outside the city. The full text has not survived, but a contemporary account says that "his voice rang out across the meadow like a celestial organ" When Bernard was finished the crowd enlisted en masse and they supposedly ran out of cloth to make crosses. Bernard is said to have flung off his own robe and began tearing it into strips to make more crosses. Others followed his example and he and his helpers were supposedly still producing crosses as night fell. On 2 July 1190, the Frankish and English factions of the Third Crusade met at Vézelay before officially departing for the Holy Land. The human settlement on the hill of Vézelay is very anterior to the Benedictine abbey. Merovingian sarcophagi were found in the basement of the church of St. Peter, and under one of them an older sarcophagus. In 2012, a Carolingian wall was discovered, under the cloister of Vézelay. Girart de Roussillon received by a favor from Louis the Pious and chose in 858 to ensure the perenniality of his possessions by transforming them into two Benedictine communities, respectively male and female: Pothières and Vézelay. He founded a monastery of women at the present site of Saint-Père. It has a villa, surrounded by large estates. The neighborhood in which the houses are located bears the name of Vezeliacus which will become Vizeliac then Vézelay. This was a tenuous start, abruptly interrupted between 871 and 877, when the Normans dislodged the nuns. Girart then asks for their replacement by a community of men. The abbey was then transferred to the hill and Benedictine monks replaced the nuns. The position of the monastery attracted many families to take advantage of the protection of the walls of the new establishment. It was dedicated to the Virgin and the apostles St. Its status is quite peculiar, for it was affiliated with Cluny, which was exempted until 1744: Some authors assert that in 882 the monk Badilon had brought from Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume to Vézelay, relics of Mary Magdalene. On the other hand, Eudes, first abbot, is mentioned in 897. The abbey of Vézelay Elected in 1037, Abbot Geoffroy reformed the abbey and convinced his contemporaries that the abbey possessed the remains of Mary Magdalene: hence pilgrimages, offerings and donations. The veneration of relics, particularly those of Mary Magdalene, proved to be a powerful magnet for religious devotion and material support. The association with this revered figure elevated Vézelay's spiritual prestige considerably within the broader network of medieval Christianity. This influx of pilgrims not only enriched the monastic community but also cemented the abbey's reputation as a site of significant ecclesiastical importance throughout Christendom. The strategic location near major travel routes further amplified this draw, making the abbey a necessary waypoint for those undertaking long religious journeys. The connection to Cluny, a powerful reformed monastic order, provided Vézelay with both administrative influence and access to extensive networks of patronage across Europe. This affiliation ensured that the abbey remained a focal point for religious life and political maneuvering among the nobility and the Church hierarchy. The development of the abbey complex reflected its growing importance, with architectural additions and expansions corresponding to periods of increased prosperity and influence. Furthermore, the abbey served as a center for intellectual life, housing scriptoriums where texts were copied and preserved, contributing to the transmission of knowledge during the early medieval period. The persistent efforts of abbots like Geoffroy to solidify the cult of Mary Magdalene ensured that the economic and spiritual viability of the institution remained strong for centuries.

In July 1919, Kamenev replaced Jukums Vācietis as Commander-in-chief of the Red Army during the Russian Civil War. Kamenev was a member of the Revolutionary Military Council of the USSR from April 1924 to May 1927. He died of a heart attack on 25 August 1936 following the Trial of the Sixteen, incidentally on the same day that Lev Kamenev (no relation) and Grigory Zinoviev were executed. Early life Kamenev was born in Kiev in a noble family, the son of a mechanical engineer at the Kiev plant "Arsenal", a Colonel of artillery. He dreamed of becoming a surgeon as a child, but ultimately chose a military career. He graduated from the Vladimir Kiev Cadet Corps (1898), the elite Aleksandrovsk Military School (1900, finished third in his class) and started military service in his native Kiev. After serving in the 165th Lutsk Infantry Regiment, he entered the Nikolaev Academy of the General Staff and graduated with 1st category honors in 1907, then served in combat roles before being assigned to the General Staff. Prior to World War I, he served as assistant senior adjutant of the staff of the Irkutsk Military District, of the 2nd Cavalry Division, and the Vilna military district. In addition, Kamenev taught tactics and topography at a military school. In the pre-war period, Kamenev participated in numerous maneuvers and field trips, which significantly expanded his horizons and training as a general staff officer and commander. During these trips, Kamenev visited the fortresses of Kovno and Grodno. He studied the unfortunate experience of the participation of the Russian army in the war with Japan. World War I Kamenev went to the front of the First World War in the rank of captain. He served as a senior aide to the operational department of the 1st Army, commanded the 30th Poltava Infantry Regiment. According to the certification in connection with the service at the headquarters of the 1st Army, Kamenev was assessed by the authorities as "in all respects an outstanding General Staff officer and an excellent combat commander", and was considered worthy of promotion to general officer rank. As the regiment's colonel, Kamenev showed himself as a firm commander, who possesses courage, orderliness and composure, loves military affairs, knows and cares about the life of an officer and a soldier. His care of the soldiers, apparently, played a role in the fact that in 1917 he was elected commander of the regiment. Kamenev held the post of Chief of Staff of the XV Army Corps (in this position he met the events of October 1917), Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army. Following the October Revolution, Kamenev transitioned his military experience into revolutionary political activities. His early involvement with Bolshevik factions marked a decisive shift from his purely military trajectory. He participated in the early stages of the Civil War, applying his organizational and command skills within the rapidly forming Red Army structures. His strategic acumen and dedication to the Bolshevik cause led to progressively senior positions within the military apparatus. The tumultuous period of the Civil War tested his leadership capabilities severely, demanding adaptability and ruthlessness in the face of overwhelming adversity. His effectiveness in operational planning and troop management became increasingly recognized by the highest echelons of the Party and the military leadership. Later in his career, his role evolved to incorporate significant political and organizational duties alongside his military responsibilities, reflecting the increasing politicization of the Soviet military establishment. He became involved in the internal political struggles within the Soviet government, a period characterized by intense ideological conflict among the leading Bolshevik figures. His tenure on the Revolutionary Military Council demonstrated his continued influence in shaping the military doctrine and strategic direction of the emerging Soviet state. Despite his military credentials, his political standing and loyalty to the central Party line were paramount to his continued ascent through the ranks. His career trajectory exemplifies the complex interplay between military professionalism and political adherence within the early Soviet regime.

Fifteen years after the Buddha's enlightenment, his foster mother Mahāpajāpatī came to see him to ask him to be ordained as the first Buddhist bhikkhunī. Initially, the Buddha refused this. Five years later, Mahāpajāpatī came to request the Buddha again, this time with a following of other Sākiya women, including the Buddha's former wife Yasodharā (). They had walked , looked dirty, tired and depressed, and Ānanda felt pity for them. Ānanda therefore confirmed with the Buddha whether women could become enlightened as well. Although the Buddha conceded this, he did not allow the Sākiya women to be ordained yet. Ānanda then discussed with the Buddha how Mahāpajāpatī took care of him during his childhood, after the death of his real mother. Ānanda also mentioned that previous Buddhas had also ordained bhikkhunīs. In the end, the Buddha allowed the Sākiya women to be ordained, being the start of the bhikkhunī order. Ānanda had Mahāpajāpati ordained by her acceptance of a set of rules, set by the Buddha. These came to be known as the garudhamma, and they describe the subordinate relation of the bhikkhunī community to that of the bhikkhus or monks. Scholar of Asian religions Reiko Ohnuma argues that the debt the Buddha had toward his foster-mother Mahāpajāpati may have been the main reason for his concessions with regard to the establishment of a bhikkhunī order. Many scholars interpret this account to mean that the Buddha was reluctant in allowing women to be ordained, and that Ānanda successfully persuaded the Buddha to change his mind. For example, Indologist and translator I.B. Horner wrote that "this is the only instance of his being over-persuaded in argument". However, some scholars interpret the Buddha's initial refusal rather as a test of resolve, following a widespread pattern in the Pāli Canon and in monastic procedure of repeating a request three times before final acceptance. Some also argue that the Buddha was believed by Buddhists to be omniscient, and therefore is unlikely to have been depicted as changing his mind. Other scholars argue that other passages in the texts indicate the Buddha intended all along to establish a bhikkhunī order. Regardless, during the acceptance of women into the monastic order, the Buddha told Ānanda that the Buddha's Dispensation would last shorter because of this. At the time, the Buddhist monastic order consisted of wandering celibate males, without many monastic institutions. Allowing women to join the Buddhist celibate life might have led to dissension, as well as temptation between the sexes. The garudhamma, however, were meant to fix these problems, and prevent the dispensation from being curtailed. There are some chronological discrepancies in the traditional account of the setting up of the bhikkhunī order. The exact timeline of the initial ordination differs across various historical and textual traditions, leading to scholarly debate regarding its precise placement within the early Buddhist narrative. Some accounts place the establishment of the bhikkhunī order much later, after a period of significant development and standardization of the monastic rules for the male order. The introduction of the bhikkhunīs into the established framework of the Sangha necessarily prompted modifications and elaborations within the Vinaya Pitaka, the monastic code of conduct. These additions were crucial for maintaining the doctrinal and practical coherence of the religious community as it expanded its scope. The relationship between the newly constituted bhikkhunī community and the existing bhikkhus remains a subject of nuanced interpretation among Buddhist exegetes, with different schools emphasizing varying degrees of autonomy and equality within the monastic structure. The very nature of the garudhamma reflects a period of institutional negotiation and careful structuring of the religious life. This negotiation reflects the complex societal context in which early Buddhism was taking root, balancing radical spiritual ideals with the practical realities of communal organization and gender roles of the era.

History Bewdley station originally opened in 1862 as one of the main intermediate stations on the line between Hartlebury and Shrewsbury. It was operated by the West Midland Railway, before that company was absorbed into the Great Western Railway (GWR). The Tenbury & Bewdley Railway opened in 1864, with its route through the Wyre Forest branching off the SVR north of Bewdley station, before crossing the River Severn over the now partially-dismantled Dowles Bridge. Thus, Bewdley became a junction station. The GWR opened a "loop-line" to Kidderminster in 1878, which meant that Bewdley had a direct link with the town and became a double junction. As a legacy of its former junction status, Bewdley station is unique on the SVR in that it has two signal boxes, Bewdley North and Bewdley South. Bewdley station was at its busiest at weekends and local holiday periods, but traffic declined with the increasing use of cars in the 1950s. As a consequence, rationalisation resulted in the end of through passenger traffic — firstly on the Wyre Forest line in 1962, followed by the Severn Valley line in 1963. Although thought by some to have been a result of the Beeching Axe, those closures pre-dated Beeching's report. Until January 1970, British Rail continued to serve the last remaining stations of Stourport-on-Severn, Burlish Halt, Bewdley, Foley Park Halt and Kidderminster. Stationmasters Thomas Appleton 1862 – 1897 George Smith 1898 – 1909 (afterward station master at Chipping Norton) Frederick Hallett 1909 – 1914 Alfred W. Cooke 1923 – 1937 (formerly station master at Cleobury Mortimer) E.T. Rose 1939 – 1942 (afterward station master at Broadway) William H. Needle until 1956 (afterward station master at Totnes) H.E. Ray 1956 – 1960 (afterward station master at Bridgnorth) Preservation Bewdley was disused for only four years before preservationists from the new SVR Company bought the land, track and buildings in 1974, enabling the SVR to extend from Bridgnorth–Hampton Loade to Highley and eventually Bewdley that same year. From 1980 onwards, occasional bank holiday services were operated to Bewdley, originally from Kidderminster and later from Birmingham New Street. The SVR's own services to Kidderminster could not commence until sugar beet traffic to Foley Park ceased in 1982, and its own station, Kidderminster Town, was opened, which occurred two years later. During and after preservation: The station clock on platforms 2 and 3 was brought from Stourbridge Junction railway station. The longer valancing pieces on the east side of the island platform canopy came from Birmingham Snow Hill station. The preserved station has undergone several restoration projects over the decades, focusing on the meticulous reinstatement of historical features to reflect its operational appearance during its heyday. Many of the original architectural elements, which suffered from years of neglect after passenger services ceased, required specialist conservation work. The station buildings themselves have been carefully maintained, ensuring they remain structurally sound while preserving their Victorian character. This dedication to authenticity has made Bewdley a significant site for railway enthusiasts and historians alike. The local community has also played a vital role in supporting the preservation efforts, often volunteering time and resources for upkeep and public events held at the location. Regular operational events are now a key feature of the site, allowing the public to experience the ambiance of a working heritage railway. These activities serve not only to raise funds for ongoing maintenance but also to educate visitors about the rich industrial and social history associated with the railway network in the region. The presence of the preserved infrastructure allows for detailed study of railway engineering and operational procedures from the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

In February 2009, Christophe, invited Kelli Ali to Switzerland, to collaborate with him on an album inspired by the short stories of the Gothic horror writer, Mary Shelley, and following several sessions between London and Switzerland, this haunting collection was eventually completed, with Kelli writing and performing the lyrics and vocal arrangements and Christophe writing and performing the piano music. "A Paradise Inhabited by Devils" was released in November 2010. Two titles of this album are used in the Japanese movie “Keibetsu”. 2012 marks the release of his latest album, “Antipodes”. Produced without any promotion in order to be in harmony with the theme of the album which means completely against current market trend today. "Antipodes" is a reflection on the current world where superficial excess and money take everything in its path. "Nos Années Troubles" is realised in October 2014. April 2017 - Three years after the album "Nos Années Troubles" (Our Troubled Years) and after 15 million plus streams on Spotify for the track "I Miss You"- Ozymandias returns with his new album "Dans Mon Monde" (In My World). Composed with influences from both Asia and Europe, the Swiss pianist's tenth solo album aims to draw you into the world that he experiences! His thirteenth album, started in February 2018 and released in December 2020 with the title 101 VISAGES (101 FACES), invites you on an inner journey as well as a rare moment of intimacy with the composer. His musical evolution demonstrates a consistent exploration of complex emotional and philosophical landscapes, moving from gothic influences to broader reflections on contemporary society and ultimately to deeply personal introspection. The integration of diverse musical traditions, evident in the Asia-European synthesis of Dans Mon Monde, suggests an increasing openness to global musical dialogues while maintaining a distinctly personal artistic voice. The numbering of his albums, such as 101 VISAGES, hints at a thematic preoccupation with multiplicity, individuality, and the myriad facets of human experience. The consistent engagement with themes of isolation, introspection, and the darker undercurrents of modern life provides a cohesive thread running through his varied output. His early collaborations, such as the work with Kelli Ali, established an early foundation in narrative-driven, atmospheric composition, a sensibility that persists even in his later, more abstract pieces. The choice of production methods, sometimes eschewing mainstream promotion, underscores an artistic commitment to thematic integrity over commercial viability. This approach positions his body of work as an endeavor rooted in artistic statement rather than market appeasement. Furthermore, the archival nature of some releases, such as the various Ramses CD volumes, documents a prolonged period of dedicated, perhaps highly localized, creative output over several decades. The inclusion of soundtracks in his discography further illustrates the versatility of his compositional style, applying his intricate harmonic language to narrative media as well as standalone albums.

These subspecies exhibit a complex pattern of geographical distribution and morphological variation, leading to ongoing taxonomic debate among ornithologists. The distinctions between these populations often rely on subtle plumage differences, size variation, and the precise geographic boundaries of their respective breeding and non-breeding grounds. Some researchers propose that the observed variations may represent clinal variation across the coastal range rather than truly separate biological species or subspecies. Further genetic analysis is frequently suggested as a necessary tool to clarify the evolutionary relationships among these closely related populations. The study of migratory patterns, particularly the exact stopover points and routes taken between breeding and wintering areas, provides additional ecological data relevant to understanding these subspecies boundaries. Differences in habitat preference between the various groups, though sometimes overlapping, may also contribute to reproductive isolation or selection pressures favoring local adaptations. The coastal environment itself presents a heterogeneous backdrop, encompassing temperate rainforests, drier scrublands, and estuarine habitats, all of which could influence the manifestation of plumage characteristics. The utilization of historical records alongside modern banding data helps paint a more complete picture of the past and present distribution of these sparrow populations.

The concert was a co-benefit for Testament vocalist Chuck Billy, who was diagnosed with germ cell seminoma (a rare form of cancer); and Chuck Schuldiner, leader of the death metal band Death, who was also battling cancer. The Master of Ceremonies for the evening was S.O.D. vocalist Billy Milano. The concert was organized by Walter Morgan. The show was announced in May 2001, and all 2300 tickets quickly sold out. The concert focused primarily on Bay Area thrash metal, a popular and influential metal scene in the 1980s and early 1990s (of which Testament played a big part), and featured the reunions of then-defunct Bay Area bands Heathen, Death Angel, Vio-lence (minus Robb Flynn, who declined to participate), Forbidden Evil, Sadus, Legacy (an early version of Testament), and then partially defunct Exodus (with Paul Baloff). As a result of the show, Exodus, Heathen and Death Angel all officially reunited and released new albums. Forbidden would reunite again in 2007 and released a new album three years later. Also appearing at the concert were Anthrax and S.O.D., who are all friends of Chuck Billy's. Lȧȧz Rockit were scheduled to appear, but had to pull out at the last minute, due to singer Michael Coons being admitted to a rehabilitation center, and were replaced by Flotsam and Jetsam. M.O.D. were also scheduled to appear, but with the show running long, Billy Milano announced that M.O.D. would play a show in Oakland the next week, and that tickets to the Thrash of the Titans would be honored. Beginning with Heathen at 3 pm, the show featured ten bands, with Legacy taking the stage just after 2am. Legacy, a precursor to Testament, featured Steve "Zetro" Souza on vocals, John Tempesta on drums, and Alex Skolnick on lead guitar. Skolnick's appearance marked his first playing thrash metal since quitting Testament in 1993, and eventually led to his rejoining the band. Also appearing with Legacy were Paul Bostaph, the original drummer of Forbidden Evil (who was then with Slayer) and Steve DiGiorgio, bassist for Sadus and formerly of Death, Autopsy and Iced Earth. Chuck Billy himself joined Legacy for the last song of the night, "Into the Pit". The show featured many other guest appearances, including Steve Souza joining Exodus and Paul Baloff for a duet on "Brain Dead". Thrash of the Titans marked one of the last live appearances of Exodus frontman Paul Baloff, who died of a stroke just six months later, on February 2, 2002. Death's Chuck Schuldiner also died of brain cancer four months after the benefit, on December 13, 2001. Performers In order of appearance: Heathen Flotsam and Jetsam Sadus Forbidden Evil Death Angel Exodus (with Paul Baloff) S.O.D. The confluence of these musical figures and the shared struggle against illness lent a profound emotional weight to the event, transforming it from a mere music festival into a significant cultural moment for the metal community. The atmosphere remained charged throughout the long evening, reflecting both the raw energy of the thrash genre and the underlying solemnity of the occasion. The Bay Area scene, while fragmented by years of internal strife and individual career paths, was temporarily unified by the shared desire to support the two musicians facing mortality. The guest appearances served to bridge generations of the genre, connecting the early, seminal sounds of the 1980s with the contemporary heavy metal landscape. The commitment shown by the bands to participate, despite the demanding schedule and personal circumstances, underscored the enduring loyalty within the metal subculture. This benefit concert stands as a powerful testament to the community's capacity for collective action in the face of adversity. The successful culmination of Thrash of the Titans solidified the legacy of many of the participating acts, providing memorable final performances for some members who would not endure to see subsequent reunions or releases.
